MARTIN LIGHTFOOT'S SONG. Come hearken, hearken, gentles all, Come hearken unto me, And I'll sing you a song of a Wood-Lyon Came swimming out over the sea. He ranged west, he ranged east, And far and wide ranged he; Be took his bite out of every beast Lives under the greenwood tree. Then by there came a silly old wolf, "And I'll serve you, quoth hc ; Quoth the Lyon," My paw is heavy enough, So what wilt thou do for me?" Then by there came a cunning old fox, And I'll serve you," qnoth he; Qaoth the Lyon," My wits are sharp enough, So what wilt thou do for me?" Then by there came a white, white dove, Flew off Our Lady's knee; Sang, " It's I will be your true, truelove, If you'll be true to me." "And what will von do, you bonny white dove? And what will you do for me?" " Oh, it's I'll bring you to Our Lady's love, In the ways of chivalrie." Be followed the dove that Wood-Lyon By mere and wood and wold, Till he is come to a perfect night, Like the Paladin of old. Be ranged east, he ranged west, And far and wide ranged he— And ever the dove w n nios honour and fame In the ways of chivalrie. Then by there came a foul old sow, Came rookling under the tree; And "It's I will be true love to you, If you'll be true to me." "And what wilt thou do, thou foul old sow? And what wilt thou do for me?" "Oh, there hangs in my snout a jewel of gold, And that will I give to thee" He took to the sow that Wood-Lyon; To the rookling sow took he; And the dove ffew no to Our Lady's bosom; And never again throve he. The greatest of all faults is to be conscious of none. lEftimtlity i 3 the roost excellent natural cure for anger in the world. Among the most blessed of all the contrivances of nature is that which prevents a man from being disturbed by his own snoring. Mankind generally seem willing to admit that the world revolves on its axis. The great mistake they make is, they think they are the axis. Over the piano in an hotel parlour dangles a placard in- scribed as follows—" Inexperienced performers are requested to deny themselves the use of this instrument." A gentleman was speaking of the kindness of his friends in visiting him. One old aunt, in particular, visited him twice a ye r, and sttved six months each time." In a recent lecture, Mr. Ruskin said—" If you want to show your country friends how the sun looks in a London fog, throw a bad half-crown into a basin of dirty water." The difttrence between war and peace has been well de- fined by one of the ancients:—" In time of peace the sons bury their fathers; in time of war the fathers bury their Bens." _ _ .

An old bachelor was recently heard saying to a young lady—" There is more jewelry worn now-a-days than when I was young, hut there is one piece I often admired which I don't often see now." What was that?" asked miss. "A thimble," was the reply. LITERARY Sera.—The young mast learn to speak by imitation of the older who already do it, or have done it. The ultimate rule is—learn so fax as possible to be intelli- gible and transparent—no notice taken of your style, but solely of what you express by it. This is your clear rule, and if yon have anything which is not quite trivial to express to your contemporaries, you will find such rule a great deal more difficult to follow than many people think. —Edward Irving, by Thomas Carlyle. TBB VALI7B OF OBSERVED FAcTs.—Firet and foremost I would advise you to get a knowledge of facts from actual observation. Facts looked at direct are vital; when they pees into words half the sap is taken out of them. You wish, for example, to get a knowledge of magnetism ; well, provide yourself with a good book on the subject if you can, but do not be content with what the book tells you; do not be satisfied with its descriptive woodcuts; see the opera. thus of the force yourself. Half of our book writers describe experiments which they never made, and their descriptions often lack both force and truth; but, no matter how clever or conscientious they may be, their written words cannot supply the place of actual observa- tion.—Professor Tyndall. DEFINITION OF HARDNESS or CHARACTER —Hardness is a want of minute attention to the feelings of others. It does not proceed from malignity, or a carelessness of in- flicting pain, but from a want of delicate perception of those little things by winch pleasure is conferred, or pain excited. A hard person thinks he has done enough if he does not speak ill of your relations, your children or your country; and then with the greatest good humour and volubility, and with a total inattention to your individual state and position, gallops over a thousand fine feelings, and leaves in every step the mark of hoofs upon your heart. Analyse the conversation of a well-bred man who is clear of the besetting sin of hardness; it is a perpetual homage of polite good nature. He remembara that you are connected wit.h the church, and he avoids (whatever his opinions may be) the most distant reflections on the establishment. Be 'stows that you are admired, and he admires you as far as is compatible with good breeding. He sees that, though y sung, you are at the head of a great establishment, and he infuses into his manner and conversation that respect which is so pleasing to all who exercise authority. He leaves you its perfect good humour with yourself, because you perceive how much and how successfully you have been studied.— Life of Sidney Smith. A DANGERons LITTLE FOE.—In situations which afford the kind of shelter in which the weasel delights, such as old walls, hedges with banks, or large heaps of stones or brickbats, the little animal will form colonies, increasing and multiplying until the community becomes a formidable one to meddle with. For no sooner does the unwary stranger strike at one individual with his stick, than the whole clan joins in repelling the attack, and by carrying the war into the enemy's camp, compels a "strategic move- ment" of retreat. As the weasels fly by instinct at the neck and throat, and their claws enable them with ease to run up the legs and body of a man, it is easy to under- stand that a simultaneous attack by some dozens of these little blood-suckers is an affair of no slight danger. The only security is in flight; and it is well if by buttoning up his coat collar, and using his hands to throw off his tor- mentors as well as he can, the fugitive escapes with no greater harm than a few bites and scratches.—That the weasel, though commonly pursuing its prey alone, will also hunt in packs, is a well-authenticated fact. The Rev. J. G. Wood mentions the case of a gentleman who seeing at a distance a number of small objects which he at first took to be partridges, crossing a field, fired and killed no less than six weasels which had come into the line of his gun. When engaged in hunting, the weasels will cry to each other after the manner of beagles, and will apparently devote a whole day to the chase. Two miles from the room in which lam writing, on a farm at Bromsgrove Lickey, belonging to Lord Windsor, a labourer saw one morning a pack numbering, as be supposed, about a dozen weasels, upon a hunting excur- sion. His attention was first attracted by the small shrill cries of the little beasts, WI they passed the spot where he was at work. The man was tempted to strike at them, but on second thoughts preferred discretion toyalour. In the afternoon be again saw the pack returning from their day's coursing.—The English Illustrated Magazine, July. AN ESTIMATE OF Joule BRIGHT.—He Is not known, and he never will be known, as a great administrator' as a great ' legislator, Or as a great master of Parliamentary detail. He cannot even be considered a debater of the first order. He LS a man, however, just as indispensable to the legislation which has been accomplished during his career as the Idinister who conducts a bill through Parliament. As an Illesrator he has acquired an equal renown in the House of -Commone and on popular platforms. Such are the power And fervour of his eloquence that it has always constituted d is force with which responsible statesmen have been compel- ., led to reckon. Disraeli once said of Cobden that "he was the greatest politician that the upper middle class of Rug- eland had produced, and that he was not only an ornament eta the House of Commons, but an honour to his country." It may be asserted of Mr. Bright that he has surpassed all e'Ais contemporaries in the art of giving simple and weighty ,e4wspression to the views and aspirations of the English mul- lieltitude. He has been called a demagogue. As a matter of e-fact no man was ever less of a demagogue. Had he been I,.aespable of pandering to the popular sentiment of the hour be Would not have resisted the Ten Hours Bill, nor would he have hie seat for Manchester twenty-seven years ago by denouncing the foreign policy of Lord Palmerston in China and in Russia. It would be unjust to say of him that he was ever the mere mouthpiece of public feeling. He has acted as the champion of the popularvincaditics: just so far as he Could Identify that cause with, ad vindicate reference to, what have seemed to him to be the eternal laws of jus- tice and right. There were Radicals before Mr. John Bright. There are, and will continue to be, Radicals after him. But as he had little in common with many of those who were spoken of as his allies at the beginning of his public life, so he has slight sympathy with the most power. fat and representative Radicals whom he sees around him as the shadows of his life begin to lengthen.—T. div.p: Nature never stands still, nor souls either; they ever go

up or go down. A man never gets thoroughly disgusted with love's young dream until he has given a girl a ring, and three days after- wards discovers that she has been to a jeweller to ascertain t its arheae lilvtge value. The . T have seen of the world teaches me to look 1 upon the errors of others in sorrow, not in anger. When I I take the history of one heart that has sinned and suffered, 1 and represent to myself the struggles and temptations it has I passed through—the brief pulsations of joy, the feverish in- quietude of hope and fear, the pressure of want, the deser- tion of friends—l would fain leave the erring soul of my fellow man with Him from whose hand it came.—Long•

fellow. &TIMELY HIT.—On a train the other day was a newly- married couple, the bride appearing to be about twenty-five years old, and the groom being a dapper little chap a year or two younger. A lady took a seat, and after a few minutes she heard the pair criticising her bonnet and cloak and general style. Without showing the least resentment in her countenance' she turned round in her seat and said, "Madam, will you have your son close the window behind you ?" The "son" closed his month instead, and the I• madam" didn't giggle again for fifteen miles. MIDDLE-CLASS FOLLIES.—But what strange folly is this which meets me in every quarter; people wanting posts in the army, the navy, the public offices, and saying that if they cannot find each posts' they must starve! How do all the rest of mankind live? If I had not happened to be engaged in politics, and if my father had not been con- nected, by very extraordinary circumstances, with public men, we should never have dreamed of having places. Why cannot P— be apprenticed to some hatter or tailor? He may do well in such a business : he will do detestably ill as a clerk in my office. He may come to make good coats : he will never, lam sure, write good despatches. There is nothing truer than Poor Richard's saw : "We are taxed twice as heavily by our pride as by the State." The curse of England is the obstinate determination of the middle classes to make their sons what they ell! gentlemen. So we are overrun by clergymen without livings, lawyers without briefs, physicians without patients, authors without readers, clerks soliciting employment, who might have thriven, and been above the world, as bakers, watchmakers, or inn- keepers. The next time my father speaks to me about P—, I will offer to subscribe twenty guineas towards making a pastry cook of him. He had a sweet tooth when he was a child.—Lord Macaulay's Letters. A VISIT TO CARDINAL NEWMAN.-9. non-Catholic American editor frpm lowa describes a visit which he paid to Cardinal Newman during a recent tour in Europe. He writes :—" You of course know that I am not a Catholic, but you also know, I be'ieve, that I feel a deep respect and reverence for the grand old Church which has in all ages of the Christian era done so much for civilisation and progress —saying nothing of its higher and more authoritative claims upon mankind. For many years—l can scarcely even guess how many—l have felt not only a very deep interest, but the warmest personal regard, for that great Prince of the Church, the venerable Cardinal Newman. The writer than briefly describes his journey to Birmingham, which he reached on a very wet evening. He at once made his way to E lgbaston, and sought an interview with one of the Fathers of the Oratory:—" In the midst of this he came in. Taking off his birretta and retaining the closely-fitting skullcap, he quickly advanced and gave me so warm and cordial a greeting that my embarrassment fled in an instant. His manner was kind, so pleasing and easy in every respect, that I seemed rather to have met an old and dear friend than an entire stranger. Motioning me to a seat, he sat down and quickly entered into a conversation which lasted fully a half-hour before I saw an opportunity to leave. He made many inquiries about matters and things in America. speaking in terms of great satisfaction Of the growth of the Catholic Church." The Cardinal's visitor, going on to de- scribe his leaver-taking. puts before his readers a picture which those who have visited the great Oratorian after nightfall will recognise :—" We rose and paned out into the long hall. He stood within the hall looking out to see me safely in the carriage, the light from burners not in sight falling all around him like the aureole of a saint. As the white.haired old man stood there in his long black robe, crowned with his red biretta, erect and straight as an arrow, despite his many years, I thought I had never seen so grand and noble a figure. I could almost imagine that the light emanated from his person, as we see the halos surrounding the representations which art has given us of the holy men of old. The reception he gave me was BO kind and cordial, his manner was so gracious, and his smile so sweet—he so grandly realised all the high ideas I had formed concerning him—that this, indeed, was one of the 'red-letter days' of my life. I had been in the principal cities of England and the Continent, but this was the crowning event of my long journey." AN ENGLISH BALLAD.—Perhaps one of the most striking and forcible of all English ballads, despite its somewhat halting metre and unpolished versification, is "The Siege of Newark," which is to be found in "The Ladye Shakerley," a Cheshire Story of the Great Rebellion. Whether it is really a production of the seventeenth century is uncertain; but it is so vivid, so powerful, and so pathetic, that to omit it in a notice on English ballads would be unpardonable. The opening lines give a picture of the beleaguered city, compassed by "three armies in the field," and the advice of the rebels to the besieged to surrender : " And we'll grant you easy terms, though you're fighting for the king"— and how " The herald answered proudly. In the name of all the rest. We know wha', the mercies of the wicked are at best; If you storm the town, we'll blow it up, but we never will give in; • And our gates will keep you long enough, false traitors to your king! "We've guns enough; we've men enough; our hearts are stout and true; We will burn the city down, but we'll never yield to you; We can do, and we can dare, but we cannot live to fling Our brave old gates wide open to you, traitors to your king! " So tell your rebel leaders we are loyal to the last. And when our bread is eaten, we then must keep our fast; We can fight, and we oan die, but old Newark's walls shall ring With no battle-cry but ours—for God and for the king I" Then, we are told "The Roundheads snuffled Psalms, and swore beneath their breath—"

A deliciously wicked little touch— " When the rebel leaders heard this challenge to the death; And they vowed they'd sack the town, for it was a shameful thing To make the godly wait so long by this fighting for the king." The besieged keep their word right gallantly, and for weeks and months hold out— "Till famine, with her hungry eyes, went up and down the town—' And men never left their posts upon the wall— They could not fall within The faces of the children that were starving for the king." The women, pale and brave, bring the food to the soldiers, and strive to smile as they see them eat it—" crumbs and all " says the ballad, with grim realism— For they knew that but for them, and the little ones within. They would die in one brave sally, for God and for the king." The sight of those pale steadfast faces—the sound of the children's wail for bread—is infinitely more unendurable to the men than their own suffering; and at last One gallant fellow said.. We can do and we can dare Aught but watching tender women, so patient, take their share •

I will advertise Prince Rupert. and our homes once more shall ring With merry Children shouting for God and for the king.'" So disguised as a Roundhead, with the flowing locks cut short, he is ready to take his life in his hand and go; but there is one farewell to utter, one last look to take, ere he departs on his perilous venture. "Then the maiden he bad wooed and won stept In amid the ring. And before them all she blessed him, for God and for the king. " He looked into her deep-set eyes, he gave her one long kiss; Then he turned unto his comrades—' I pray you, grant me , this ; If the foe—' he could not speak It. but he touched his pistol

spring, And they swore to do his bidding. by God and by the king." He reaches Prince Rupert's forces; he tells of the bitter need; and the warrior prince dashes to the rescue— . '4 So cheerily at midnight blew Prince Rupert's bugle horn, And old Newark rote before them, as rose the early morn' Then he looked upon his troopers, and his troopers looked on him, And he knew to death they'd follow, for God and for the king. "They have gained the Beacon Hill, and the town before them lay. The rebel armies round the walls gathered in close array; The grand old castle still from her battlements did fling The Royal Standard proudly, for God and for the king. "And the river by the castle still murmuring did run, For ever ever murmuring and glittering in the rim. Unheeding of the turmoil and the strife and tears within, Of those who still fought bravely, but were starving for the king. "They are seen upon the hill-top, all dark against the sky, They are dashing down the hill-side, to death or victory, They have burst upon the rebels, and Newark heard the hymn (It never sounder sweeter). 'For God and for the king " Then comes the struggle— " They are round him, all those Roundheads, they surround his little band, They are fighting against hundreds, they are fighting hand to hand; And ever in the thlokest fight, where shot Ilke hall poured in, Rose loud and high that dauntless cry, • For God and for the king V " The foes are forced to retreat; the gates are opened; the victorious Prince enters the city; and Newark is saved! "As he entered the old gates, the cry of triumph rose, To bless and welcome him who had saved them from their foes; The women kiss his charger, and the little children sing, Prince Rupert's brought us bread to eat from God and from the kink But, amid all the burst of maddening joy, there is one heart that is beating fast and thickly with a fear that is not to be quelled; one face that has worn a look of heart-break ever since it watched the entering ranks, and found not what it sought. "And that brave young cavalier, ready to do and dare? She will find him near the bridge—she has gone to seek him there, Close beside old Newark's walls; but he never heard them ring— With merry children shouting 'For God and for the king l'" —Aunt Judy's Magazine. ego ea. iltt etkiodOn.l{, LiverElF Ar t in es 3 lo T.LlVERComplaints, tR.:IB,SIL. - Mr. Leopold de Rothschild has remitted to the tenants on his Buckinghamshire estate 15 per cent, of the rents due on Lady-Day last; and the tenants on the estate of Kinfaans, Perthshire, have been allowed by Mr. E. A. Stuart Gray abatements of from 10 to 20 per cent. \ Tills ARTISTIC MANIPULATION OF BUTTER.—Lady Bee- tive, who offers prizes for the beat butter at Kendal (with- out sal t),has acceded to a wish of the farmers' wives attending 1 that market, and is giving special prizes for the artistic manipulation of our chief dairy prodact. tier ladyship suggests that the design should not be too elaborate, but , should be directed rather to the improvement in the art of , making up batter, and to the production of such specimens as would be best suited for the breakfast table. DAMAGE BY licrwriwo.—Sir Henry Selwyn-Ibbetson has announced that the Essex Hunt, of which he is Master, will , regularly compensate farmers for damage done to their crops and fences by huntsmen, if claims be sent in before June in each year. This coarse he recommends to other hante, and they will do well to adopt his advice. At pre- sent a farmer who sends in a claim is regarded as rather mean; yet, in these bad times, few farmers can afford to suffer the damage undoubtedly caused by hunting. ENSILAGE EXPERIMENTS.—A record of experiments in feeding cattle with silage at Portinore is very satisfactory as far as it goes. The increase of live weight in cattle fed on silage and cake was obtained at the cost of rather less than rik per lb., reckoning the silage at £1 per ton; while that in cattle fed on turnips, valued at 12s. 021. per ton, and cake, cost a llttle over Bicl. per lb. Sheep fed on a daily ration of 21b. of silage with a run of grass, did as well as another portion of the same flock which had the run of a turnip field by day and a grass park at night, similar to that on which the sheep fed on silage were kept. The weekly ration of silage was valued at Id., against sd. or 6d. for the turnips. DR. PLOWRIGHT ON RUST IN WHEATS.—Dr. Plowright, of King's Lynn, in reply to an inquiry as to whether he has investigated the nature of the rust that is so prevalent 011 the wheats this season, writes to us as follows :—" I have seen nothing on the wheats yet bat Uredo rubigo-vera, the early spring rust, which has been exceedingly abundant. It appeared here as early as the end of March, and lam gone on increasing. It won't do the wheats any appreciable harm. The Ured,o (linearis) puccinia graminis I have not yet seen this year. I don't expect it will trouble us much if this dry weather holds. By-the-by, the dry weather has had but little, if any, retarding influence upon the spread of U.rubioo- Vera. I have had some communication from Australia con- cerning the mildew there, which I intend sending a note of to you when I can find time." NEW METHOD OF SALTING BUTTER.—MI. A. S. Kings- ley, of Indianopolie, has been putting the salt in the churn in the shape of strong brine, instead of working it into the butter afterward. He gives the following as his method of batter-making :—" The cream was about three days from the cow when it WAS put into a mass, and so nearly sweet that it was barely thickened, and tent in a room at 55 deg. and churned at .62 deg., the churning requiring about an hoar; and when the batter had all come, but not gathered, two gallons of skim milk, at a temperature of about 50, was thrown into the churn, when only a few minutes were re- quired to gather it. There were sixteen gallons of cream at the start, and there was about that amount of water at a temperature of 52 deg.. thrown into the churn after the but- termilk was drawn off. The churn is a revolving box. The churn was then turned rapidly for a moment, and then the water drawn off and about two gallons of strong brine was put on with the salt and the churn turned slowly for about five minutes, when the brine was drawn off and the butter packed in the pail, and you get it in that condition." The American Dairyman has been trying a sample-of this bat- ter and pronounces it delicious - salt enough for the market, but without any, streaks or =Wings, and with the butter- milk thoroughly worked oat. • TSB FIRST SCOIVI CLAIM UNDER THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT.—The first °Latin made in the Inverness dis- trict, under the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act has just been enrolled for settlement in the Inverness Sheriff Court. The claim is made by Mr. Alexander Fraser, Solid- tor, Inverness, late tenaut of the farm and lands of Faillie, in the vicinity of Inverness, against the proprietor, Mr. H. S. C. Smithson, of Lentran, and asks compensation to the extent of £897 19s. 6d. Mr. Fraser says that, having within the ten years preceding the commencement of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act, 1883, without being tinder any obligation of contract or otherwise to do so, made improvements in the sense of the Act on the farm and lands of Faillie, occupied by him, he is under the Act entitled to receive from the landlord at his outgoing at Whit-Sunday, 1884, such compensation for said improvements as fairly represents the value of them to an ingoing tenant, or to the landlord if he be the successor in the occupancy of the farm. His claim is made up of the following sums :—Unexhausted value of lime applied in 1882 to farm, £55 7s. 61 ; cost of draining done in 1883, £l2 125.; unexhausted value of hay crop consumed on farm during the ten years, £250; unex- haasted value of feeding stuffs, £100; unexhausted value of artificial manures, £180; total, £897 19s. 6d. Mr. Smithson, proprietor' states that he has already paid the first two claims, and holds the receipts, and points out the unreasonable nature of the other claims. He calculates the total amount in name of compensation at £25 23. Od. ' In terms of the Act, Mr. Smithson has asked the sheriff to appoint an oversman, and has named Mr. Mollison, factor, Dochgarroch, while the pursuer has named Mr. John Gor• don, farmer, Baleatichy, Fearn, Ross-shire.—Land Agents' i Record. THE FLAMM OF CATERPILLARS IN SOUTH WALES.—A 0 Cardiff correspondent writes that the great swarms of cater. , pillars which have suddenly appeared on the mountains in ' South Wales 'have produced an extraordinary sensation in that part of the country. The insects measure about an Inch and a half in length, and are of a brown colour, with black stripes. The head, which is furnished With a pair of mandibles, is of a dark yellow colour. The insects are re- markably lively, and eat all the green herbage in the vicinity. - Many of the farmers have fired the mountains_ with the view of destroying the insects hut the visitation . is too widespread to allow of this expedient succeeding. The whole of the mountains lying between the greater Rhondda and Maesteg, a distance of twelve miles, are liter- ally swarming with the insects, as well as the ranges of I mountains and valleys intervening. Millions of the insects , are found buried in the peat holes, getters, and mountain brooks in some of the localities. The crows feed on them, and it is feared that this will result in the pest being car- ried to the fertile valleys, and there attack the young grain. ' Anxiety is felt lest the insectivorous pests should get into the wool of the sheep, and the flocks are being driven from the mountains to other districts.—aliss Eleanor Ormerod writes :—" From specimens sent to me I find that they are I grass-feeding caterpillars of a moth, about the size of the • common turnip moth. Whether they are all of one kind is not certain, but probably the greater part are the cater- pillars of the ' antler moth,' so called from the markings on ' its fore wings, a kind remarkable for appearing from time ' to time in vast numbers in some one special district, which ' js the case at present. They will do boundless harm to grass, and, probably, if in their line of march, to growiog . corn; but as for being 'insectivorous' or hurting sheep, even if they got stack fast in the wool, there is certainly no , foundation in any scientific observations that have been published on their habits to suppose they will behave in any such way. Probably they will soon go into the chrysalis ; state now, and towards August be represented by a great : appearance of reddish-brown moths, with gray hinder wings. 1 lam not aware they often appear in great numbers a second year in the same locality." 1 Scrinunif DAIRY Scatoor..—Lord Vernon having consented to the use of his dairy as a school for the technical instruc- tion of young men and women (especially the sons and i daughters of small farmers) in the details of butter-making and cheesemaking, the following rules for the organisation and working of the school have been drawn up by Mr. H. M. Jenkins, secretary to the Royal Agricultural Society, and have received his lordship's approval :—(1) Applies- ' tins from those who wish to be received as pupils must be addressed to Mr. Algernon Fawkes, Estate Office, Sudbury, Derby, and must be accompanied by a certificate of good character from the clergyman, or minister of any denomi- nation, resident in the same parish as the applicant. These applications must be received by Mr. Fawkes, before Augnet . Ist, and the first course of instruction will commence on August 15th. (2) No applicant will be received as a pupil who has not completed his or her eighteenth year. (3) On the acceptance of the applicant as a pupil, information will be given of the date fixed for arrival, which date must be strictly adhered to. (4) Lodgings will be obtained for the pupils in advance of their arrival at one or other of the farmhouses or cottages on the estate, or, in the case of young mtn, if necessary, at the village inn. The payments for board and lodging must be made in advance to the oc- cupier of the farm, cottage, or inn, and at the rate of not more than 10s. per week for girls, and probably about 12s. per week for men (5) Daring working Ivairs every pupil will be under the direction and control of the manager Of the dairy, and will be expected to work at the several dairy operations in the same degree as paid servants. (6) The milking of cows will be taught at the farm-houses where the pupils lodge, or on other farms, where special arrangements will be made for the purpose. (7) The pupils will be in- structed in the dairy itself in the best methods of skimming milk by hand, and in cream-separating by machinery, as well as in the practice of the methods of butter-making and ' cheese-making ordinarily pursued, and the reasons for each operation will be explained to them. (8) Lectures on the theory of the several branches of dairying will be delivered as occasion may seem to require, if a anfficient number of pupils should attend to warrant the expense, which will be met by a proportion of the fees paid by the pupils. (9) The complete course of instruction will extend over three months, but pupils may enter for any shorter or longer period by special arrangement. (10) The fees for instruc- tion will be as follow :—First month (or less) £3, second month £2, third month £l, being graduated in that manner In anticipation of the increasing value of the pupils' set.- vices in the later periods of their stay. (11) The maxi- mum number of pupils under instruction at any one time will rarely exceed twelve, and future pupils will be taken in the order of date of their applications to be received as such, except under very special circumstances. (12) At the com- pletion of every quarterly course there will be a "Leaving Examination" in both the principles and the practice of dairy-work, and certificates according to degrees of merit will be awarded to those pupils who satisfy the examiners. —lt must be understood that while the principal feature in this dairy is the making of butter, yet that the making of cheese from both whole-milk and skim-milk is largely prac- tised, more especially in the summer months.
"John, what is the best thing to feed a parrot on ?" asked an elderly lady of her bachelor brother who hated parrots, "Arsenic !" gruffly answered John.

And here we may deal.with a question which has repeat- edly been asked by correspondents, namely, how to tell fer- tile eggs. This we believe to be impossible before they are put under hens or into an incubator, except by breaking them. Then, if one be an expert, he can tell for a certainty whether the eggs would have hatched. The proper way is to set the eggs, and within a few days the fertilised eggs can be divided from the barren ones. The eggs that will hatch appear dark; there is a dark spot, which may readily be distinguished when held against a strong light, and that spot is the embryo chick. On opening a fresh egg that is fertilised the germ can be discovered on the yolk. It is about the size of a small pea and frequently, though not always, floats to the top of the opening. When without the shell this germ is supposed always to remain uppermost, and daring the period of incubation receives the greatest amount of warmth. The examination of eggs against a strong light is a safe guide as to their condition. When the whole shell is fall and dark, the egg is within a day or so of hatching, and if the chick is alive it may be heard by placing the egg to the ear. If all is still and dark probably the chick is dead. Often the little thing dies owing to the toughness of the shell, or to a sudden blow received whilst in the nest. Fresh eggs may be separated from stale ones by examining them in the way known as "candling." If fresh, the air bladder is seen to be small, not much larger than a pea; if stale it will be much larger, and if very old will take up about one-fifth of the whole space within the shell. Sometimes the shell indicates the freshness of the ' egg, and a very old one can generally be discovered in this way. There is a bloom on a fresh egg which cannot be I described, and the veriest novice would have no difficulty in telling it from a stale egg. But ills not easy to say whether an egg is a day or a fortnight old merely by the outward appearance, and it is also rather a risky way of de- ciding—not one that we should care to stake much upon when comparatively fresh eggs are concerned. As already stated, hens vary greatly in their productive powers, and some breeds are more noted than others as layers. There is so much difference in this way that even 1 some families of the seine breed are more noted as layers than are others, which proves that fecundity is a charac- teristic which can be developed in the same way as can out- ward characteristics. "Like produces like" in this respect, and there is a great deal in the old henwife's theory of always breeding from good layers. These distinctive breeds and families give us a very great help in getting the class of fowls that we want, for we know in what direction to turn for them. But it should be the object of every poul- try breeder to improve his stock, and he can do this by selecting those fowls that best meet bin ideals or needs. 1 - SEASONABLE HINTS. Signs will now soon become evident that some of the older birds will be beginning to moult before very long, and it is all the more necessary, on this account, that the stocks should be looked over, and those fowls that it is thought de• sirable to get rid of selected and put on one side to be got rid of forthwith. Those birds that are to be kept should have a little iron put into the drinking water, and a hand- ful of hemp seed given occasionally, as both these have the effect of loosening the feathers and helping on tbe moult. I don't believe in porcupine forgiveness. There are saintly fellows who, when they forgive, first worry and harass the one who craves forgiveness; then they pierce him with quills and heap damnation on his head, and say, "1 forgivd."—Newman. CAPTURE OF A DYNAMITARD IN THE POTTERIES.— On Saturday, Police-Sergeant Beirne, of the Staffordshire con- stabulary, arrested a uotorieus character named Jos Gratton, who was living without any visible means of subsistence in a disused railway carriage on a lonely road at Norton•green, near Hanley. Thirty-six packets of dynamite, some caps and several yards of fuse were seized. Gratton, who is 64 years of age, was charged before the Potteries Stipendiary at Hanley, on Monday, with having the dynamite caps and fuse in his possession for an unlawful purpose. The pri- soner refused 0 give any account of how he came into pos- session of them, or for what purpose they were intended, beyond the fact that he got them from Yorkshire. The pri- soner, who is a notorious gaolbird, having been convicted 24 times, was remanded. PRINCESS LOUISE AND GYMNASTICS.-- On Saturday, a selection, numbering between four and five hundred, of the boys in attendance at the schools of the London School Board were assembled in Hyde Park to take part in the an- nual drill competition. The Princess Louise and the Mar- quis of Lorne drove to the ground, where they were met by the Duke of Buckingham, I ord Reav, the Chairman and other members of the School Board, Sir Francis Sandford, Sir U. Kay-Shuttlewortb, Lord Alfred Churchill, Mr. S. Morley, M.P. and others. The challenge banner was awarded to the Soho boys, and the Princess Louise pre- sented it to them. Mr. Buxton proposed a vote of thanks to the Princess, and the Marquis of Lorne, in responding, said the Princess attached the greatest importance to physical exercise both for boys and girls, and espe cially.recommended the Swedish system for the girls. Not only were these exer- cises healthy, but they fostered a national spirit. The boys were afterwards entertained in the Health Exhibition at the invitation of the Executive Council. FISHERIES ON THE RIVER MERSEY
—— IN 1755. The following statement is printed from a manuscript, and is contained in a Case prepared in 1755, upon which the opinion of Counsel (Mr. R. Wilbraham, of Lincoln's Inn) was taken.

"on the River Mersey, which is navigable, and Sloops and Boats have free passage at Spring Tides from Lever- poole to Smalley, and which divides Lancashire and Cheshire, are several' antient tfishwares which have been enjoyed time immemorial, and to which River no claim was ever made by Lords of Mannors or others, save the Earl Rivers to 3 yards of the mid stream for the passage of Boats from Halton to hold the Courts at .. in Cheshire, but not made use of in the memory of Man, tho' the said Earl and his successors have always had the Royal Fish taken at the said Weares, for which they pay es. Bd. for each Royal Fish.

"The-part of the River in dispute was map'd at low water, and is near 30 miles from the Sea, and there are few Tides (if any) except Spring Tides, that flow within seve- rail Miles of the same, and the Land Owner of the lands, being qualified to kill game, insists that he has a right to fish in the said River, as it is navigable, it he was not ewner of lands on either aide of the said River, where he was fishing, provided he did not land his net but upon his own ground. "A. is a fishware which has been used as such time im- memorial, and enjoyed by the Tenants of the land marked B. and D. without obstruction. The owner of the land C. has sett up a claim of drawing in the River from his own I land with a nett, which is conveyed or drawn by a Boat across the said River, or within a few yards of the opposite side at B, by which method he never lands his net upon the land 8., but upon his own lands, C. Bat the owner of the land B , apprehending he has a right to one-half of the Stream, which haa always been claimed and enjoyed time immemorial by the Land Owners adjoining to the said River, insists that he the said owner of the land C. can't use his nets there except from his own land, to the middle stream, without the consent of the owner of the land 8., as he does not only prevent the fith from passing up the River to the antient fish ware, but also takes the fish out of the River to the great damage of the owner of the said antient fishware, as well as drawing his net upon that part of the river which the owner of the land B. apprehends belongs to him.

"Query.—Can the Owner of the Land C , or persons em• ployed by him, make flee of a Nat to kill and destroy Fish in the said River beyond the Mid Stream at Low Water, for those Nets are not used at any other time and the Banks on each aide are the Lords' or Owners' of the land adjoining thereto?

"Answer.—ln all Rivera not naturally navigable the Lord Owners of both sides the River de communt jure own the River; that is, the owner of each side owns the soil to the .ifylum aqua, and they own alternately the fishery on each side the River; but tho' the soil of the River, as high generally as there Is constant flax and reflex of the Sea, is In the King, and the right of fishing in such River is gene-I rally com'on to all the King's Subjects, yet particular Per- sons may Claina it by prescription. And as in this part of the River the 0 wnera of lanui 811 eastb side cic; gT,nerally claim the fisheries, usque ad Alum aqua, I think that this Is the right which will probably prevail. So that I incline to think that as this lies above 30 Miles from the sea, it can't be said to be a River that is an Arm of the Sea, or a River which continually flows and mitoses. If then this River is not a public's River in which all Mankind have a right of fishing, then I think that the owner of the land called C. can only fish on his side of the river, and can't Justify fishing or setting Nets or Engines on each side of the river or beyond the midst of the stream." There are in the MS. other queries and answers Its to the best legal means for determining the dispute and for arrest- ing encroachment.

In September next a professorship of geography is to be instituted in each Russian university. The Italian Government has asked for a credit of £7,000 in order to found a central magnetic observatory at Rome, under the direction of the Meteorological Office. In addi- tion to the above sum, the Government asks also for an annual grant of £220 for the general expenses; and £460 for the salaries of the personnel of the pronozed observatory. A SUFFERER Facor HAY FIVER writes that a few years ago, acting on the principle that like cares like, he began in spring to take strong Scotch snuff as he felt hi a unwel- come annual visitant coming upon him. He found it effec- tual, and in future years, when he resumed the snuff-taking in the spring, confirmed the cure. He has recommended it to many sufferers with great success. . . . • . .

An original portrait of Handel has come into the posses- sion of Hamburg Library. It was painted in 1745 by Hud- son, and seat by the composer to one of his relatives at Halle. Later on it belonged to Chrysander, the historian of Handel, and from the etatement that it had been handed down to a Dr. Senff of Halle, whose wife was a descendant of the family of the great musician, we conclude that this portrait is one of• the many painted by Hudson to which Mr. Rockstro refers in his "Life of Handel," under the head "Do Reliquiis."

PARASITES IN MEAT AND FISH.-At a lecture on para. Sites in meat and food by Dr. T. Spencer Cobbold on Wed. nesday at the Health Xxhibition, as to parasites in fish, special reference was made to the scare which was raised by the asserted unwholesome condition of mackerel. In reply, Dr. Cobbold stated that there were fourteen kinds of para. sites which attacked fish of all kinds; of these twelve were intestinal, and two limited their attacks to the gills. In every species vitality was destroyed by a temperature of 115 degrees Fahrenheit. The evil effects attributed to the mackerel parasites consequently must be nonexistent. THE PRICE OF Picxuans.--It is interesting just now, when every one is talking of the enormous prices obtained for pictures, books, furniture, and faience at recent sales, to recall the sums which were paid at one of the most sensa- tional sales on record—that of Charles the First's pictures. Every one knows that the Raphael cartoons were saved to the nation at a cost of £3OO. Correggio's "Antiope" fetched £1,000; the "Venus del Pario," of Titian, £600; Raphael's "St. George," £130; and a "Portrait of a Young Man," likewise by Raphael, £2OO. Titian's portrait of Charles V. was sold for £l5O as was also the same painter's " Hero- dias with the Head of the Baptist in a Charger." One of the the highest prices realised at the sale—£l,ooo—was paid for Correggio's "Apollo Flaying Marsyas," which is now in the Louvre. Rabene's allegory of" Peace and War," now in the National Gallery, was literally "given away" for £loo.—St. James's Gazette.

CIVILISATION AND TEN SIZE OF TEETIL—Most people I know that the teeth of anthropoid apes are considerably larger in proportion to the size of the skull than those of human beings. A few are also aware in a vague and general way that The teeth of savages are larger, as they are more free from disease than the teeth of the civilised races; but this latter proportion had never been really tested by scien- tific measurement; hence the great value of a paper read by I Professor Flower at the last meeting of the Anthropological Society. Professor Flower has carefully measured the teeth of over 3,000 skulls belonging to different races. He took a certain line from ths nasal point to another point at the base of the skull, as giving on the whole a measurement least affected by mere differences of shape; then he ascer- tained in each case the proportion which the four last molars in the lower jaw. bone bear to this measured line. The results are most interesting and curious. In the average Englishman the proportion is as 41 to 100, in Europeans generally 405, In ancient Egyptians 401, in Polynesians 401, and in the Inhabitants of Central India 404. These form what Pro- fessor Flower calls the small-toothed group. Next comes the Chinese with an index of 42 6, the American Indians with 428, the Malays with 433, and the negroes with 43-9. These are classed as middle.size toothed races. The third group is formed of the large-toothed. These are the Mela- nesians, with an index of 44.2, the Andamanese males with 444 and females with 46.5, Australian males with 44-8 and females with 461, and Tasmanian males with 475 and females with 48.7. The great difference between males and females in the lower races is very remarkable, because it does not occur in the higher races, and also because it has been observed in the anthropoid apes. For the purpose of comparison it may be mentioned that the proportion in an- thropoids is as 50 to 100. It will thus be seen that in re- spect of her teeth a Tasmanian woman is not far removed from an ape—in fact the whole series of figures abound with points of interest, as, for instance, the high place taken by the ancient Egyptians and the folynesians—and as indi- cating a new basis for ethnological classification will doubt- less give rise to much comment and criticism among scien- tific men.

To the Lancashire and Cheshire Antiquarian Society, Mr. J. E. Bailey has announced that the Duke of Devonshire had undertaken, at his own cost, to publish the cartularies of Furness Abbey. This announcement, Mr. Bailey said, would be hailed with pleasure by all antiquaries. Lord St. Leonards, convicted at the last session of the Central Criminal Court of assaulting a servant girl, at Brentford, in May, was on Saturday sentenced to be im- prisoned for seven weeks from the date of his conviction, which was May 19. The effect of this was that Lord St. Leopards was discharged the same day. THE FORTHCOMING CONSERVATIVE CONFERENCE At SHEFFIELD—This Conference is lo be held at Sheffield on the 23rd inst. Lord Randolph Churchill will preside, and 'he and Earl Percy are both candidates for the office otpresi- dent next year. The contest will be close but it is believed Lod Randolph will be elected, as he had the majority at Birmingham last year, and is in favour with the Sheffield delegates.

THE HULL AND BARNSLEY RAILWAY AND DOCK : STOP- PAGE OF WORKS.—On Saturday, o wing to the directors of the Hull and Barnsley Railway and Dock Company having failed to raise the additional capital required b complete the undertaking, the works were stopped, and about 2,0001 workmen paid off. If some arrangement is not made in a few days to tide over the difficulty, there is every reason to fear that the whole of the works will have to be stopped at the end of next week.

_ HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4.15. DEBATE ON THE FReNC RISE BILL. There was a very large attendance of peers; the peer- sues' galleries were crowded; and the spaces at the foot of the throne and outside the bar' as well as the Strangers' Gallery, were fully occupied. The Prince of Wales, the Bake of Edinburgh, and the Duke of Cambridge were on the cross benches. After a preliminary demand by Lord Hardwicke and Lord Relesdale thae the Government should e state what concessions they were prepared to make, Lord KIMBERLEY rose to move the second reading of the Representation of the People Bill. Having briefly stated the provisions of the bill, he explained the general results to be that the franchise was placed on the broad foundation of household qualification—one which he hoped would wear for many years. The measure would add two millions to - the three millions of voters already on the franchise roll The number it would add in Ireland was 4000)0. He ad- rutted that at first sight this seemed Is be an imminent and great danger; but the Government had had to determine What on the whole appeared to be the path of safety. He was sorry to say that there was in Ireland a large party vio- lently hostile to the connection of the two' countries and wishing to sever the connection, and he admitted that under this bill the number of those wise supported Mr. Parnell in Parliament was likely to receive a considerable accession. Such an accession would show that the true feeling of Ire- land was not now represented in Parliament, where it would be better to•have that feeling to deal with than it was to encounter it elsewhere. The consideration, however, Which weighed With him was that, if Ireland were not in- cluded in the bill, the enemies in that country of the , British connection would receive the support of a large Party in this country who were strongly devoted to a gene- ral extension of the franchise. Corning to the amendment Of Lord Cairns, he asked whether the bill was not "a well considered and complete scheme for the extension of the • franchise." Repeating pretty nearly Mr. Gledstoneei sketch of the Redistribution Bat contemplated by the Government, he stated that they intended to introduce it next year if they remained in office till that time, and the bill before their lordehips was not to come into operation till January, 1886. Re pointed out what appeared to him the dangers of an as- sembly like their lordships' House rejecting this measure at the Present time, when revolutionary ideas were making such formidable progress. Their bitterest enemies were . longing and praying that their lordships might throw the measure Out; but he hoped they would not decide upon tak- ing so perilous a step. Lord CAIRYS, in moving his amendment, combated the • aesertion of the Government that there never had been a corn- Plate scheme of reform such as the Opposition now required. That assertion, he contended, had no other foundation than the fact that different portions of the United Kingdom had beau dealt with ley different Bills, because each of those • Bills either contained a redistribution scheme in itself, or was accompanied by a measure of redistribution. He cited Lord Derby and Lord Hertington as authorities against the eourse taken by the Government in this instance. if the . Government were prepared to accept an amendment that this Bill should net come into operation sooner than their Redis- tribution Bill, they bad only to say so; but as they had refused that amendment in the House of Commons, the Peetponemeat to the Cemmittee stage of such a resolution would be only to postpone the i.sue on the Bill. He be- lieved in the sincerity of Mr. Gladstone's promise to bring in a Redistribution Bill next Tear, but circumstances might defeat his intention. He believed in the sincerity of the right hon. gentleman's promise to give the House of Corn- ORS a day for the Vote of Censure; but the day was not , given, and Mr. Gladstone was reported to have complimented • his supporters on their good sense in bringing about that , result. Having pointed out that those political organizers who were masters of the situation might tell the Govern. fluent that they were quite satisfied with the extension of the franchise without a Redistribntion Bill, he said it was stated that their lordships were going against the country. They : appealed to the country, and seised to be jueged by the . country. They had received a considerable quantity of advice and some menace. The latter had corns mainly from • one quarter, and, coming from that quarter, it was neither • fitting nor constitutional. He asked their lordships to be neither deterred by menace from supporting his amendment or Provoked by menace to support it if they did not think it was one which the House ought to approve. He placed it before their lordships in the belief that it would inset with .; the approval of the great majority of their lordships as he , believed it would that of the country. ' The Duke of ARGYLL, in an earnest speech, celled on the ' independent members of the Hones to support the second reading. While admitting that it would be desirable to have a Redistribution Bill before them, he held that the effect of the Franchise Bill of itself must be to increase the Power of couisty voters. Judging from speeches made some - time ago by two of the Radical members of the Cabinet, he felt sure that it was not without difficulty the majority of the Government had succeeded in bringing forward so 'Moderate a measure. He expressed his opinion that if the yowe rejected the measure because it was not accompanied leT a Redistribution Bill, its action would be •mieunderstood and tnisrepresehted. The Duke of Itemeolen strongly supported the amend- Meat, and argued that without considerable improvement and a good measure of redistribution the bill would be in- itirious to the best interests of the empire. The Earl of JERSEY said the course which was being taken tile Earl Cairns was the only one which would prevent a , Itedistribution Bill being brought up. (Ministerial cheers.) t as the right of the House of Lords to pass any amend- 'lent they believed to be a good one, and their Lordships ehottlei insist upon the insertion in the bill of an amendment Postponing the operation of the bill until after the passing Or! a Redistribution Bill. He objected to the motion of -e'er! Cairns because It favoured nothing but the rejection of the bill. Could it be rVat for their Lordships to refese a lecond reading to a bill which had passed the other House Without opposit'on to its main principles, and were they to confess their in tbility to amend a meisure in Committee? (Ministerial cheers). He warned their lordships that what- ever might barmen this session the question of reform would nOt slumber. THE FRANCHISE DEBATE.—REJECTION OF THE

div.head: BILL.
div.p: BILL.

The adjourned debate on the second reading of the Repre- sentation of the People Bill was resumed by the Earl of CARNARVON, who commenced by observing that the Reform Act of 1832, though in many respects it effected satisfactory alterations, amounted to an absolute revolution. Many abuses were removed by it, but it swept away the small boroughs which gave admission to public life to the greater names that history recorded. It substituted for the repre- sentation of classes the representation of mere numbers. ' Between 1832 and 1867 labour was represented less than previously. The intellectual level of the House of Com- mons had been lowered, and there had been in increasing ratio an absence of that continuous policy without which a country could not hope to maintain its prosperity, The Act of 1868 in some respects went too far, and in offers in did not go far enough. The safeguards with which it was sur- rounded disappeared. The redistribution which accompanied it was not commensurate with the amount of the enfran- chisement, and it converted members of the House of Com- mons into delegates. The lesson which the two Acts taught was that in touching the Constitution they should endeavour to avoid great shocks. They should make the changes gradual, and seek as far as practicable a representation of the divers interests and classes which were the strength of the country, and Endeavouring to make the House of Commons a mirror of the people, He was prepared honestly to accept the facts of the present day, and to give effect loyalty to their consequences. He was prepared to accept a large extension of the franchise upon the basis of household suffrage, but that extension should be fair, and should involve such succeeding redistri- bution of the electoral power as would give full play to the different opinions in the country, fair representation to the different interests, and make safe the Constitution at home and

abroad. This bill gave a large extension of the fran- chise, but omitted many things which he considered essen- tial. He congratulated the Hollse that it was not intro- duced with a promise of finality, by which the country had been many times cheated; and knowing the agricultural labourer well, he was ready with an ungrudging hand to give him the vote. Looking at the state of Ireland and the certain results of the bill, he congratulated the Government upon a tremendous act of course's in including that part of the kingdom in 10 provisions. It was a grave omission that the measures made no provision for the representation of minorities, but the most serious omission was that it did not deal with redistribution, which Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, Mr. Fawcett, and Mr. Trevelyan had in past times spoken of as by far the most important part of any scheme of Parliamentary reform. Their lordships had been threatened with the anger of the country, but he could not understand the country being angry at being asked to ex- press its opinion on the subject. The action of the House of Lords if it adopted the amendment, might be misrepre- sented, but it could not be misunderstood, and the Govern- ment had the power even then at the eleventh hour, if they had the will, to settle the matter in conformity with what be believed to be just and expedient, and to be, also, the almost unanimous feeling of their lordships' House. Better that the House of Lords should cease with unstained honour than that it should pretend to exercise functions whieh it leased to discharge. (Cheers)

div.head: Earl of DERBY considered it a remarkable and satis-
div.p: The Earl of DERBY considered it a remarkable and satis-

factory feature of the discussion that though the House was asked to decide who should in the last resort be the deposi- tory of supreme power, there was absolutely no difference of opinion among their lordships as to the principle of the measure. That being the case. he should scarcely have thought It worth while when they were making a change which was acknowledged to be inevitable, to provoke a colli- sion between the House of Lords and the majority of the nation—(" No, no*" and cheers)—by insisting upon the adoption of one mode of proceeding rather than another. The supporters ef the amendment declared that tiny were not opposed to reform • but, if so they were takiog a very grave step. They would be judged, not by their words, but by their acts. The agricultural labourers would be told that a bill was brought forward to give them the vote, but that their lordships rejected it. The fact would be remembered when all their qualifications were forgotten That their lord- ships were bound to accept the general indications of public opinion was a penalty they paid for their maiden. A mem- ber of the House of Commons who found himself in antag- onism to his constituents could not long retain his seat, but in giving their votes upon important questions their lord- ships nad no such guide, and must endeavour to act upon those indications of public opinion which reached them. Noble lords opposite declared that that was all they intended to do by the amendment, but if they expected to be sup. petted by any considerable popular force, he could only hope that the awakening from that delusion might not be rougher than any of their lordships desired. (Cheers.) In 1880 the constituencies thoroughly made up their minds on the question. The ground upon which the amendment had been submitted was the applehension that if this bill passed leisure might not be found in the present Parlia- ment for passing a Redistribution Act. But he reminded their lordships that there would still be eighteen months for the work. Ho admitted that it would be inconvenieet and undesirable in the event of an earlier dissolution that the appeal should be to the extended constituencies before a I redistribution scheme had been passed, but in making the calculations for a budget it was not the practice to take into account the possibility of those calculation ti being disturbed by a war. They must in most matters be content with something less than certainty, and he did not see why a measure of reform should be an exception to that rule. He

would suggest to the Opposition that they would put them- selves in a rounder position if they allowed the bill to be read a second time and proposed in committee a resolution suspending its operation till a Redistribution Bill had been

div.head: 'I lir-EXAMINER SATURDAY. JULY 12, 1884.
div.p: 'I lir-EXAMINER SATURDAY. JULY 12, 1884.

passed through. That course would be fraught with con- siderable inconvenience. Supposing a Redistribution Bill were brought forward, it might be rejected year after year, and it would be impossible to suspend the exercise of the new franchise for an indefinite time. The curse which the Government proposed was that which they believed would be attended with the least inconvenience and the most likely to secure the desired result. If the two bills had been brought in together the chance of passing either would have been destroyed. If one was hung up till the other !Imam law that would be attended with difficulties, and the only alternative was to make an ample allowance of time for the completion of the work. He did not deny that he should, have liked to see the whole subject dealt with in one bill, ' but it was a question not of what the Government would like to do, but of what was practical. Lord BRABOIIENE was of opinion that if the Government were in earnest they might have dealt with redistribution I first and extended the franchise afterwards, Though he I considered it a mistake to have moved the amendment at that moment he felt bound to support it. He felt bitterly having to say no to a proposal for the extension of the franchise. The Earl of ROSEBERY could scarcely understand the anguish of Lord Brabourne in voting in a different lobby from the Government when he remembered how frequently the noble lord had placed himself in that position. • The Liberal party regarded the measure not only as one of ex- pediency, but as one of high justice, and also of possibility; while it would have been wholly impossible to have passed a Redistribution Bill in connection with a Franchise Bill through the House of Commons. The fact that redistribu- tion had been disposed of by a majority of 130 did not pre- vent the leaders of the Opposition from supporting it at the last stage of the bill a proposal for admitting 500,000 women to the franchise. If the Government bloke their promise to deal with redistribution in the present Parlia- ment, the Liberal Peers would give an almost unanimous support to any-Vote of Censure the Conservatives might bring forward. He denied that the House of Lords had any moral justification for rejecting the bill on the second read- ing, and wanted to know what their lordships' feeling would be if, after they had passed a bill for reforming theinselvas, the Commons were to throw it out. By adopting the amendment they could not prevent the measure from pass- ing, awl the only effect, of the vote would be indefinitely to strengthen the present Government. The weight and authority of the House of Lords were at stake, and he ap- pealed to independent Peers to pause before endorsing the action of Earl Cairns, and to the Bishops to assist in giving the franchise to the two millions of men to whom the bill would extend it.

The Duke of RUTLAND supported the amendment. The Earl of DALHOUSIE opposing it, declared that the ex- treme Radicals were dancing with joy at the expectation of the rejection of the bill by their loroships. If it were re- jected it was not likely that they would again see so moder- ate a measure of reform.— Lord Ravxwswourn acknow- ledged the unanimity of opinion in favour of equalising the borough and county. franchise, but there was equal unani- mity in the admission of the imperfections of the present measure.—The Marquis of HUNTLEY supported the second reading of the bill—The Earl of GALLOWAY had no con- fidence that a measure of redistribution of the colossal form shadowed forth by the Prime Minister could pass in the present Parliament —The Earl of CamPsrt- DOWN observed that Lord Cairns was throwing a serious re- sponsibility upon the House of Peers in asking them to reject the bill on the second reading when, as it seemed, they were all favourable to an extension of the franchise. He should be glad to support a motion for adjournment if he thought that would bring about an arrangement which would save the bill.—The Earl of WENITS3 disputed the statement that the question of the extension of the franchise was before the constituencies at the last general election, and viewed with anxiety the introduction into the con• atitnency of two millions new voters. Still he felt it his duty to vote against the amendment and for the second reading of the bill. The Archbishop of CANTERBURY. like others, could have wished that Redistribution had been included in the mea- sure, but did not regard that as a ground for the rejection of the second reading. The principle of the bill had been conceded long ago, and had been re-aflir med in such a manner that the present measure was not so much a mea- sure of reform as an expansion of a reform introduced long ago. The Church trusted the people, and used its beet efforts to educate and elevate them, and he believed the people wonld be true to the constitution as long as the con- stitution was true to them.

_ The LORD CHANCELLOR pointed to the experience of 1831 and 1832 to show that it would have been impossible to have passed in the present Parliament a bill dealing with Enfranchisement and Redistribution at the same time, and mentioned that even when the bill of 1832 went up to the Lords with the support of an overwhelming majority of a House of Commons elected to pass "the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill," it was nearly wrecked by an amendment of Lord Lyndhurst, which turned upon a pro- pesition the reverse of that new sebmitted by Earl Cairns. The bill of 1867 took in its progress from the 18th of March to the 22nd of July, though it did not deal with redistribution in a large and satisfactory way, and it must be remembered that the machinery of legislation moved much more smoothly and easily than it did in these days. If their lordships did all they could cordially ant gene- rously to pass the bill, they would place themselve in a position of enormous advantage, if any Ministry were so forgetful of its duty as to propose a measure of redistribu- tion framed for selfish or party purposes. The rejection of the bill would give an opportunity to eirtreme men to use language which would tend to set class against class and irrerest against interest, and to attack and villify their lord- ships' House. The Marquis of SALISBURY had the same admiration for the working-men as the Archbishop of Canterbury had ex- pressed, and believed they might, with perfect safety to the institutions of the country, be entrusted with the franchise. The question before them however was, how was political power to be so distributed that all classes might receive their due position in the State, and how might mince Ries have that power of expressing their views which was essential te the protection of their interests. They were asked to as- sent to a measure which was abolutelv unprecedented in the history of the country. Never had any Government before dealt with the question of the extension of the franchise without dealing at the same time with the redis- tribution of power. Speakers in defence of the measure had attached little importance to a General Election under the new franchise without redistribution, but it must be borne in mind that the effect of the measure would be to project into the rural coestituencies a great number of urban voters, and thus falsify and efface the opinion of the rural portions of the country. The urban voters had already political power abundantly and oven superfluously, and it was now proposed to give them more, to the effacement of a class which had done more than any other to give to the Eng- lish character its solidity. The warning that the effect of the ballot in Ireland would be to take power out of the hands of those who were attached to the English con- nection had proved true, and he warned the Government now that this measure in its present incomydete form had the disadvantage that it seriously menaced the integrity of the Empire. It had been said that the object which Lord Cairns had in view might have been attained by an amend- ment in committee, but they knew perfectly well, from the emphatic language of the Colonial Secretary and the Prime Minister, that no such clause would be accepted. He gave the Government eredit for perfect honesty of intention to carry a Redistribution Bill next year, but the question was whether they had the power to iulfll the promise. They had not had much power over their proceedings during the last four years. What the Opposition wanted was a Redis- tribution Bill, which, if it was.unjust, they could modify; but they could not modify it with this pistol at their heads. If the bill passed in its present form they would not have a free hand in modifying the scheme of redistribution. They were told that terrible things would happen if they did not pass the bill, but if so why did not the Government agree to insert a clause which would prevent the bill coming into operation until after a scheme of redistribution had been passed? If they did that the whole difficulty would be at an end, and if they refused upon them and not upon the Opposition would rest the responsibility for whatever might happen. (Cheers.) The my of danger to the House of Lords was nothing more than a Liberal contrivance, and if the action of their Lordships was misunderstood it would be owing entirely to the careful and persistent menaces of her Majesty's Government. The Opposition did not as a party measure desire to force a dissolution, but he urged upon the Government the justice of consulting the people upon the question of enfranchisement and redistribution. Earl GRANVILLE *lid not attach any great weight to the warning founded upon experience that the ballot in Ireland Ibad taken away the power of landlords to coerce their ten- an's to vote against their own convictions. He had very great doubt whether the House of Lords had a right to arro- gate to itself the prerogative of the Crown so far as to dic- tate the time of a dissolution. He was ready to accept the assurance that the Conservative party was not opposed to an extension of the faanchise, but he found a difficulty in arguing that point with persons less credulous than himself, and the discussion that night would not render the process easier. Fears had been expressed of the new voters, and he should have thought that if the votes of the farmers were to be swamped, the change would have been exceedingly dis- tasteful to the Marquis of Salisbury. Great indignation had been expressed with regard to Mr. Gladstone's supposed threat to the HOMO of Lords, but it was not the case that the words of the Prime Minister were unprovoked. Great pains had been bestowed upon the measure, which was ad- mitted to be temperate in character and Conservative in Lone, and while it Was still before the House of Commons the noble Marquis had gone about the country giving good reasons why the House of Lords should reject the bill, and others had pronounced it as dead as a door nail. He ap- pealed to their lordships even at that late period to think' for themselves, and come tea statesmanlike conclusion. THE DIVISION. Their lordships divided on Lord Cairns' amendment-- Contents 205 Non-contents

Majority against the Government.. 59 The bill was therefore lost. The result was received with loud cheers. The amendment was then ag,reed•to with the alteration suggested by the Earl of DIINIIAVEN. substituting "The principles of representaCon contained in this bill," for a "well considered and complete scheme for the extension of the franchise."
