The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. MIDHST PASHA'S DEATIL—In reply to Mr. Jerningham, Lord E. FITZMAIIRICE said that it had no doubt been stated that Midhat Pasha and other exiles had been starved to death at Tait, but the Government had no reliable informa- tion on the subject. Tam KOIIRRASH IN E.:limn-4n reply to Mr. Wm. Corbat, Lord E. FIIZMAIIRICE said that instructions were now being framed which would in future secure that the Kourbash should only be used in a manner consistent with justice and humanity. The Kourbash was no doubt used under the rules, established by Mr. Clifford Lloyd.—ln answer to Mr. Coleridge Kennard, Lord E. FITZUAIIRICE said that Mr. Clifford Lloyd would not return to the scene of his labours in Egypt. FRENCH AND ENGLISH SHIPBUILDING.—In reply to Cal. Gourley, Mr. Cmaransauatx said that the total increase in the tonnage of ships annually built in the French ports, from 1872 to 1832, was only 6.000 tens. The tonnage of ships anaually built in British ports daring the same period was 300.000. tons. That was in spite of the bounties given by the French Government fqr the encouragement of French shipbuilding. GENERAL Gounow.—ln answer to Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, the Marquis of HARTINGTON said that the last information the Goa ernrnent had had from G-eneral Gordon was an un- dated telegram, in which he stated that they were provi- sioned at Khartoum for five months. They had already stated that it was not their intention to send an expedition to Khartoum unless it could be shown that this was the only means by which General Gordon and those attached to him could be relieved. They had no information which led them to depart from that intention. LONDON GOVERNMENT BLLL. The adjourned debate on the second reading was resumed by Mr. R. N. FOWLER, who, in. supprtitag the amendment, reminded the House of the saying attributed to President Lincoln, that it was unwise to swap horses while crossing a stream. He applied this quotation to the effect the passage of the bill might have in throwing upen a new and untried authority the administration of important sanitary laws at a time when cholera had appeared in a neighbouring country, and might bkexpected at any moment in England. He expressed surprise at the small amount of popular sup- pert given to' this bill. There had been comparatively few -petitions in favour oaf the bill, but there had been 210 against it. Sir 8. WATERLOW entertained a strong sense of the im- portance of a measure which proposed to extend to upwards of 3i millions outside the boundaries of the City of London 1 the same municipal privileges that were enjoyed by the in- habitants of every other large town in the kingdom. In giving his support to the second reading of the bill, he in- sisted on the necessity for the establishment of a central authority as a means of procuring that uniformity of ad- mietration which was so greatly needed in the metropolis, and the absence of which accounted for so many extraor- dinary anomalies. Lord G. HAMILTON complained that the scheme embo- died in the bill was unsatisfactory, inasmuch as it would deprive the ratepayere of each district of that direct con- trol over the levying and expenditure of rates at present exercised by them through their local representatives. It would be as sensible to attempt to pass a Local Government Bill for England with a central and controlling authority in London. _ .

Mr. S. BUXTON supported the Bill, mainly on the ground of its creation of one great central authority, whereby uni- formity of government of the large area of the metropolis would be secared.—Mr. Bonen, in opposing the Bill, sug- gested as an alternative that system which divided the me- tropolis into six municipalities, with a central council of 50 members, as the equivalent of the present Metropolitan Board, would he more workable.— Mr. L. STANLEY, who was interrupted at the outset and again a few minutes afterwards by unsuccessful attempts to count out the House, con- tended that the bill was needed to remedy the existing chaos of local governments in the metropolis.—Sir J. Euas re- garded much that had been said against the malpractices of the vestries and other local authorities of London as greatly exaggerated. The reasons advanced in support of the bill were not sufficient for upsetting the entire government of London and substituting a new and experimental system. Mr. G. RUSSELL, speaking on behalf of the Government in support of the bill, replied to numerous objections against the measure, and entered into some details in proof of the charges that had been made as to jobbery in con aection with certain of the London vestries, the way in which the sanitary arrangements had been neglected in poor district!, and the fact that meetings in favour of the present bill had been disturbed by persons who were paid for that service. Sir J. M. GABEL noon taunted the supporters of the bill with having ,ailed to prove the alleged chaos in the govern- ment of London, and defended the Metropolitan Board of Works against the attacks made upon them in the course of the debate. He hoped the Government would postpone the bill.
THE FRANCHISE BILL-GOVERNMENT STATE- MEN r.--AurumN SESSION PROPOSED. _

The PRIME MINISTER, in stating the intentions of ,the Government, remarked that their first duty was to secure by proper constitutional and regular methods at the earliest possible moment the passing of the Franchise Bill, the prin- ciple of which had received in terms—in the House of Com- mons by positive votes, and in the House of Lords by words not deficient in force—the assent of both Houses of Parlia- ment. The Government wished early next session to proceed with the Redistribution Bill. They did not see any way in which these two c•bjects could be obtained except by the method of advising Her Majesty—and she has been graciously pleased to consent—to assemble the House in the course of the autumn for the purpose of considering' the Franchise Bill. It was qnite clear to him that it would not be his dray, even if it were possible, either morally, socially, or physically, to obtain such a sac- ' rifice as would be involved in attempting to proceed with all the bills before the House. That being so, and having stated that the passing of the Franchise Bill and the fat- fitment of the Government's engagements with regard to re- distribution were to be made their paramount object, the Go- vernment had come to the conclusion that they had no option except to make a sweeping and very impartial sacri- fice of the bills before them. There was one exception that the Government proposed to make, in the case of the bills that had passed through the Grand Committees. The bulk of the labour of the House having been spent upon them, the Government thouarfat they ought not to be lost. That was especially their view with regard to the Corrupt Practices at Municipal Elections Bill. With respect to the Law of Evidence Bill the Govern- ment reserved their decision. The other bills which they could not ask the House to proceed with included the Lon- don Government Bill, the Railways Regulation Bill, the University (Scotland) Bill, the Education (Wales) Bill, the Irish Land Purchases Bill, The Irish Sunday Closing Bill, the Coinage Bill, the Police Superannuation Bill, and the Criminal Law Amendment Bill. Upon the Medical Act Amendment Bill he did not give a final decision. They would make it their first duty to proceed with Supply. It was the view of the Government that it was of vital im- portance that they should concentrate their attention on the Franchise Bill, and go forward on the first opportunity with the question of redistribution. (Cheers.) Sir S. Nowracorn moved th adjournment of the House in order to allow the consideration of the Prime Minister's statement. Assant having been accorded, the leader of the Opposition proceeded to ask the Government to give a clear understanding that redistribution should be before the House in the autumn in the shape of a bill before they were called upon to decide the question of the franchise. He wished to know what was to be done in reference to any debate on Egyptian affairs.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the burden which redistribution imposed upon the conduct of the fran- chise question was far more formidable than-it had been hitherto, and it was impossible to hold out any expectation of the government changing their course. But the Govern- ment considered it their paramount duty to pass both the Franchise Bill and the measure of redistribution. The pie !gee of the Government with reference to the discussion of the affairs of Egypt was wholly unaffected by the state- ment which be had made. He was sanguine that the de- liberations of the Conference would be over in such time as to give liberty to Parliament to consider the conclusions presented to them.—Lord R. Carnacuru. said that the Prime Minister had said it was the intention of the Government to call Parliament together to cm- eider the Franchise Bill and redistribution.—Upon this Mr. GLADSTONE remarked that it was the intention et the Government to deal with the Redist ibution Bill next see- BiOn.—Lord R. Canucataa, resuming, said if the Prime Minister had not denied the statement everyone in the House except the Liberal party would have believed it. If the Prime Minister liked he could aring in a Redistribution Bill in October, complete the whole scheme of reform, and take an election upon the new constituency. It was obvious to him that the whole legislative programme of the Government which had now been abandoned was a gigantic humbug. The right hon gentleman had denied the independent legis- lative rights of the House of Lords, and threatened them with practical abolition unless they consented to become a registration office for Liberal legislation. Lord Randolph proceeded to contradict a statement made on the previous night by Sir C Dilke, and a very animated and personal dis- cussion followed, in the course of which Sir M H Beach re- pudiated a charge of obstruction brought by Sir C Dilke. , Subsequently Sir W HARCOURT joined in the debate, and stated that nothing could be more contrary to the intention of the Government than to try to pass a Redistribution Bill in the autumn session. Their object was simply to pass the Franchise Bill this year, and the Government would keep before the country the Franchise Bill and that alone till it was passed. He charged Lord R. Churchill with using inflammatory language and attempting to exasperate party spirit. From this time forth, in the House of Commons and out of it, the Government would have only one object, and that was to prosecute before all things to the end the passing of the bill for enfranchising two millions of people.—After considerable discussion, the Irish members ref need to let the motion for adjournment be awithdrawn, and it was negatived. The House tly_n went into Committee of Supply.

ROME, gIINDAY.—Two cases of cholera occurred yesterday among the fugitives from Toulon in the lazaretto at Saluzzo. Both patients were kept completely isolated. One case ter- minated fatally. SPREAD OF THE CHOLERA.

TOULON, THURSDAY, 945 AM.—There was ten deaths from cholera here last night, two occurring in the suburbs, two in St. Mandrier Hospital, three in the Civil Hospital, and three in the city, among the victims in the latter case tr,ing the Superioress of the Sisters of St. Maur. The sister who was attacked by cholera at the Marine Hospital is now convalescent. MARSEILLES, THURSDAY, 10 A.H.—Twenty-five deaths from cholera were regietered here last night. div.head: DEMANDED.
div.p: DEMANDED.

PARIS, MONDAY.-At a Cabinet Council held this morn- ing, it was decided that in consequence of the violation of the Treaty at Tientsin committed at Langson, France I should demand a war indemnity from China. This decision has already been telegraphed to M. Patenotre, now at Shanghai, and will be immediately despatched by the French Minister to the Chinese Government at Pekin. The amount of the indemnity demanded by the French Government is stated to be 250,000,000 francs (£lO,OOO 000). In to-day's sitting of the Chamber of Deputies, M. Jules 'Ferry announced that he had received the text of the Treaty of Tientsin' bearing the Chinese Imperial approval. The Chinese had broken the treaty under circumstances which made their proceedings amount to nothing less than an ambush. Reparation was therefore necessary. The French Government, after having relinquished the idea of demand' log an indemnity in May last,now felt bound to remind the Chinese Government that similar treaty violations cost dear or require reparation. The Premier said, in conclusion— "We await the reply of the Chinese Government, and, meanwhile, are in a position to make treaties respected. We shall act with moderation, but with a firmness that nothing will shake." (Applause.) _

Penrs, WEDNESDLY.—The—Com—mittee of the Senate ap- pointed to consider the bill for the revision of the Constitu- tion has elected M. Dauphin as President. This choice in- dicates that the Committee will not agree to the bill without serious guarantees that the revision will be limited.

The commanders of two Portugese war vessels which recently proceeded to the Congo River have annulled the treaties concluded by Mr. Stanley with the natives, by the terms of which the International African Association were granted sovereignty over territory declared to be neutral. GREAT FIRE IN MORAVIA.
VIENNA, TUESDAY.—A grext fire has occurred at Polan, in Moravia, destroying 31 farm houses. A child perished in the fl Imes. •

div.head: PIRACY IN THE BLACK SEA.
div.p: PIRACY IN THE BLACK SEA.

ST. PETERSBITRCH, SUNDAY.—The Odessa Messenger states that for some time past pirates have appeared off the Anatotian coast of the Black Sea. They have already plundered two sailing vessels, which were _proceeding from Batoum to Constantinople with valuable cargoes of silk goods. Resistance was out of the question, as the pirates, from fifteen to twenty in number, had fast cutters and were well armed. Their nationality is unknown. THE UNITED STATES. NEW YORK, MONDAY.—The schedules in bankruptcy of Messrs. Grant and Ward have been filed. The liabilities are set down at 16,792,000 dollars; the nominal assets at 27,139,000 dollars, and the actual assets at 67,000 dollars. The official assignee, in his report upon the affairs of the firm, condemns in the strongest terms the method pursued in business by the bankrupt house. A CRISIS AT PANAMA.

NEW YORK, WEDNESDLY. —Desp-a—tcresfrom Panama an- nounce that, notwithstanding the nomination of an inde- pendent President, Senor Cervera refuses to resign, and that in order to prevent disturbance be Aral be allowed to continue in office until his term expires, provided that he consents to make certain changes in his Cabinet and to meet the other demands of the Opposition. Perfect tranquility prevails. INDIA,
Bo:No.1Y, MONDAt—Great anxiety is felt with regard to the crop prospects in the Bombay Presidency owing to the want of rain.

THE HUNGARIAN ELECTIONS. TUESDAY.—The elections to the Hungarian Diet have now been concluded. 231 Liberals, 60 members of the Moderate Opposition, 77 Independents, 17 of the Anti- - ' party, 16 ..N.tionalists, and nine other members not or belonging to any particular party, have been re-
turned.
DISTURBANCES IN BELGIUM.

AT ( BELGIUM), WEDNESDAY.—The Clericals haying organised an electoral procession in this town last night were violently assaulted by a mob, which tore their flag to pieces, and subsequently wrecked the premises occupied by the local Catholic club. • CHILI AND PERU. LIMA, WEDNESDAY.—tieneral Iglesias and General Caceres have con:e to terms. The new Congress will meet on December 9, and the general election will take place in September and October. The candidates for the post ef President are Generals Iglesias, Cac,res, and Pierola. " WILLIAM THE stLENr." Darxr,TauttsneY.—The tercentenary celebration of the death of" William the &lent " commenced here to day by a s)lemn service in the church. The Prince's tomb was magnificently decorated with funeral wreaths, including one in silver offered by a deputation of Freemasons. The church was filled by a numerous congregation, all the miaisters and the principal civil and military authorities being pre. I sent.

BOUM AFRICA. CAPETOWN, THURSDAY.—Thabinchu, a place in the Orange Free State, has been attacked by a force of Basutos and Batalongs. The town was burned, and the Comman- dant of the place narrowly escaped. Troops have been des- patched from Bloemfoatein to the scene of the occurrence. THE DUKE OF HESSE'S MARRIAGE.

DARMSTADT, THURSDAY. The Suore—m—e—fri—bunal of Hesse yesterday delivered judgment in the case of the mor- ganatic marriage between the Grand Duke of Hesse and Madame de Kolomine. The court decreed separation.

div.p: GgNPARAL NEWS.

SUICIDAL MANIA AT Rllntimollem.—Fire persons were on Monday placed together in the dock at the Birmingham Police Court charged with attempting suicide. Henry Simms, a coal merchant, who tried to cut his throat through heavy losses in business, was handed over to his friends; as also were Mr. Fellows and Charles Devonport, a groom, both of whom took vermin killer, on Saturday night, as- signing shortness of work as the cause of the attempt upon their lives. Sarah Brown, a young married woman, was re- manded for attempting to drown herself at midnight in Peb- ble Mill Pool, having previously taken off all her clothes but her chemise.- The fourth man, William 13ayfield, who attempted tc cut his throat while intoxicated, was dis- charged. THE GERMAN EitrrEnon.—ROlttaNTlC STOILY.—The Ber- lin correspondent of the Standard telegraphs—The Emperor, who on Sunday quitted Ems for the present season, was en- thusiastically cheered en his way to the station by a numer- ous crowd that had assembled to witness his departure. The extraordinary freshness and vigour of the Sovereign, who is now in his 88th year, was the subject of general re- mark. During his stay in the charming watering-place on the Latin, the Emperor 'nide the acquaintance of a private gentleman, with whom he was frequently seen walking and conversing. Curiosity was natnrally excited as to the stranger who was theobjectof such'distinguished attention, and it has now transpired that be is a Belgian gentleman, M. Peer- block, of Verviers, who once saved the Emperor's life in the summer of 1854. His M ijesty, the then Prince of Prus- sia, was staying at Ostend, and one day, when bathing in the sea, fainted. M. Peerblock, who .was standing near, observed that there was something wrong, and he at once plunged into the water in his clothes, and brought the faint- ing Prince to shore. The name of his rescuer never came to the Emperor's knowledge till this summer, when M. Peerblock happened to be staving at Ems at the same time as His Majesty. THE DYNAMITE EXPLOSIONS.-110 repart of Colonel Majendie and Colonel Ford, her Miij esty's Inspectors of Explosives, on the exp,osions at St. James'e-square and Scotland Yard On May 30th, is issued. The Inspectors trace an undoubted connection between these and previous explo- sions, and attribute them to the same agency. The dyna- mite found on the same evening in Trafalgar-square 18 identical with that discovered at the railway stations last February—Atlas Powder,—and the Inspectors are enabled to state that all the dynamite was unquestionably manufac- tured at Repauno Factory, Philadelphia, which factory was mainly destroyed by an explosion last March, and, that the dynamite was obtained all at one time.—. 4 anti, er Discovery. —lt having come to the knowledge of Inspectors Wall and Vicars, officers at Hanley, under the Explosives Act, that a large quantity of explosives was secreted at Bucknall a village near Hanley, search was made on Monday even- ing, which resulted in the discovery of a considerable quan- tity of one of the most dangerous compounds of nitro- glycerine. The ovfner absconded, but a warrant has been issued. The Birmingham Watch Committee, on Tuesday, promoted Detective Steven s'.n from the Fourth to the Second Division, in recognition of the ability he had displayed in tracing the dynamitards. It was Stevenson who arrested Daly at Birkenhead, and the Chief Constable said he bad done hts duty remarkably well.

Twelve hundred jute workers at Barrow struck work on Thursday against a reduction of 5 per cent. The South Staffordshire miners have resolved to continue the strike until the old rate of wages is conceded. The late Duke of Albany's personal estate is sworn under £413,000. He leaves all his property to his beloved wife for her own use. • Two boyenemed Mills and Hutchings, living at Ealing. „ were drowned while bathing on Wednesday evening. in the t Grand Junction Canal, near Collets Wee.d. Hanwell. Earl Granville and Earl Sydney arrived at Windsor, on - Wednesday evening, from London, and proceeded to the , Castle, where their lordships dined with Her Majesty. At Hull, on Tuesday, a Jew named Abraham Goldstein was committed for trial for wilfully setting fire to his shop. from which a large quantity of goods had been removed. HER MAJESTY has c9nb.rreci 'the honour of Knighthood upon Professor Roscoe, of Owens College, in consideration of the services rendered by him in connection with the Technical Education Commission. At Carrick-on-Shannon assizes, on Thursday, Roger Tan- sey, charged with the murder of William Mahone, game- keeper, at Ballyforan. County Galway, was found guilty, and sentenced to be hanged. On Thursday morning a young man named Frank Sam- son, 21 years of age, was at work on some scaffolding at the New Birmingham Art Gallery when his foot slipped and he fell from a dazzling height into the street. When picked up he was dead. At °Ahem, on Thursday, a woman was committed for trial for the manslaughter of her grandchild, whose mother is a domestic servant in Liverpool. The medical evidence showed that the child, an infant 11 months old, had been neglected and had died of starvation. Mr William Liddell, a Belfast linen merchant, was shot at on Wednesday while driving from Lurgan railway station to his residence. He was not hit, but a number of pellets entered the face of his wife, who was with him. A farmer's son has been arrested on suspicion. A synod was held on Wednesday in the Roman Catholic church of St Mary's, Aberdeen. The proceedings were, of course, private, and the one fact of importance to be recor- ded is that until now no Roman Catholic synod has been held in the nerthern city since the Reformation. In his charge to the Grand Jury at the Lancaster Assizes on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Mathew said that in mskitig the new circuit arrangements the Judges had found themselves considerably hampered by the state of the law. The present arrangements were only provisional and temporary. The Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster has declined to appoint the Mayer of Ashton to the magisterial bench because he is a licensed victualler. Mr. Dodson shows that he is acting according to precedent; but at a meeting of the Town Council lost evening a hops was expressed that the matt.r would not be allowed to rest as it now stands. THE NEW ROLES OF LEGAL PROCEDURE.— 'the Press Association learns that the Lord Chancellor is about to ap- point a committee consisting of judges, Queen's counsel, members of the junior bar, and solicitorsla inquire into the operation of the new rules of procedure and the cause of the block in chambers and of the delay in the trial of wit- ness actions. ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A SOLDIER.-1 deliberate at- tempt te murder is reported from Sheerness. A gunner named Eastwood, who has been reduced from the rank of sergeant for drunkenness, went into the sergeants' mess on Wednesday night and shot Sergeant Hunter through the body. The assassin attributed his reduction•in reek to the reports sent in by former comrades. A FATAL LOCOMOTIVE EXPLOSION occurred at Balloch I Station, D,umbartonshire, on Saturday. A goods train was leaving the station when the boiler of the engine exploded, partially wrecking the station building. A gentleman named Jack, who was standing on the platform, was mostally in- jured, and the driver (Andrew Paterson) and stoker (John Dempster) were severely scalded. Several other persons • were injured less severely. BUTCHER IMPRISONED.—At Hyde, on Monday, Charles ' Blount, butcher, was charged by the inspector of the • Hyde Corporation with selling on September 17th 14 pieces of beef which were putrid and until for food. After - the meat was seized the prisoner absconded. and was are. prehended lest week in Macclesfield. In 1879 the plisoner was fined £l5 at Hyde for a sin...:lar cffence. The Bench said it was a bad case, and committed the prisoner for three months.

SHOCKING SCENE IN A INTExaoerag.—A. shocking scene was witnessed in Edmonds's (late Wombwell's) Menagerie, at Wrexham, on Monday. An attendant was employed cleaning out the lions' cage, and placing his right arm in- side the bars, one of the lions snapped at it and tore it off at the elbow. A panic at once ensued, and in the attempt to escape, a number of persous were more or less seriously in- jured. The injured attendant was taken to the infirmary, where he remains. AN ALLEGED FEMALE Sr y IN DUBLIN.— A few days since it was reported that a lady, described as prepossess- ing and with plenty of means, had been in Dublin as a Government spy, bat had returned to England after being victimised by certain parties from whom she had sought in- formation. United Ireland to-day devotes two columns to the movements of Ibis lady, who it appears is a MN. Tyler, and according to United Ireland was sent over by Mr. Jen- kinson as a decoy duck. THE REPRESENTATION OF PrrEntortonasr.—The Pete:. borough Liberal Association have replied to the Hon. H.l W • Fitzwilliam's refusal to submit his future candidature to that body. They say that Mr. Fitzwilliam's letter has grieved those who had hitherto been his political friends, and de- lighted those who were nominally his political opponents. His allegation that the Birmingham system rested upon the dictation of a section was erroneous, and that he does not understand liberty as they do. THE MEDICAL ecr.—Mr. Mandel's on Wednesday re- ceived a deputation from the Licentiates of the Apothecaries Society, who urged the desirability of providing in the Medical Amendment Act Amendment Bill for a representa- tion of the Society on the Medical Board. The Vice Presi- dent of the Council informed the deputation that the Go- vernment had never intended to omit the Sleety from the - bill, but that Lord Salisbury had in the House of L )rds in- "1 sisted upon the provision for repres.ntation being struck out. The claim of the apothecaries is to receive "careful consideration." ROYAL SOCIETY FOR THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO , ANIMALS.—Lord Aberdare presided at the 60-h annual meeting, held at St Jam's Hall, London. on Monday. There were also present—Lord and Lady Wolseley, Lord and Lady Aberdeen, B troneas Burdett-Coutts, and others. - The report showed that 4,618 convicdons were obtained last 't year, being an increase of 137 on the previous year. Baroness Burdett-Coutts distributed the medals presented by the Queen, and Lady Wolseler presented the prizes , offered by the society for Efilys written by teachers and ' scholars on cruelty to animals. DEMONSTRATION OF DCRRAM MINERS.—The annual demonstration of Durham miners took place on Saturday, on Durham Race-course, and was largely attended. Mr. John Morley, M. P., said the House of Lords would neither reform itself nor let the House of Commons do so. He ad- vocated agitation to ensure the preservation of the Franchise Bill in the same shape as it left the House of Commcns. Mr. Burt, M.P., and Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., also spoke, and resolutions were adopted expressing a hope that the Gov- ernment would not dissolve Parliament until the Franchise Bill has been put in operation, submitting proposals for restricting the output of coal, and advising amendments. of the existing Mines Act. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND THE RAILWAY GUARDS.— The Prince of Wales presided at the ninth triennial festival of . the Railway Guards' Universal Friendly Society at Willis's Booms, London, on Saturday. and spoke on the ad- vantages accruing to railway servants by participation in the benefits offered by such societies. In responding to the toast of his health, his Royal Highness took the opportunity on that, the first public occasion on which he had presided since the death of the Duke of Albany, to express in the er name of the Queen and all the members of the Royal Family their thanks for the kind sympathy which bad been Omen to them in the sorrow they bad experienced, tie felt sure in the mortal life which was before him that to receive 4i' sympathy in what was sad and support in what was agree- •. able would do much to help him through the duties of life which it might be his lot to perform. THE BISHOP Or PETERBOROUGH AND THE CIERTCAL SCANDALS.—With the view of preventing the sc4ndals which have recently occurred in Preston, Manchester, Sheffield, and elsewhere, the Bishop of Peterborough has issued circu- lar letters to the beneficed clergy and churchwardens. He reminds them of the language of the 50th and 52nd Canons, and then states that "every incumbent engaging for more than one Sunday the temporary services of a clergymr not having the Bishop's license or permission to officiate in the diocese, is required to signify the name of such :clergyman, and his reference to the Bishop before permitting him to I officiate any longer." The same duty is saddled upon the churchwardens during any vacancy in the benefice. • It is hoped that by these p-ecautions clergymen who have proved themselves unfit for the ministry, and impostors, wilt be prevented from occupying the pulpit—still leas unlawfully solemnising marriages. Tun STORids• ' —Lo,s or Lim.—Thunderstorms, cauairg losssof life and destruction of property, are reported frOm : various parts of the country. On Sunday, Holy Trinity Church, Walton Breck, Liverpool, was struck by lightning, causing considerable panic, which brought the service to an abrupt conclusion. A woman was killed by the lightning in the Canterbury district, and a crofter met his death in the same way at Fortwilliam. On Wednesday afternoon a thunderstorm of great violence passed over many parts of the country. At Royton, near Oldham, a hut in which some navvies bad taken shelter was struck by lightning and two of the men were killed on the spot and three others rendered for a time unconscious. A colliery engine driver at Both- well was killed by lightning, and two of his fellow-workmen were injured. Several CMS are reported in which cattle perished, and it is feared that the damage to the hay ere? will prove to be very serious. DROWNING CASES —EIGHT LIVS.S 'WM—Jaws Watson, joiner, aged 19, of Eaglesham, was drowned at that Plane on Sunday whilst bathing. George Mills, 13, Was drowned .in the Forth and Clyde Canal on Sunday night. Be dived and never rose again. A first year's medical student of Edin- burgh, named Frank Merivaleos hen bathing in Loch Lomond. On Saturday became seized with mum), and was drowned, Two boys named JaS. Young, aged 5, and Dant,' Morrison, aged 12, bathed out of their depth near Eledn on Sunnily. and when rescued life was extinct. Wm Qu'nn, a tail7r, .?40 years old, of Hankier-streot. Glasgow, lo,t his life while bathing near Row Poict on Saturday. A young man named William Jotin Longridge, who had gone with a Sunday fCIIOOI excursion party in connection with the Donegal Pres- Lyterian Church, Belfast.to Antrim Castle, the seatmf Lord hlassereene, was drowned on Saturday while bathing in Lough Neagh. In most cases companions of the deceased tried to save them.

CONSTABLES AND FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.—An in- stance of the value of constables receiving,instruction ill first aid to the injured was demonstrated in St. Helens, on Saturday night. A man named Robert Rimmer, residing at 41, Glover-street, whilst in drink, struck a window with his fist, and, breaking it, cut the main artery of his wrist. Police constables Simpson and Temporal, who were near, and who had been members of the St. John's Ambulance Asso- ciation Class,lound up the arm of the man and stopped the bleeding. On the arrival of a surgeon the constables were warmly complimented upon their efficiency, they having probably saved the man's life. OUTRAGEOUS ASSAULT CH A SCHOOLMISTRESS AT RAIN. 'ORD.—Before Mr. William Pilkington and Dr. Twyford, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday forenoon, Alice Wilkinson, of Rainford, was summoned for assaulting Mary Phillips, head mistress of the girls' school at the Rainford National Schools, on the 27th ult.—Mr J. 0. Swift appeared for the complainant ; and the defendant, who was unrepre- sented, pleaded guilty.—Mr Swift stated that the defendant, Mrs. Wilkinson, was the mother of a girl named Hannah Wilkinson, who up to the 27th of June was one of the scholars at the Rainford School% On that day Miss Phil- lips had occasion to correct the girl, and, from the evidence he had, she corrected her in a proper manner. The girl was stupid, and doggedly refused to answer the questions put to her, and Miss Phillips accordingly sent a note to Mrs. Wil- kinson asking her to come to the school and talk the matter over. About half-past one o'clock Miss Philips, on return- ing to the school, saw Mrs. Wilkinson with her girl. Miss Phillips told her that the girl had been stupid, and Mrs. Wilkinson said "I won't have my child beaten." Miss Phillips said she had not beaten her improperly, but the mother said that in the previous week her child's ears were bleeding, whereupon Miss Phillips said she ilid not do that. At that moment a little girl asked Miss Phillips to be let off for the day, and Miss Phillips turned round to speak to her, when without any warning or provocation the defendant struck Miss Phillips two violent blows in the face with her fist. Mies Phillips was stunned and staggered a little, and the defendant snatched Miss Phillips's umbrella, and with the handle struck her several violent blows. The complain- ant was unable to go into the echo 1 in the afternoon, but went to the house of the Rev. J. Barnacle, where her head was bathed. She afterwards went to see Dr. Milner, who found that the left side of the head was very much woollen, as well as the left side of the face and the left eye. For two or three days Miss Phillips suffered considerably from the shock and blows she received. There had'been a little difficulty about the Rainford schools, and a week or two ago at Prescot, Miss Phillips was a witness in a case where a little girl bad had her ears boxed. That might have caused some feeling in the village, but if the defendant's child had been chastised, Mrs Wilkinson had her proper remedy.—Mr Pilkington : This is not the same girl ?—Mr. Swift replied that it was not. The assault was a very serious one and ought to be dealt with more severely than common assaults were.—Miss Mary Phillips was then called and corroborated Mr Swift's statement. In reply to Mr Swift, witness said she did not ilium the girl.—Mrs klarritt deposed that she saw the assault com- mitted. She did not see Miss Phillips do anything to Mrs Wilkinson.—The Chairman said the Bench thought the condact of the defendant had been outrageous to society in general and from the silly way in which she seemed to treat it they were led to think she was possessed of only half her senses. Anyway, they must protect parties who were in authority like schoolmistresses, and the defendant would be fined £1 and costa, 19s tld, Of 21 days imprison- ment.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 12, 1884.

THE Tory Peers would seem to be deter. mined to " die game," for they have rejected the Franchise Bill, after two nights of debate, by a majority of 59. It is true that Lord SALISBURY'S following is not so large as was expected, and it is lust possible that it may melt away in the heat of the contest which will undoubtedly ensue, when, after a an- tumn session, the Bill is, for the second time, sent up to the House of Lords for acceVance or rejection. What the Tories want is a dis- solution upon the present register, but al- though they have not had the hardihood openly to take their stand upon this ground, the desire has been made manifest in the course of the debate. Lord CAIRNS said they wished to appeal to the country, and to be judged by the country—an echo of what Lord SALISBURY had been dinning in our ears for some time past. The proposal to appeal, as Lord GRANVILLE observed, is a large thing behind an amendment, and it might be asked. What in the world has it got to do with it? Lord CAIRNS'S amendment was to reject the Bill because it did not include Redistribution —not because it was deemed desirable to ap- peal to the country on the question of an ex- tension of the Franchise. The latter would have been a clear and distinct issue, but the House of Lords has not dared to face it, preferring to hide itself behind the flimsy screen of a demand for Redistribution—a de- mand which, we do not hesitate to say, is utterly hollow, for if there is one thing which the Peers fear more than household suffrage, it is a fair redistribution of seats. Some time back Lord SALISBURY did contend, with the reckless audacity what characterises him, that there was no question of the extension of the Franchise before the country at the last Gen- eral Election, and that there ought therefore to be an appeal to the people. It was asserted again and again that no reference was made to the subject during the Midlothian cam- , paign ; but Lord ROSEBERRY stopped Lord SALISBURY'S mouth on this topic on Tuesday by the followinz quotation from one of Mr. GLADsToNE's speeches :—" It was almost impossible to say anything new about the county suffrage, but he hoped and believed it would form one of the earliest measures which the new Government would present to Parliament." ,There was nothing new to say, but for all that, barring Mr. GOSCHEN, we venture to assert that not a single Liberal was returned to St. Stephen's in 1880 except on the understanding that he would vote for an assimilation of the borough and county franchise. And yet it is suggested that on this issue there should be an appeal to the judgment of the country. Be it so ; the Lords will get an indignant answer, and may find that they have fallen into the pit which they , had dug for another.
—Notwithstanding the repeated statement of the Government that it was impossible to carry a Bill through Parliament in one ses-

Ision including an extension of the Franchise land Redistribution—a statement the truth of which is obvious to those who have paid any attention to Parliamentary affairs—the Opposition in the Lords, as in the Commons, have feigned to disbelieve the assertion, and practically discredited the distinct pledge of the Cabinet that next session would be de- voted to Redistribution. But the nation .is

not to be deluded by such tactics, for, as the Earl of JERSEY confessed—and he is a Con- servative—the course taken by Lord CAIRNS was "the only one which would prevent a Redistribution Bill being brought up." What a satire upon the Opposition I They are so eager for a big load of Reform that because

M. GLADSTONE puts it on two waggons knowing one cannot carry it—they block the way and overturn the load ! Lord SALIS- BURY talks of the " absolute certainty of being able to carry a Franchise and Redis- tribution Bill through in one session, and yet in the same speech, when it suits his purpose to point the moral of the danger of delay, he asks—" Have they (the Gc.ve nmen) the power to fulfil the promise which they make? We all know that they have not had much power over their procedure for the last four years." If this is not a case of eating one's own words, there never was such a thing. His lordship has essayed the impossible task of trying to go up two streets at one time, and, as others have done before him, he has made himself ridiculous in the attempt. He would taunt the Government for not carrying both measures through this session, and he would-scoff the hope of carrying one of them through next session. He has been too eager, and he has let the cat out of the bag ' by confessing the difficulty of the situation. Well, he has his way for the present, but what of the fixture—the immediate future? As far as we can divine the situation it comes to this: If the Three Millions who are en- franchised, and the Two Millions who are looking to the Reform Bill for an acknow- ledgment of their birthright, are content to be ridden over roughshod by haughty barons as in the bad days of old, the Lords will re- peat the performance of Tuesday night, and we shall have an election early next year, with, possibly, a Tory Government as the re- sult. But if on the other hand the Five Mil- lions—or the bulk of them —arise in their might and majesty, they will tell the startled Lords that the day of reckoning with them has at last come; that they have completed the cycle of their existence as an hereditary and irresponsible body of Obstructionists; and that, having themselves deliberately pro- voked a conflict for which they are wholly unequal, the only terms of peace are a radi- cal Reform Bill and a radical Reform of the , House of Lords.

THE working of the new Bankruptcy Act, involving, as it does, issues so numerous and far-reaching, has not unnaturally excited a considerable amount of attention. It came into operation with the present year, and before January was out it was noted that the percentage of bankruptcies was much smaller than usual. The reason for this, as stated by those who were sceptical as to the working of the Act, was that, in dread of its stringent provisions, a large number of shaky tradesmen "scheduled," before the year was out, under the old law. But the falling off has been con- tinuous up to the present moment, and by way of further explanation we have been told that the Act was being dodged by means of private arrangements with creditors which did not come within its scope ; the failures, it was said, were as numerousiand the Act it- self was a failure in that neither debtors nor creditors cared to resort to it. It was easy, of course, to make these assertions in the ab- sence of comprehensive data, and impossible to confute them; but a new light has just been thrown upon the subject by the publication of a preliminary report of the Inspector-General in Bankruptcy, Mr. JOHN SMITH, who gives the results of the operation of the new Act for the first three months. It may be at once admitted that it would not be wise to tie our- selves to conclusions obtained upon this limi- ted experience, but there is no reason why we should not accept them as far as they go; and it must be gratifying to Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN that they are highly favourable to his handiwork. With regard to the number of bankruptcies, it appears that the average of the last five years has been just over ro,ooo per year; but under the new Act, if-the present rate is maintained, there will not be more than 3,000 for the year. It is likely that there will be an increase upon this, but between 3,000 and ro,ooo there is a great gulf. The special point of interest in the matter is how far this extraordinary reduc- tion has been brought about through an in- crease of private arrangements that is whether with the falling of one scale there is a proportionate rise in another. As to this there is necessarily a lack of evidence cover- ing the whole sphere of operations, for pri- vate arrangements are to a large extent kept private. Still some figures are given by way of a test, and they go to show that the increase in Private arrangements is, compara- tively speaking, very small. A certain Grocers Association referred to has an ac-

count of 99 private arrangements made dur- ing the first three months of 1883 ; while for the corresponding period of the present year, the number is 6—an increase of r 7 only. The Manchester Trade Protection Association furnishes a return which is equally suggestive. During four months of the presentrtpar their agents attended 39 meetings of creartors, but for the same period of last year they were pre- sent at no fewer than tor meetings. These figures include both private and public ar- rangements; they are therefore complete as a means of comparison, and they indicate what is suggested by the total returns, namely, that bankruptcy proceedings have been reduced by more than one-half. This is surely something in favour of the new Act. But to turn to another feature; where meet- ings are being held the creditors are re- ceiving more money than formerly. Under the old Act not more than three debtors in the hundred paid above ros. in the pound; now eight times the number, or 25 per cent., reach that figure. -There is a similar result to report as to the lower ranges of figures so that taking the Act all round—the reduc- tion it is effecting in the number of bankrup- tcies, the lessened cost of proceedings, and the increased return from compositions with creditors—it must be pronounced, up to the present, to be a triumph of legislation.

The Mass Meeting of the Liberal party ill Warrington, which is to be held in the IPublic Hall, Rylands street, on Wednesday evening next, promises to be highly success- ful. There has, since the meeting was announced, been an unusual demand for tickets, the great body of the electors being "on the tiptoe of expectaticn " t, see and hear Mr. W. Crosfield, T. P., the new Liberal candidate for the borough. The interest

in the demonstration has now bee'n inten- sified by the political crisis in the country, Produced by the suicidal action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill ; and it is not unlikely that the attendance will be SO crowded as to necessitate an overflow meeting. After the chairman (Mr. S. Rigby, J. F.), has explained the objects of the .gathering, Mr. W. Crosfield will be called upon to address the meeting, following upon which a resolution will Will be submitted adopting him as the Liberal candidate and pledging those present to help to secure his return to Parliament at the next general election. The second reso- lution will have reference to the present poli- tical crisis; it will express confidence in the Government, and a determination to render the Ministry every, assistance in placing the Franchise Bill upon the statute book. Lord DALHOUSIE will be asked to respond to this resolution, and, as he is a member of the Ministry, we need hardly say that his speech at this juncture in the affairs of the nation will be listened to with uncommon interest.

THE Env. S. LOCKWOOD 07 HALTON has been gazetted to the chaplaincy of the Earl of Chester's Riles, and was in camp on Thursday. THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN. —At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday. before Mr. JAS. Handley. Michael Murphy, captain of the schooner Eclipse, surrended to his bail on a charge of having, on the 17th of May, done grievous bodily harm towards Wm. Stringer, a labourer, living in Portland-street. A letter was read from Mr. Edmondson, solicitor, Fleetwood, - asking for an ad- fournment of the case, as he was suffering from a cold and could not attend. The prisoner was reminded until Monday, bail being allowed as usual. • UNITED METHODIST FREE CHUHCH SUNDAY SCHOOL AT WIDNES.—The children attending this school bad their annual treat on Saturday last. To the number of 200 they assembled in the schoolroom at 2 o'clock, and headed by the Mill-brow brass baud, Runcorn, marched in processional order to the Central station, whence they were rapidly con- veyed to Hough Green. Here, in a field kindly lent by Mr Joseph Longton, the time passed pleasantly.until evening. During the afternoon the childrey were supplied with a good tea, and about 150 friends, wfir had put in an appear- ance, also sat dawn to tea. Rollason, Walter Calland, John Rigby, Patrick McQuire, and Michael Metier were each fined 5s and costs for drunk- enness.—For i similar offence Mary McCafferty was fined 7s 64 and costs; while Eliza McDermott and Sarah Ann Taylor, who had been frequently before the Bench, were each sentenced to a month's hard labour.—ln default of finding sureties to keep the peace, Jas. Cowley and Bridget O'Toole were each sent to gaol for 14 days. PAWNBROKERS' LICENSES AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. F. Gossage and Mr. H. Oaskell, janr., at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, Mr. J B. Testimonials as ta his character were put in and proved, and the applicant was placed in the box and stated that be had for the past twenty years resided at Wigan, where be beld an, outdoor beer license. He owned property there.—The application was granted. NEW TEMPERANCE Mostar; HALL FOR WiDszs.--From an announcement in our advertising columns it will be seen that to-day the memorial stones of a Temperance Mission Hall will be laid- The building, which will occupy a site in Ifibbert-street, Widnes-road, will be the property of the members of the Hope of Appleton Lodge, through whose efforts it is being erected. The large room will accommo- date 250 persons, and while being specially the head quar- ters of the lodge, it will be available for meetings of a re- ligious and philanthropic character. The coet is estimated at £250, and towards this stun the lodge expects to raise £lOO. depending for the rest upon the generosity of the public. Mt F H (image, J,E, and Mr T S Timmis have each contributed £lO towards !tie fund._

ROBBERY FROM Wernties Pawn SHOP.—Mary of 17, Walmsley-street, Widnes, was brought up at Widnes Police'Court, on Satitrday, charged with stealing a shawl, value 6s 6.1, the property. of Mr. Neil, pawnbroker, Ann- street. The shawl was safe in the shop at half-past four on the2Blh ult, but half an hour afterwards Mr. Neil discovered Peet it had been rcrnoyod, and geve 111 re. jatneeon, pawn- broker, a description of. the article. On Wednesday, the 2nci ins; the prisoner went to Mrs. Jameson's and offered a shawl in pledge for 58. As it answed the description given Mrs. Jameson sent for Mr. Neil, but in the meantime the prisoner ran away, leaving the shawl behind. She was subsequently apprehended by P.O Snowdon, at St. Helens, and was now sentenced to a month's hard labour. A LIVELY YOUNG WIDNES APPRENTICE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, OR Wednesday, William Bolton, 15 years of age, was brought up under an adjourned summons charged with committing a breach of his apprenticeship in- dentures with John Pye, tool maker, Widnes-road. It ap- peared that during the past five weeks the defendant had absented himself for eleven days, and on several occasions he had stayed out all night. One night, inetead of going to sleep at his maeter'e house, he broke int, the woriishoa and slept there. The Complainant claimed Li 2s damages, but stated his actual lose was much greater.—The defendant, who had nothing whatever to say in extenuation of his con- duct, was ordered to pay the amount claimed and fulfil his contract, and he was informed that otherwise he would have to go to gaol. A &mom; PAttnelgoNittni.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions,- on Monday, John Oultram, a boatman, was charged with having, on the 27th June, committed a breach of the peace. Dr. McDougall Said about seven o'clock on the Sunday morning in question he was aroused by a loud noise In the neighbourhood. The disturbance continued for about half an hoar, the noise becoming gradually louder and louder, a good deal of obscene and unpleasant language being used. , Looking through the window he saw the defendant fighting with a female in Lock-street. He saw the defendant strike the woman twice. There were a good many people in the neigh- bourhood. Every Saturday night from twelve till two there was an incessant brawling going on in the neighbourhood between loose characters who converted the streets into a pandemonium. Whenever they saw an officer coming they ran away. "They were a perfect nuisance. Defendafit was bound over to keep the peace. A YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNEM.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Peter O'Toole, 15 years of age, was charged with having, on the 2nd July, stolen a coat, value 16s, the property of James Henry.—Complainant said he was a plumber, and resided at 34, Market-street, Widnes. The coat produced was his property. He saw it safe in the lobby of his house on the day mentioned.—Annie Jameson said I she was a pawnbroker carrying on business in Anne-street West. On the 2nd inst. the prisoner pledged the coat at her shop for Sc. He said his mother had sent him.—The prisoner was then charged with having on the let inst. stolen la coat worth 15s belonging to James Curley,a labourer resid- ing at 30, Major Cross street. The coat was miseed from the lobby of the house on the Illnd July, and on the same day the prisoner pledged it at Syred's pawnshop for 2s 6d. He was apprehended by P.C. McDonald, and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour on each charge. SCANDALOUS INJURY TO CROPS AT RtYNCOßN.—Before Mr. Josephetiandley. at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, ' Elizabeth Houghton, a woman who tramps about the country, was charged with having on the previous day stolen She. of potatoes, value 3d, which were growing in a Reid at Weston Point, belonging to Thomas Geffs, farmer. I —The prisener pleaded not guilty. It seemed that on the previous afternoon a young man named Martin Galligan, who lives in Cooper-street, was walking along Percival's- lane when he Raw the prisoner and a man enter Mr. Get's' field. The man plucked up seyeral roots of petatoes, plac- ing the vegetables into the woman's apron. Gall igan inlor- med P.C. Finney of the occurrence, and that officer followed the thieves. The man, however, managesd to escape, bet the 1 woman wee captured, and placed in the lockups.—The pri- soner alleged that her husband purchased the potatoes at the I Market and gave them to leer.—Mr. Gale was called and I said that his fields had been frequently robbed of potatoes; I and especially in the night-time daring the past month. Not ;long ago three square roods of roots of potatoes were pulled up although there were no potatoes at the end. Theelamage done was scandalous—His Worship fined the prisoner 20s including costs, but as she failed to-pay she was committed to gaol for 14 days. FATALITY ON TRH RAILWAY AT WIDNES.—A. fatal accident occurred at the Lagedele level crossing on Wed- nesday night to a man named John Langford, 67 years of age. Langford was a farm labourer, and lived at Mersey View, Hale Emile. For a conside4le period he'had been out of employment, and occasionally he was strange in his mind. It was his custom to go to Widnes once a week to get shaved, and in consequenee of his manner on Wednes- day his wife did not want him to go, but he was very determined and went. About six o'clock on Wednesday evening Langford was seen attempting to get upon the rail- way at Ann-street crossing, and thei signalman, John Davies, went to him and asked him where he wanted to go. Langford appeared to be deaf, and made no reply, so Davies placed Wm in the street. Two hours later Langford was again at the crossing and after examining the gate closely walked down Earle-street in the direction of the Gas Works. At ten minutes past nine Lengford wile OR the 'London and North-Western 'Railway near the Lngsdale-road crossing, walking clear of the rails towards the signal box. A geode ' train was on its way from Widnes to Tebay, and Ralph Cleworch, the signalman, saw Longford walk across the metals in a sloping direction. He was caught right in front of the engine, knocked down, and killed. Mr. B:Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Stanley Arms on Thursday afternoon, and evidence in accordance with these facts having been given, and it also having been proved that the deceased was a trespasser, the jury returned a verdict of accidental death. Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH. WIDNEC: v...IENEROUS DONLTIONS. —We extract the following from the " Pariah Messenger :" —The new church of St. Paul. The opening day is drawing very near. The seats are nearly all in position, and a very natural anxiety is felt about the chancel furniture, which is not provided for in the contracts. We have to acknow- ledge the gift of a handsome Communion rail from Mr. T. Sutton Timm's, Esq , and the promise through him from Mrs. Nicene of an eagle lectern in oak. The want el a pulpit has, however, long been a problem difficult to face, and the cost of one in harmony with the church could be no light matter, and seemed utterly beyond our reach, This problem, then, has just received a most happy solution. Moe Deacon, IL Wade Deacon. Esq., and Allan 'Deacon, Erg, have most generously undertaken to provide one. Once more, the beautiful carved font, standing already in its place, is the offering of G. t7'ilkington. Esq., LP. The want of a wall is ever pressing upon us. What maet soon be the aspect of the simple but ecclesiastical exterior here in Widnes, without even the slightest fence? 'Tie enough to make the rudest sorrowful • hat the cost Of a wall to sur- round that acre is between £5OO and £6OO, and that mak-s the most pitiful atone -dumb; for have we not yet £14.00 to raise for contracts nearly completed? How happy, therefore, mast we be to report that once more our good friend, T. Sutton Timmie, Eerie has come to our relief,— yea, rather to the relief of God's hew, by the preventing of its imminent external desecrating —he has promised to pay for the building of a wall himself. Truly a noble of- fering. In the light of it we must work with redoubled vigour to raise the sum before named, and then? Why then for the other surroundings. The.se donors, Messre. Sutton Timmia, Wade Deacon, and G. Filkington, are all Widnes enanutacturers, and members of the Church Build- ing Committee. Another member of that Committee has promised help in furniture. Vet wanted : Communion plate, holy table, and cloth for same, chancel•chaZrs, service books, hymn books, and prayer books (Hymnal Companion) for choir and body of churih, and vestry furniture, Who will help us to these?
