SUDDEN DRATII OF A CHILE AT WIDNIS.—The police report the sudden death of Margaret Dunn, six months old, daughter of John Dunn, chemical labourer, living at 11,, Caroline-street, Widnes. The infant had been healthy from birth, but was suddenly taken ill on Thuredly morn- ing, and at one o'clock had a fit. She was taken to Dr. O'Keeffe's surgery, but the doctor was absent from borne and the child was taken home again. The doctor saw the child, however, at sefen p.m., when he gave directions for its treatment. The child continued to'have fits until half-past four yesterday morning, when she succumbed. There is no suspicion of foul play, but Dr. O'Keeffe refused to certify as to the cause of death, and the coroner has been acquainted with the circumstances. WARRINGTON AMALRAMATED /SOCIETY OF OPERATIVE BAICIDIS.—The anniversary ef this Society was celebrated on Saturday last, when 41 members, of whom 23 hailed from Runcorn, journeyed to Overton in waggonnettes. They arrived at the Ball's Head Inn about four o'clock, and here, having replenished the inner man with a substan- dal meal, a meeting Was held under the presidency of Mr. Burroughs. Mr. Jenkins, of Manchester, Secretary to the Society, delivered an excellent speech, which was followed by an interesting presentation. The Chairman, on behalf of the Society, handed to Mr. William Houghton, of Run- corn, a handsome emblem as a token of the respect and es- teem in which he is held by the members. Mr. Houghton is about to leave the Warrington branch. Subsequent to these proceedings, the members viewed the natural beauties of the locality, and retarning to the Inn, spent the evening in a convival manner, arriving home safely about eleven o'clock. A Row me GRINROD Sai.RE Ittnicoma.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Camp- bell and Mr. G. L. Davies, Rebecca Baxley, a woman with a child in her arms, was summoned on a charge of assaulting Alice Newton, a married woman living in Grinrod Square, on the 30;11 Jane. The complainant said that the defendant's husband beat thu, defendant, and she fled into complainant's I house. She was just then removing a pan of boiling water from the fire, and the defendant caused the water to go upon the loor, and it was 'a wonder they were 'not all scalded. The defendant challenged her out to fight, and threatened that if she did not come out she would break all the windows in the house. At that time her (the complainant's) husband came in, and than went for a policeman, whereupon the de- , fendant entered the house, seized her by the hair, and I punched her in the eye. She used her behind the door worse than a dog.—The defendant alleged that the CORI. plainant's husband was continually acting indecently toa wards her. On the day in question the complainant threw some boiling water upon her, and struck her before she retaliated.—Mary Jones, a married woman, corroborated.--. The Bench imposed a penalty of 53 and costs lls 63. THE MOTHER-IN-LAW AGAIN: A WIDNES CASE —ISM Livingstone, a strapping young fellow, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, charged with as- saulting George and Hannah Newbrooke.—Mr J W Knowles defended.—lt was alleged that on the sth inst. Newbrooke, who is a printer by trade was standing in the doorway of his house, when the defendant came up to him and struck him twice on the face with his fist. He then pulled his coat off and attacked Newbrooke again, a struggle taking place on the ground. The defendant also knocked down Newbrooke's wife, who is a delicate person. In cross- examination by Mr Knowles, Newbrooke admitted that the woman was not his wife, but his housekeeper. They had lived Webster, d shearaane inniaanstl wife for 13 years. Her real name w the defendant's mother-in-law. —John Kinsey deposed to seeing the defendant commit the assaults; arld for the defence Mr. Knowles pointed out / that the elefendant was a retipeci.e.f,; Man ra...622,4"iirea in Widnes far 17 years. His mother-in-law by her conduct With Newbrooke had disgraced both him and his wife, and the two complainants had also set about scandalous reports about the defendants, and also his wife's character. He contended that the assaults were merely a mutual scums between the parties.—The Bench imposed a fine of 103 and costs in each case; in default of payment defendant to go to gaol for 14 days. Tyra PROPOSED FRANCHISE DEMONSTRATION AT RUN- ooltie,—There is every prospect that the demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill which last week we were en- abled to intimate was under considstation, writ ben -me an accomplished fact. The 1.4 t: of commencing an agitation in Runcorn, and showing the "Upper House" that the calm attitude of the industrial classes on this question was not one of apathy, but quiet determination originated with one of the " unenfranchised millions" who has on previous occasions by his example endeavoured to inculcate habits of thrift and a desire for knowledge in his fellow working- men. At his instigation a representative committee of working-men were called together, and they are making the arrangements for the demonstration in conjunction with the Liberal committee. The programme includes a monstre procession through the streets of the town, accompanied by three bands of music whose services have been proffered, to conclude with a mass meeting on Runcorn Rill. Next Saturday afternoon, the Nth July, is the time fixed upon. Mr. Leadam, one of the candidates for Mid-Cheshire, has already consented to deliver an address, audit is confidently expected that Mr. T. Rigby, of Sutton, wl-o is also contesting Mid-Cheshire at the next election ; Mr. Tomkinson and Mr. Duncan, Liberal candidates for West Cheshire. Mr. T. Snape and other prominent politicians will be present, and speak to the assembled thousands. Should only the unen- franchised classes in Runcorn take part in the demonstra- tion it would be of an imposing description, because had the Franchise Bill succeeded in passing the House of Lords, the number of electots in the town would have been in- creased from 850 to considerably over 3,000. It is earnestly hoped, however, that the working-men who wish for votes, and even those who are in possession of the benefits of the Franchise will come from the surrounding districts.—Wid- nes, St. Helens, Warrington, Earlestown, Zee., and take part in the proceedings.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board Offices, Allforde Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon , last. There were present Messrs. Gossage (chairman), I Wright, Midwood, Ciaskell, Manley, Pankhurst, Forster, Dutton, Handley, Houghton, J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higgin. son (surveyor), W. W. Copland (resident engineer), T. Carr (gas engineer), and J. Dickson (nuisance inspector.) I A Comaxeriox.—On the minutes of the previous Board meeting coming up for confirmation Mr. Forster ',Ad he wished to correct a statement which had been made at the , last meeting to the effect that he in his position of chair- man of the Gas and Water Committee had sent a letter to each member of the committee asking that the minutes might be altered.—The Chairman: Bo you wish through the Press to deny some statement whkh has been made or is said to have been made 11—Mr. Forster: Yes, I do not wish to carry it farther, but I with the Press to record my denial. —Mr. Mldwood said he did net quite understand Mr. Forster's request. If he said that 801110 member of that Board made a misrepresentation, then he (Mr. Midwaod) thought Mr. Forster was wrong. He did net know to whom Mr. Forster was referring, but he did knew he was one of the parties in connection with the matter.—The Chairman said he must call attention to the fact that what Mr. Forster complained of did not appear, on the agenda paper nor was it in the minutes. Mr. Forster complained of something that was in the public prints which was not correct, inasmuch as he did not write a certain letter which he was said to have written. —Mr Sadler: Doer he make any charge against any mem- ber of this Board for eayirg so ?—The Chairman: I den't this'll he has mentioned any name.—Mr Midwood : I am prepared to prove that he -sent a letter.—Mr Forater said he did net say that he had not sent a letter; what he said was that he had not Bent a letter for the purpoea represented in the public prese.—The Chairrrian said Mr Forster had better read what he complained of.—Mr lForster then read the ex- tract he referred to and said that what was stated in it was not correct.—Mr Gaskell submitted that the discussion was not in order. The business was simply the confirmation of the minutes, and the question was were the minutes a cor- rect record of what took place at the previous meeting.—, Tne Chairman thought that Mr Gaekell was quite right, and, he thought he could not hear the matter further as it did not appear in the minstes at all.—The minutes were then con., firmed and the subject dropped. Amman TAMPERING WITH %Pmts.—The following letter ; was read :—Sir,—At a meeting of the Widnes Owners' and Occupiers' Association, held ,on the 26th April lact, it was alleged that persons had tampered with voting papers at the last election of-members of your Board, whereupon it was resolved: *That as this is a constantly recurring evil, it is advisable to prosecute -such persons with a view to , checking the practice in future. The undersigned 1 were appointed to carry out this resolution, and upon refer- ence to the Public Health Act of 1875 we find that the Local Boardis empowered toprosecute, and as this is a matter that affects the town generally, we venture to suggest that your Board ,being the proper body, should take action in this matter. We may add -that we have such evidence against several persons as will in our opinion prove sufficiently con- clusive to ensure convictions, and we are prepared to lay it before you upon hearing from you that you have decided to take action. Kindly being this matter before the Board at your early convenience, and oblige, yours obediently, FRANC GASHEIL and JOHN W. Waanntrai.—ln answer to the chair- man, the ,Clerk said the Board could take action if they liked in that matter; or any aggrieved person could take action as well as the Beard.—After a short silence the Chairman said he was willing to hear any member of the Board who had anything to say on that subject.—Mr. Wright said his firm conviction was that it was a case that would cut both ways, and he thcught the less said about it the better. Of course as far as he was concerned, he had never been a party to such things, but he should , be glad to see the party, whether in local matters or par- I tnamentary matters that was altogether free from such practises. lie moved that the letter be allowed to lie on the table.—Mr. Sadler seconded this proposal.—Mr. (Laken said he knew very little about that matter, but he thought that in cases if that bind that Board ought certainly to take action to stop the abuse. They bad seen the same thing year after year, and no action had been taken. The Asso- ciation of Local Boards had bad the matter under considera- tion, and they had seen the importance of it and were now doing their best to get a Ballot Act passed. It would prob- ably be some years before that could be done, and until a a Ballot Act was passed they should have to go on with the present iniquitous system of voting. Ile thought that Beard ought to take some steps to ensure that tampering with voting papers and other illegal proceedings be put an end to. He should propose that the matter be referred to the General Purposes Committee that they might hear the evidence for and against, and get as many cases as they could; and if they found cases to prosecute, let thetn prosecute and not let the matter drop. He (Mr. Giskell) thought the com- mittee ought at any rate to hear the evidence and bring it before that Board.—Mr. Forster seconded Mr- Gaskell'it

amendment, as he thought something ought to be done with regard to that matter.—On Mr. Gaskell's amendment being put to the meeting there voted for it Messrs. Gaskell; Fors- ter, Handley, and Pankhuret ; for Mr. Wright's motion there voted Messrs. Wright, Sadler, Mid wood, Motley, and Dut- ton. Mr. Houghton did not vote. The motion that the letter lie on the table was consequently declared carried. Tax NEW °Moss: A Cowersaner.—it letter was read from Mr. Shelmerdine, architect, Liverpool, referring to the award of prizes for the most suitable plan of new Board offices. He (Mr. Sheluterdine) had seen from the news- paper& that considerable alterations had bad to be made le Messrs. F. and G. Holmes' plan to make them euit their requirements, thus increasing the Cost of the building. In awarding the prize after these alterations he thought the Board bad acted in an exceedingly unfair Manner, inasmuch as the instructions issued had limited the cost of the build- ing, and it was stated that anyone exceeding this cost would be disqualified. Mr. Shelrnerdine therefore thought that he was entitled to the first priza—The Clerk said he bad written to Mr. Sheltnerdine, stating that the Board had re- served the right to alter the plans, and that the altered plans ' still conformed with the Board's requirements.—Another letter had since been received from Mr. Shelmerdine, asking that the matter might be laid before the Board.—lt was agreed after a short conversation that the clerk should be ins,ructed to inform Mr. Shelmerdine that they considered his (the clerk's) former letter a sufficient answer to the com- plaint. PROPOSED PUBLIC LIBRARY.—A letter was read from Mi. It. 11. Davies asking if, now that the Board had passed a proposal regarding the building of public offices, they would permit him to suggest that a room or rooms be pro- vided in it for a free public library and reading-room. 'He understood that hitherto the difficulty in founding a library in Widnes had been in finding a TOOIII suitable to the pun, nose. The first cost, he thought, would be small, and he had no doubt that many wouldmontribute books for a com- mencement, and a rate of Id. in the Z would be amply suffi- cient to cover the working expenses and additional books. He thought the chairman would agree with him that such an institution was much needed in Widnes, and by providing it the Board would Ise consulting the best interests and wel- fare of the p ople.—Tbe Chairman thought the levet Might bo referred to the General Purposes Committee.—Mr. Hand- ley believed there was a room to spare in the public offices that might be used as a reading-room, if it was thought well to have one. He moved that the letter be referred to the General Purposm Commht Pankhurst seconded this proposal, which was carried. GAS AND WATER COMHETTEE.-10 the minutes of the Gas and water Committee, it was stated that a letter had been read from J. W. Wareing and Co. complaining about the sale of tar by tee Board; and that instructions had been given by the committee that no sales were to be made at the gas works —The Clerk explained that the Board had entered into a contract with Messrs. Wareing and Co. for the sale of their surplus tar, and they complained that the Board had been selling in cornitetition with them. There had been a small quantity of tar sold outside the contract, but instruc- tions had now been given that no tar was to be sold in any quantity in that way.—The minutes were adopted. HIGHWAY Coaturrent—The minutes of this committee eontained the following r-.-Sewers: The Surveyor instruc- ted to examine those to Ann-street and Victoria-road, as early as possible, ant report. Instruclons given to prepare a statement of expenditure at Helton View.—Stseet Mak- ing: Letters 21st June, from the St Helens and Sutton, and St Helens and Reinford Building Societies, asking that the work be delayed. Instructions given to reply that the Beerd bay deeideel t bays' certain streets made—Letter 18th Lae, from It Whiteside, On behalf of two property owners, stating that Margaret and Wellington-streets have been put into proper order.—Adopted. HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.—In the minutes ef the Hospital Committee it was stated as follows :—Patients at last meet- ing, 1; admitted since, 1; discharged, 1; sent to the work- house, 1. Recommended that the tender of W Kershaw, £6 15r, for the pointing as per specification be accepted. Re- commended that the tender of Samuel Merritt as follows. be accspted: £5 for pointing and dressing the front and ream walls as per specification, and 7d per yard for any work seeteael " khe bioli walls as per specification,—Adopted, Two PROPOSED SEWERAGE Words. The minutes of the Sewerage Committee contained the following : tuition of lifain Sewer: Plans and estimates for the follow- ing works submitted by Mr Copland, examined and ap- proved—From Simm's Cross, along Whines and Albert. roads, to the junction with Peelhouse-lane ; from Albert- road along Peelhouse-lane to the junction of Derby-road; from Kent's lamp along Lugsdale-road to the junction of Pooleatreet; from Ann-street level crossing to Lugsdale- road ; from Lugsdele crossing along Warrington-mad to the junction of Best-street; Moss-bank,irom the outlet into the river, brick sewer beneeth the canal and railway, from the latter point along a private road through Sullivan and Co.'s works, to a point in Moss Bank-road, and from the latter point along Moss Bank-road. - Recommended that applica- tion be made for borrowing power for the works as follows: --SiOem's Cross to Peelhouse-lane £5,500. Albert-road to Farnworth-street £6,000, Legsdale-road £2.900 or £2,500, Ann-street £450, Legodele crossing to Warrington-road £6,500, Moss Bank £3,270; total, £24,120 or £24,22o.—Re- commended that Mr Copland's salary be increased £25 per per atinum.—tt a meeting of the Committee held 30th June, the following business was transacted :—No I Con- tract: Letter 27th June, from J Evans asking for definite orders as to the reconstructing of the defective work put in by Mr Jeffreys (about 40 yards, estimated to cost £5 per yard) if it is to be done by hfm.—Recommended by a majority of the committee (3 to 2) that the nedessary Work be done. Contintsation of Main Seteer : Mr 'Copland instructed to proceed with the plans for the sewer in Albert-road and Moss Bank, the others to be held over pending the inspection by the Highway Committee.— Mr. Handley moved the confirmation of the minutes with the exception of those referring to the continuttion of the main sewer, which he wished to be sent back to the corn- ml' further consideration —After some delay, owing to lidwood and Mr. Dutton, who are members of the Committee, refusing to second Mr. Handley's pro- '? Gasket' said he would second them with the . ion Mr. Handley had mentioned.—Mr. Houghton asked what was the reason of the committee's recommend- ing an increase in Mr. Copland's salary.—Mr. Wright moved that not only the portion referred to by Mr. Handley be referred back, but also the recommendation to increase Mr. Copland's salary and the paragraph instructing Mr. Copland to proceed with the plans for the sewers in Albert. road and Moss Bank.—Mr. Houghton seconded Mr. amendment.—Mr. Mid wood then severely criticised proposals contained in that portion of the minutes which . Handley had proposed to refer back. lie maintained eat the greater portion of the proposed new sewers would not be required for many years to come. With regard to the proposed increase of Mr. Copland's salary, he thought it was a very unwise course to take, and one which he went very much against. The engineer had £2OO a yes: at the present time, and it was not so long since his salary had been increased £5O. The Board was paying something like £7OO in the surveyor's depart- ment, and what were they having done for it? Siraply keeping the roads.insorder, and some people would say they were net even doing that.—The Chairman: Mr. Copland's salary is the thing you are sneaking about; you are wander- ing away.—Mr. Mid wood said the engineer was really in the surveyor's department, and he had a right to say anything affecting the department with which he was connected.— The Chairman said Mr. Midwood should cetrfine hinesel( to what was on the agenda.—Mr. Midwood thought he had been confining himself to what was on the agenda, but if the chairman ruled him out of order be would of course stub- mit. He said they were spending £7OO Mid on the depart- mint—The Chairman (intereuering): I shall certainly rule you out of order unless you stick to the point in ques- tion.—Mr. Midwood then further briefly criticised the :minutes, after which Mr. Handley said it had not been in- tended to carry the whole of the sewerage at once, but as the minutes were to be referred back, he did not know that it was worth while making further remarks. As to Mr. Cop- land's salary. Mr. Copland came to the Board nine years ago for a special object. Five years ago he had his salary increased to £2OO, and had not had it increased since. Mr. Copland was getting on in life, and he (or. Handley) did not think the members of that Board thought that their officers ought to always continue at the -same salary--Mr. 'Wright's amendment WAS then put to the meeting and car- ried, Meesrs. Wright, Houghton, Midwood, Martley, and Houghton voting in it* favor.—Mr. Sadler moved a further amendment that the minetes included in Mr. Wright's amendment be .net merely re- ferred back, but withdrawn tmconditionally.—Mr. Wright said he preferred this areendrneat to his own.—Mr Mid- wood seconded Mr Sadler's proposal, which, on being put to the vote, was carried, there voting (or it Messrs Sadler, Midwood, Manley. Wright, Dutton and Houghton; against, Messrs 'Handle',', Haskell, and Par4ahurat. Mc Forster did not vote.

THE Cramsa,.—On the minutes of the Health Committee, which contgined nothing of public interest, coining up for .confirmation, Mr Gask-ll referred to the condition of the .canal, which he said was very little better than an open -sewer. It was worse than a cesspool, as it was practically tlied tip with most offensive matter. He was td that this was owing to sewage coming from St. Ifelens. Re thought -it was of the utmost importance when they had smallpox a Liverpool and cholera approaching with rani* strides that some steps should be taken.—Mr Dutton said he had in- tended to bring the same question before the Board.—The Chairman said he might mention that he had already written to the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany about the canal on his own account, at the smell down at their works was dreadful. fie suggested that they -farther -consider the matter when they went into ,cemmittee.--The Board then went into committee.

and get some allowance for the plaintiff.—ln cross-examina- tion by Mr Sparrow, the plaintiff said he was not paid any wages unless be worked. He had seen the dog before the day in question at Mr Billington's. He could not say whether the dog tore h's trousers or not. His leg bled very much. David Worral/, labourer, of Kingsley, in reply to Mr. Burton said he kr.ew the defendant, and knew that be had had a sheep dog all the present year. He had seen the defendant Out oith the dog in the early part of this year. fie said to Billington " This dog of yours has bitten me," and Billington replied that it was a queer dog, and it was only his ploy. Lie had seen the dog once since.—John Birkbiil, labeurer, Kingsley, said he was passiog the fl.rse Shoe Inn, Kingsley, on the sth of March last. He 8.1 41 the defendant with a fight brown sheep dog, which ran at him, and would hnifil bitten him if he had not kept him at bay with a bag he was carrying .tt the time. He had alien the dog once or twice about the defendant's house.—Dr. Robin- son said be saw the plaintiff in March last. He examined his leg, and found a wound about ene inch in diameter and surrounded by inflammation extending upwards. He saw him subsequently. His charge was 7s dd.—Mr. Sparrow, for the defendant, submitted that the plaintiff must be non- suited on the ground that the identity of the dog was not established.—His Honour held that there was evidence of identity.-.114r. Sparrow then submitted that the evidence of scions was not eetablished,and quoted a case in support of his contention.—His Honour, hostever, held that there was suf- ficient evidence to justify the case going on.—George Bil- lingtor, the defendant, in reply to Mr. Sparrow, said he had never had any complaints about the dog before. He con- sidered the dog a very quiet and sensible one, lie remem- bered being with Worrell, one of the witnesses, when the dog came and jumped up along aide of both of them, but he did not see the dog attempt to bite. it was sibply playing. In cross-examination by Mr. Burton, the defendant said that Worrell did say something to him about the dog having tried' to bite him.—Mrs. Billington, defendant's wife, said she reared the dog, and never had any complaints about it. —Mr. Sparrow then addressed his Honour on behalf of the defendant.—His Honour, in summing up, said that with regard to the savageness of the dog he must say that the bite inflicted npon the plaintiff was a savago and severe one, and, taking the evidence of Worrell and Birkhill together, confirmed him in the view that the dog was ferocious. The plaintiff was entitled to something for his suffering and for his loss of time, and he considered that in case of bites something substantial must be given. He should give judgment for the plaintiff for £5 10s.—Judgment for this .arnount, with costs, was entered.

At Runcorn County Cou—rt-c-M-T. uesday, before Mr Wynne Ffoulkes judge, Joseph Hughes, labourer, Kiegsley, 'sued George Billington, of the Horse Shoe Inn, Kingsley, for the sum of £lO d trnages through having been bitten by the defendant's dog. Mr Burton appeared for plaintiff, and Mr Sparrow, barrister at law, of Liverpool (instructed by Mr A Linaker), for the defendant. After Mr Burton's open- ing statomen, Joseph Hughes, the plaintiff, was called and said he was 72 years of ..ge. He was passing Mr Billing- tons early in Much ef the present year, about ea o'clock in the morning, when he saw a dog standing near the defen- dant's house. The dog followed him and bit a piece out of his leg and then ran away towards Billington's house. He was off work a fortnight and at the end of tat time he could only work a day now and then. He also had to have i-xtra nourishment. He saw Billington the same day he was bitten by the dog, and informed him of what had occurred. He then said he would get rid of the dog, and would try

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, when there were present—the Revs. John Lock- wood (in the chair) and J W N Tanner; Messrs. James Warburton, E A Walliogton, John Weir, Henry Linaker (clerk), Dr Adams (medical officer), and James Farrington (nuisance inspector). A NUISANCE AT STEETTON —A letter dated the 4th inst., frum Mr James Marson, of Hill Cliffe, was read complain- ing of the pollution of a" watering pond" at Stretton Lower Hall Farm. It was alleged that a sewer telonging to the Highway Board was the cause of the nuisance.—Mr Far- rington stated the sewer was not the cause of the nuisance. There was no =AI at the pond. The question of disposing of the sewage in that district had been a great trouble for a length of time. He suggested the appointment of a com- mittee of three members to investigate the matter.—This suggestiou was acted upon. Frwarrcn —Cheques amounting to £712 7s 10d were signed for .the payment of midsummer accounts and salaries, MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr Adams, the medical officer of health, presented his quarterly report, which stated that during the qaerter ending June 3011, 1884, tbe Re- girerar's return recorded 171 births and 91 deaths inthe four registration sulidistricts comprised in the Rural Sanitary District of the Runcorn Union, Of the births 90 were miles, 81 were females ; birth rate 8 7 per thousand per quarter, against 153 births, with a birth rate of 7 9 per thousand, in the corresponding quarter of 1883. Of the deaths 46 were males and 45 females; death rate 4.6 par thousand, against 91 deaths, with a death rate of 47 per thousand, in the cor- reaponding quarter of 1883. Of the deaths 24 occurred in persons under five years of age, 18 of these being under one year of age, while the remaining 67 occurred in persons of five years of age and upwards. The death rate was some- what increased by the boating fatality on the Mersey, whereby four persons, not residing in the district of the Au- thority, lost their lives by the capsizing of a but. The deaths from zymotic diseases comprise five from scarlet fever, one from diphtheria, one from whodping cough, two from typhoid fever (in the .Sutton outbreak), and one from diarrhosa, a total of ten deaths from these causes. A tabular form of the causes of death included: Heart disease, eight; blood poisoning, through opening a cow suffering from splenic apoplexy, one; stickle by banging, one; acci- dentally drowned, five; accidentally overlain, one. Tim SIITTOS OUTBRE&K —Dr. Adams also presented the i following special report:—' Gentlemen, I have to report to you the death from typhoid fever, on June 25th, of Ann antrebus, aged 67 years, who resided at a cottage at Sutton, situate near the railway station. She had been in close per- sonal attendance upon Mrs. Johnson (see case No. 2 in special report of June 9th), and succumbed to the disease in ' a few days from its c)mmencement. The disease in her ease had, in my opioion, arisen through direct personal infec- tion from Mrs. Johnson. I have also to report the death of Clara Emma Kemp, aged nine years, of Grange Lodge, Halton, from scarlet fever. I received no intimation of the disease in this C 498 until the registrar sent me notice of the death. I have also to report the occurrence of scarlet fever In the undermentioned places, notification of which I hare received from a medical practitioner t—Ernest and Waiter Manning, at a house in Halton Village, occupied by Joseph Manning; Esther and Mary J. Wirral!, at a house occupied by George Worrell, situata in Wood's-row, Halton-road; J. H. and A. Walker, at a house occupied by Henry Walker, situate in Astmoore. These are all simple cases, and are all doing well, three of them being convalescent. They are I properly isolated and supplied with efficient disinfectants, and Mr. Farrington will 'receive notice when the premises are ready for final disinfection. lam also informed by the same medical gentleman who gave me information in these cases that two children of George Leatherwood's, residing at Astmoore, have been attacked by measles, but are now convalescent. The premises will shortly be disinfected by your Inspector." I The other business was not of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD:
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD:

_ The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Ceme- tery Offices on Wednesday. Mr. G. Moss presided, and there were present Messrs. Whittaker, Norman, and Cole- burn, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). THANKS TO Ma. Moss.—Mr. Norman moved that the best thanks of the meeting be accordel to Mr. Moss for his valuable services in the chair during the past six months. He observed that Mr. Moss had attended very regularly to the duties of the Board, and had filled the position of chair- man with credit to himself and advantage to the ratepayers. —Mr. Coleburn seconded the motion in complimentary terms, and it was carried unanimousty.—Mr. Moss, in acknowledging the compliment, said it had been very agree- able for him to preside ever the Burial Board, where the pro- ceedings had always been of such a harmonious description. I He had felt it to be an honour to occupy the position he did, and hoped the business would be conducted in the future as In the past years. Emscrtos or Cnatataratr.—Mr. Norman proposed that Mr. James Handley, J.P., shoed be chairman during the ensuing year, remarking that that gentleman had worked with much energy and intelligence on lochalt of the rate- payers. On that Board, and In other positions in the town, he had proved himself highty useful, and he felt that in appointing him chairman of the Board they were placing him in a position the duties of which he wonld discharge in an eminently satisfactory -manner, not only to the Board, but the ratepayers generally.—ln a perch couched in com- plimentary terms Mr. Whittaker seconded the motion, which was also supported by Mr. Coleburn. Mr. Handley, said the latter gentlemen, bad as a financier proved himself of great service to the Board, and they could always depend upon tris abilities in times of emergency. He felt sure they could not do batter than appoint Mr. Handler, who had al- ways taken a deep interest in local matters —The motion was tarried unanimously.—Mr. Moss then moved the ap- pointment of Mr. P. Briscoe as vice-chairman during the ensuing year. Mr. Briscoe, he observed, was one of the eldest inhabitants in the town, and the oldest member on the Board, and in whatever post of responsibility the ratepayers had been pleased to place him, be bad acted in a manner which gave general satisfaction —The proposal was seconded by Mr. Norman, and carried newt:con. FINAROL COILKITTER.—On the motion of Mr. Coleburn, secoaded by Mr. 'Whittaker, theVinance and General Pur- poses Committee was formed as follows :—Messrs. Moss, Coleburn, Norman, Rogerson, and the chairman (ex-officio). A TINDER —The tender of Mr. Grayson, of High-street, for the painting of the cemetery property at nO 101 was ac- cepted on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Cole- burn. Mr. Norman and Mr. Whittaker were appointed to see that the work was satisfactorily performed. A DRINKING FRUNTAIN FOR CNN CRYETERY.—Mi:: Nor- man introduced the subject of erecting a drinking fountain in the cemetery grounds, and he advocated that an orna- mental fountain chould be ereeLed near the entrance of the cemetery, where it would prove a benefit to the thirety, and Also be of use to the persons who wished to water the plants .an graves —The Board generallymoncurred in Mr. Norman'e Yiews.—The secretary produced a deeitn for a fountain On the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, it was decided to erect a fountain, and a committee, consist- hag of the chairman, Messrs. More, Coleburn. and Norman wee appointed to inspect designs out of which a selection should be made, and also to have the work carnal out. RKPAIRS WANTER MeSSIS T T Barry and Son, archi- tects for the cemetery building., wrote that he had recently visited the new church that was being erected in Greenway- road, and he went across to the cemetery chapels, the fabric of which seemed to rtgeire some attention, and he recom- mended various repairs to be done. The Secretary and Mr Norman were directed to make arrangements with Mr Pen- nington, who was at present 'employed on the cemetery wall, to have the work dune at. as cheap a rate as possible :trans-rms.-The Secretary reported that the interments for the three months ended on the 25th June bad been 86, as against 81 in the corresponding period last year. The fees :eceived for the same period this year amounted to £BB us lid, last steer. £B2 4s.

This concluded the business. TRI MAYOR'S PORTRATT We understand that the Mayor of Warrington (Aidrrnan Harrieon), has purchased the porbait ptinted rec ntly by Mr 8 titmmond, of. 205, wiewiek-toad, at the prie4 asked, anti has expressed entire uttieraction with the work.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Mr. Gladstone's statement this afternoon was listened to in a crowded House, though what be had to say was news to less than one half of the assembly. The Liberals were fresh from the enthusiastic meeting at the Foreign Office and were at liberty to sit and watch the effect of the announcement upoa their opponents. It was unmistakeably disappointing. Up to the last, with characteristic fatuity, they have hoped that ministers would play into their bands And forthwith dissolve. On the Liberal side there were some advocates of this step upon the ground that no one can say what may happen in Egypt, and that it would be well to take the election now whilst affairs are moderately quiet. This is a consideration of which Conservatives also nave taken account. But with them nothing can outweigh the dread of the result of the Lords once more throwing out the Franchise Bill at the autumn session formally announced by the Premier to-day. That, they know, is an act that would in the popular mind at election time outweigh all considerations of misfortune in Egypt. From this course as far as the Lords are concerned, there is but one alternative—to yield in' October after blustering in July. Either course must be fatal to whatever remnant ,of political influence is left to the Lords. But of the two I the latter is the least immediately calamitous. If they throw out the Franchise Bill a second time there is no doubt ' that a Elation whose will has been twice insolently deed, will make such speedy account with five hundred men who have flouted it. If they pass the bill they will become an übject of public derision. Still they will keep their posi tion and may hope to live down ridicule. Therefore th belief gains ground that they will yield in October. In the meantime the injury they have accomplished is irreparable. In the 'House of Commons to-day, Mr. Glad- stone announced the withdrawal of all the bills upon the ministerial programme with the exception of those before a grand committee. That means practically, the waste of a whole session. The Franchise Bill has been the lean kius that :has eaten up all the rest. If it had passed it would have been a worthy achievement for a session. But not only by the action of the Lords is the bill destroyed, bat all others go with it. We shall in time, within this year I begin to think, get the Franchise Bill. But the wasted see- sion can never be regained. The question is, is a cycle of the House of Lords worth a session of the House of Com. none?

The debate in the Lords will not compare with some ethers that have taken place within its walls at great crises. The explanation of this is obvious. There was no question to debate. Ministers were urging forward a Franchise Bill, and the Conservatives were prepared with an amend- ment, in which they declared that they accepted the princi plea contained in the measure. What else they had to say was that a Redistribution Bill should have been brought in at the same time with the Franchise Bill, and failina that ministers should now consent to the insertion of a clause making the enactment of the Franchise Bill contempora- neous with a edistribution scheme. But these were not matters upon which debate was possible. The first is a puiely childish assertion disproved by cotorious facts. If, , introducing the Franchise Bill alone, ministers were unable to pass it through the Houee of Commons before the end of June, the Lords being engaged in discussion of it on the 7th of July, where would they be with the more controversial matters of a Redistribution Bill added As to the other I claim put ferward, it had been urged at every stage of the ' Bill in the other House, and had been rejected by over- whelming majorities. Its real meaning, as I endeavoured to explain in a former letter, simply is to insure a condition of affairs in which redistribution shall not be arranged by the present House of Commons, but by one in which with a possibly reduced majority a Liberal Government would be at the mercy of combinations between Tories and Parnel- -1 lites.

Lord Rosebery lifted the &bite above its level by a speech of quits unexpected power. Beyond this the most remarkable contribution to the debate was Lord Salisbury's speech which,delivered at an early hour of the morning, has scarcely attracted the attention it deserves. It is a common thing to talk of Lord Salisbury's hopeless incompetency as a leader of parties or ef men ; but it was a new revelation to hear him in the first hour of yesterday morning sneering at the very people to whom he was urging Ministers to appeal, talking about the possibility of getting up copular demonstrations as long as there was a balance at the credit ,of the promoters, and jeering at the working-man who gives up a day's pay in order to uplift his voice in a great political question in which he is nearly interested. As Lord Rosebery's speech was sufficient to make a reputation, so was Lord Salisbury's sufficient to sink one. In quiet times, and amid the truth-inspiring influences of a copious dinner, we are accustomed to hear Tory squires talk in this way. But to have the responsible Leader of the Conservative party, almost on the eve of a general election, thus grossly insulting the bulk of the electors suggests mad- ness. The Conservative peers cheered Lord Salisbury where they could; but at this passage in his speech they sat omi- nously silent.

The fete at the Healtheries last night was at once the most audacious and the most successful ever given in Lon- don. Over five thousand people were invited to come in evening dress, and were informed that no provision would be made for receiving cloaks, hats, or Umbrellas. This, of course, meant that people were to walk in and out as they might from their own dining-room to the drawing-room. But what if it had rained? All day long the air had been thunderous and ominous clouds hung over London. Some hours after the last guest had found his carriage the Heavens opened and the rain descended in that tumultuous manner which marks cur July. Inside the exhibition there was scarcely any crush, its vast area absorbing the population that momentarily streamed into it. It was a fairy scene, all the gardens being illuminated, the fountain-playing, ladies in rich evening dress strolling about, whilst the bands of many countries played soft airs.

The Maori King is, in the regrettable absence of Jumbo and Cetowayo, the hero of the season. He goes everywhere, and beitig of robust frame and endowed with a great gift 0 enjoyment, he manages to get along. I met him the other night in a well-known drawing room. He was sitting on the sofa with his hands crossed before him, a great bouquet stuck in his button-hole, and a broad smile on kis tattooed face. His compatriot was on hie feet singing a most mono- tonous strain, lapsing into a moan, indicating a kind of pathos which possesses a jaekall when it has had nothing to eat for three days. But though the strain was melan- choly the humour of the song was evidently keen. Ihe tongster (whose name I cannot spell) was grinning from ear to ear, whilst his Majesty, with his chin buried in his bouquet, was smiling scarcely less broadly. If on the invi- tation it had not been plainly set forth 'To meet the King of the Maoris," I should have thought these were two es- teemed members of the Christy Minstrels engaged for the evening. In repose, both the King and the songster had honest, ingenious faces, always ready to break into a broad grin. They were thoroughly enjoying themselves, and in the space of an hour ate more ice-creams than would kill two English ladies. Mr. Irving has scored another success at the Lyceum. There is little doubt that Ticelfth Night will carry him over to the time when he is due to return to the States, and will leave behind thousands unsatisfied in the desire to have seen the piece. The comedy itself is one of the most charming in Shakespeare's book. Ellen Terry adorns every character she undertakes, and in Viola is not less charming than in Beatrice. It is a more difficult matter to fit Mr. Irving with a part. But in the many sided character of Malvolio he has found a success. On Tuesday night the theatre was tilled with the remarkable assembly that always occupies stalls and boxes on the occasion of bringing out a new piece at the Lyceum. "The Foundation of Death," of which I spoke the other week, is now out. It is a truly remarkable volume, pos- sessing a curionsfaseination. At the Garden party at Lam_ heth-place, on Saturday, the Archbishop of Canterbury, talking about it, said it had kept him up half the previous 1 night, th,,ogh be had opened it only with the intention of idipping into its contents. It is, tbe most remarkable and powerful contribution to the generally unattractive drink question that has ever appeared.

The extraordinary heat has already produced singular ehanrres in London customs and costumes. Hansom cabs I go about with white linen stretched on their roots looking extremely cool and inviting. In the Park, men stimulated by sunshine, have adopted a new iress. There are com- paratively few light coats worn, but white duck trousers, a vest of the same material, and a black coat is certainly a novelty, and as black and white stripes (called • I are in.t. now fashionable costu mes for ladies, we are thus of both sexes. 1 protui*ed a uniformitr of colour in the dress " magpies ")

lAt the same time I hear of a novelty in hair cutting. For I don't know how many decades, men have had their hair cut after the same pattern. It might be longer (4r shorter, according to the wearer's taste, but the shape was always the same. Now there is a change. Men are bcgirming to wear—dtes it sound funny to read it ?—fringes. The h Air is cut away at the temples and allowed to be a little long in front. It has long been the fashion in France and Italy, where it is called a laVandyek, but is quite new in Eng- land.

I I bear that the authors of "Silver King" are agaic in collaboration lhe new play is to succeed Claudian, now at its hundredth night, and yet showing little signs of de- clining interest. What the new piece is to be has been kept a secret. Mr. Barrett, like Mr. Gilbert, knows the value cf mystery. Still I should not be greatly surprised if the sub- ject were an historical one, and if the hero of the play were llarold.

SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A LABOURER. A shocking affair occurred at Warrington, on Wednesday when a man named T. Bates, aged 46. shot himself through the head with a single-barrelled gun at lam house. No. 1, Appleton-street. The deceased, who was a labourer, bad been employed at Dallam Forge. It appears that he had been drinking more or less for the past seven or eight weeks. and in consequence of that he lost his situation at the forge. On Saturday he remarked to his wife "I shall not live long; I shall not want this shirt any more." On Wednes- day morning the bailiffs were put into the house for rent due, and that apptared to trouble the deceased, who, after speaking to one of them, went upstairs. Shortly afterwards the report of a gun was heard, and upon a neighbour going upstairs she found the deceased in the back room, lying on his back on the bed, with his brains blown out. By hie side was a single-barrelled gun. Yesterday afternoon Mr Husband, deputy coroner, held - an inquiry relative io the occurrence at the Horse and Joc- key Inn, Winwick-road, when Alice Bate, the widow of the deceased, said that her husband had taken to drinking for the past few weeks. On Saturday last she was hanging up a clean shirt for him, and seeing it, he said to Albert, their son, "Albert, you have the shirt, as I shall not want it any more, nay days will not be long." Witness told him that "he was haying her on, and that he must net talk like that." On Wednesday morning bailiffs were put in the house for rent that war in arrear, the amount being £2 2s 3d. Her husband took the matter very much to heart, and went up stairs to awaken his sons to see if they had any money. Directly afterwards she heard the report of a gun upstairs and ran out of the house. Deceased had bad his leg broken about two years ago at the forge, and she thought that he must have received a severe shock, as he has been some- what queer since. His father was buried two months ago, and he was considerably upset by that and losing work in consequence. The gun produced was in the Mouse at the time. —Mary Hamersley, wife of William Idamersley, Apppleton- street. deposed that on Wednesday morning she WAS in the house of the deceased when the bailiff was there. The deceased seemed very mach put about in consequence. Sub- sequently she beard the report of a gun.—Edittt Blackburn, wife of John Blackburn, engina driver, Russell-street, said that she was at the house of the deceased on the day in questim. She met Mrs. Bate in the entry, and Mrs. Bate said that her husband had shot himself. She went into the bedroom and found deceased lying on the bed. She touched . him on the shoulder, and said " Mr. Hate, what have yen done." He then turned his head towards her and tried to speak, but was unable to do so. His lips quivered, and that was all. The gun produced was by his side, and there was a wound on the left side of his head ; his whiskers were blackened with smoke.—Verdict "That the deceased com- mitted suicide whilst in a .fit of temporary insanity."

WARRINGTON TRICYCLE CLUB —The members of thfi club, which was formed a few weeks ago by a few local tricyclists, have had a number of very enjoyable runs of late, which have been done in good time and with comfort. The night runs are on Mondays and Thursdays, and bay° comprised, amongst others, runs to Hollinfare, Hainhill, Hoo Green, Golborne, Lvmm, High Legh by way of Lymin, and back on the Knutsford-road, Norton Priory, Presto' Brook, &c, The Saturday runs have, itacludei Hale. Liver- pool,m 't - Rostberne, Altrincha , and outsr ord ; and on the programme there are runs to West Derby, Denham Massey, Budworto, Bowdon, Rostherne Mere, Runcorn, Altryncham, t&c., yet to be done. On Tuesday evening a meeting held at the headquarters, the Patten Arms Hotel, for the purpose of re-considering some of the rules, and seeing what further steps could be taken to increase the membeiehip of the club. Eleven tricyclists were present, and as a siart it was resolved to advertise the fact of the exis,ence of such a club, as the opinion was expressed that there were many in • Warrington who would be glad to join and take part in the runs if they knew of such a club. As will he seen by the advertisement in another column, gentleneen baying machines are requested to apply for information to the Lore sec., Mr. 0. F. White, Bank Villa, Warrington.

RAINHILL.

flour Surnosor Scaloot.—The annual summer treat and tea party of this school took place on Saturday last. The children having assembled at the school, marched through the village, headed by the Nutgrove Temperance Band, and returned to a field kindly plazed at their disposal by Mrs. Jackson, of the Holt Palm. Here they were joined by Mr. Darbyshire and a number of friends from West Leigh. After partaking ef a substantial tea, the evening was spen- in dtncing and playing football and cricket. Great assistt lance was given by the Rev. J. Johnson, of Prescot, Mr. W. Evans, and Mr. Derbyshire. Remain NATIONAL &atoms —The enlargement of these ectiools was commenced last week by Mr. D. Pickering, builder and contractor Rainhill. It is intended to remove the front part of the schools and to re-erect it close to the parapet, thus adding twelve feet to the length of each room, and providing extra accommodation for nearly ninety chil- dren. The prenent rooms for some time past have been found to small for the increased attendance, their crowded state calling for the following entry in the School Inspec- tor's report for this year:—" The schools are so crowded that it is cliff:knit to conduct them with the very satisfac- tory efficiency which now marks them, without undue effort anti strain on both teachers and scholars." The Prescot Highway Board have kindly consented to make all the ne- cessary alterations to the drains and water courses. At the last examination of the schools in May, W. B. Coward, Esq., L1.M.1.5., awarded the excellent merit grant to the boys' and girls' schools and the good merit grant to the in- fants' school.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. COMMONS' COMMITTEE. The Select Committee of the House of Commons ap- pointed to inquire into the Manchester Ship Canal Bill sat on Monday. Mr. Sclater Booth presided, the other members being the Marquis of Tavistock, Mr. Lewis Fry, and Mr. J. A. Campbell. The principal petitioners against the Bill were the Corporation of Liverpool, the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Corporation of Birkenhead, the Corpora- tion of Bootle, Miss Watt, Garston Land Company, Sir H. de Trafford, the Cheshire Lines Committee, Mr. Vyner, Messrs. Naylor, the Cheshire Justices of the Peace, the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, the War- rington Water Company. the Justices of the Peace of Lan- cashire, the London and North-Western Railway Company, the Great Western Railway Company, the Garston Local Board, the North Staffordshire Railway Company, and the Lancashire and Cheshire Coal Association. The promoters and opponents were represented by the same counsel as ap- peared when the Bill was before the Duke of Richmond's Cornanittee.—The Chairman, before calling upon Mr. Pember to open the case for the promoters, said it must have occurred to learned counsel on both sides that the time before the Committee was very short I in which to carry through such a trial, so to speale, as had been carried through the House of Lords this Seeeion, and the House of Commons last Session. The Committee, there- fore, relied upon learned counsel on both sides to do the utmost in their power to narrow the issue, and not to put the Committee and themselves to the trouble of going ex- haustively into all the details of the Bill.—Mr. PEMBER, Q.C., proceeded to open the case for the promoters, and at the outset remarked that it said a great deal for the comb's tency of the people of Lancashire to find them continuing their appeal to Parliament to pass this canal scheme. He then described in detail the physical features of the low water channel of the propose I canal. In navigable width and depth the canal would equal the Suez, which would ac- commodate steamers of over 5,000 tens. It would, therefore, , be open, practically, to the mercantile navy of the country, I with the exception ef large passenger liners. The total estimate of the works was £13,904,185. The share capital was £8,000,000, and the borrowing powers would be £2 000,000, making altogether ten million. The margin of capital might seem unusually large, but it provided for the purchase of the Bridetewater Canal and the Mersey and Dwell Navigation undertakings. Whatever of the two millions they spent on the Bridgewater and Mersey and Irerell undertakings must not be taken to add to the costli- ness of the project, because they bought them as going con- cerns, and would derive an income from them. With regard to the suggested dangers to the estuary of the Mersey they would never have heard a word about them had it not been for the commsrcial fears o' Liverpool. The promoters would deal with only one-tiftieth pert of the cub- ical capacity of the estuary of the Mersey. Every force of nature would be left free to exert itself as at present. The estuary of the Mersey had been very grossly neglected, and it was a cry of disgrace to the country in general, and to Liverpool in particular, that the condition of the river was what it now was. Liverpool did not care two straws about what became of the upper Mersey, and shw did not seem to care as much as she ought about what became of the bar at the mouth of the river. In consequence of neglect the height of low water at spring tides was only Oft. Having a monopoly, Liverpool had been content to leave things alone. The Dock Board urged that nothing should ba done lest harm should come of it. But why should the Mersey be left in its present mi,erable condition, with tortuous and shifty banks and channels, whilst other rivers had been greatly im- proved Y All the works of the promoters were to be carried out under the supervision of the Mersey Commissioners, who would have absolute power of interference and control. Pro- ceeding to refer to tables showing the population of Lance- shire.—The Chairman, interposing, said the committee could take that for granted, as they were familiar with the outlines of the case presented to both Houses of Parliament. —Mr. Pember having concluded his speech, the committee adjourned. On Tuesday Mr. Daniel Adamson, chairman of the Pro- visional Committee of the Ship Canal promoters, was the first witness. He handed in a number of resolutions in favour of the scheme passed by various public bodies, in- cluding the Chamber of Commerce and the Corporation of Manchester. He also pranced tables showing the eetimated traffic upon which the undertaking was based. One of the grievances of which they complained was the high rate of charges for carriage of goods between Liverpool and Man- chester, in addition to the high charges of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board for dock purposes and for town dues. A careful comparison showed that the rates in the case of Liverpool were excessive as compared with other places. With the exception of London, Liverpool was the dearest port in the United Kingdom. He estimated that the scheme would effect a grand saving to the cotton trade of £514,411. He regarded the engineering features of the undertaking as exceedingly simple, and in his views, its construction would tend to improve the estuary of the Mersey. There would not be any difficulty in raising the necessary* capital. It was his own impression that if the capital were twenty mil- lions, and Lancashire saw that there was a prespect of rea- sonable remuneration, it would find the money for this great work. He had not a doubt that there would be a good return for an expenditure of ten millions. Asked " What about the telegram stating that £6,000.000 had been raised," he replied that he didn't know of any telegram of that kind —that no such telegram wah sent to him. On Wednesday great progress was made in the examina- tion of witnesses. To one of Mr. Marshall Stevens's obser- vations that Liverpool would really lose nothing, but would gain by the canal, Mr. Aspinall, counsel for the Liverpool Corporation and the Mersey Dock Board, said there was no dieoute about that, for his clients also held that Liverpool would lose nothing commercially. Amongst the other evi- dence taken was that of Mr. Walmaley, president of the Cotton Spinners' Associetion, Mr. Reuben Spencer Sir Jos. Lee, and Mr. Alderman Bennett. The last-named gentle- man said be had no hesitation in saying that the capital would be found. Mr. Pember announced that in view of the shortness of the remainder Of the session and the crisis in Parliamentary affairs he had determiued to close at once the commercial part of his case and to pass on to enginw- ing evidence, and Mr. Leader Williams had been flat in the witneass box before the committee adjourned for the day. On Thursday, Mr Leader Williams, the principal engi- neer to the scheme, was further examined. He said the balk of the steam shipping trade was vessels of moderate tonnage, and for cargo steamers the masts were of small im- portance, and there would be no difficulty in such steamers passing under Runcorn Bridge. Witness gave details as to the canal, stating that the canal proper commenced about a mile above Runcorn Bridge, and terminated at Manchester, the total length being twenty-one miles two furlongs. The minimum width of the bottom of the canal was 120 feet, as compared with 72 feet in the Suez Canal. The canal would do away with ordinary floods, and tend to diminish the effect of great floods. The Bridgewater Canal, which the promoters had power to purchase, would be, both for water and traffic, a valuable feeder to the ship canal. It would tale eight hours for a steamer to get from Liverpool to Manchester.

SANITARY AUTEIORITY.—A special meeting of the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority was held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday afternoon, when there were present: Messrs. Leatherbarrow (in the chair), Newsome, Meadows, Tyrer, Hill, Eatock, Gilbody, Griffith, W. B. Longtpn, Syder, Kenwriglit, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).—Proposed Infectious Diseases Ho,pital.—The Clerk explained tfiat the meeting was called to consider what steps should be taken to carry out the resolution passed at the last meeting with respect to the erection of an infectious diseases hos- pital. Mr. Gordon Smith, architect of the Local Govern- ment Board, would attend next Thursday, and he (the clerk) thought it would be as well if they postponed their decision until after the visit of that gentleman.—Mr. Meadows thought it advisable that all infectious cases should be isolated, but he did not think it necessary that they should erect a special hospital. He thought some cottage at present erected might be utilised for the purpose. —Mr. Tyrer said as they might have either the cholera or smallpox in the district shortly, it was advisable that that they should take some steps—After some further dis- cussion, a committee was appointed to confer upon the matter with Mr. Gordon Smith and the Medical Officas of Health for the district. Hartley (clerk).— Workhouse Master's Report: The new Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale) reported there were 389 inmates this week, against 396 last week, and 454 in the corresponding week of last year; 39 vagrants had been relieved, against 34 in the corresponding week last year. There were 441 boys and girls at Kirlaale Scheol.—Appoinfment of Master and Matron: The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the appointment of Mr. and Mrs. Hale as master and matron of the Present Union Workhouse, and approved of a salary of £lOO per annum to Mr. Hale and a salary of . £6O per annum to Mrs. Hale. with rations and other allow- ances .assigned to them by the Guardians.—A Religious Question : A. discussion took place upon a letter from the Local Government Board, who wished to know what reason the Guardians had for altering the creed register in the case of two children named Sarah and Mary Lewis. The Rev. .Father Finegan said the children had been brought up Catholics and they had since said that they had been made to be Protestants. He thought the Guardians should haste and repair the mistake that had been done. The Clerk said Father Finegan was labouring under a mistake. As a fact the father had been a Protestant, and by Act of Par- liament they were compelled to enter the religion of children coming into the Workhouse in the religion of the father, if it could be ascertained. When the children had attained the age of 12 they could themselves elect which religion they would embrace. It wasultimately decided that

EARLIISTOWN FOOTBALL3RS AT CI-MAR.—OR S'alßlday afternoon five membors of the Earlestown Association Foot- ball Club journeyed to Crewe in order to take part in a five a-side football contest, in connection with the annual sports under the auspices ef the Crewe Alexandra Athletic Club. The football contests excited the greatest enthusiasm, as they were among the chief attractions of the day's proceed- ings. The names of the Earlestown players were.F. Emmett I (captain), J Ellison, R. Bowker, J. Sims, and W. Rich, and in the first round they were drawn against the team repre- senting Northwich Victoria (winners of the Cheshire chal- lenge cup.) The game was very even, and hotly contested to the finish, when the Earlestonians retired defeated by two goals to one. The subsequent contests resulted as follows : —Stoke beat Goldenhall three goals to two ; Crewe Alex- andra beat Port Vale one goal to nothing; and Preston Zin- gari beat Crewe Britannia one goal and one touchdown to one goal. Second round Northwich Victoria beat Preston Zingati one goal to nothing; Crewe Alexandra beat Stoke one goal to nothing.
