HEAVY THUNDERSTORM: HOUSE STRUCK BY LIGHTNING. —On Tuesday evening a thunderstorm passed over Eerles- town, Newton,. and the surrounding districts, and though brief in its duration it exceeded in intensity and violence any which has visited the neighbourhood for a great number of years. Toe first evidence of an approaching etorm was about six b'clock in the direction of Warrington, and low, rumbling thunder was heard in tb,e distance. In less than half an hour the storm was at its height, and it was one which will be long remembered. Rain poured down in tor- rents, and almost gave the streets the appearance of rivers, while the thunder pealed and rettled overhead with a terri- fying continuity, and the lightning flashed with a vividness and rapidity that lit up the district, temporarily shrouded in darkness. After the lapse of about fifteen minutes the storm was succeeded by a calm, which continued for the rest of the night. In the course of the storm a cottage in Crow-lane, near the Common, occupied by a Mrs. Horeley, a widow, and tiff si4 children was struek ty th?. 1 lightning and considerablii damage Was oocaeloned. In addition to a large hole being made in the ceiling near the stairs, the stone mantle-piece over the fire was smashed to bits; the cupboard doors were wrenched off their hinges; the sofa was greatly damaged, while several glasses and pots about the kitchen were smashed and scattered about the floor. Mrs. Horsley and her children happened to be in at the time. The woman was knockel to the their and ren- dered insensible; and ene of the children called in several neighbours, who rendered what assistance they could. For- tunately none of the children were hurt, but the occurrence created the greatest alarm. SAD DROWNING FATALITY.—On Tuesday morning James Puyvus, six years of age, residing at 25, Manchester-row, Vulcan, was drowned under circumstances of a sad and painful character.—lt appears that he, along with two other lads about his own age, named Griffiths and Houghton, went to play on the bank of the St. Helens and Warrington Canal. They afterwards proceeded to play near a pit in a field bor- dering the canal, and deceased took off a portion of his clothes and entered the water. He immediately began to sink, and called out to his companions "Pull me out and I'll give you some toffey." The lads were unable to render any assistance, however, but Griffiths ran to a man named Beta who was working in a neighbouring field, and informed him what had occurred. Bent went to the pit, but Could see nothing of the deceased lad, and the water was quite still. He sent his dog into the water in search of the body, but this attampt proved unsuccessful, and Bent went to the Vulcan Irofnoundry where the lad's stepfather was working. The two men returned to the pit, and commenced to drag for the body, but they were unable to recover it until a lad named Joseph Rigby dived into the water, and found the de- ceased lying at the bottom with his face to the ground. The body was conveyed to the side, and was afterwards taken to the lad's late home to await the inquest.—Mr. S. Bri - house, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the dee' at the Wargrave Inn, on 'I hursday. After formal eviden identification had been given, the lad Griffiths was called t the room, and he made a statement substantially simil what appears above. But the next witness, Harry Bent, stated that on the morning of the day in question be was working in the field when the deceased came towards him with his shirt over his head. He had been attempting to null his shirt off to enter the water, but he could not get it off. He (wit- ness) put the shirt on properly, and ordered the lads to go home. About half an hour afterwards he was going towards the pit with the intention of driving two lads away, when one of them said that there was a lad in the pit. He threw a stone in the water in the direction where it was said the lad had sunk, and sent his dog in to search, but the dog did not bring the body out. He then, went to get assistance, and the body was recovered by a boy who dived in the water. The Coroner expressed the opinion that the death was purely an accidental one; and the jury accordingly returned a ver- dict to that effect.
THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL: EXTRA- ORDINARY SCENE: RESEUNATION OF TUE CURATE.

The scandalous disput-e;-w—hic-b- have taken place at the Church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown, during the last six months are being brought to a climax. In the ccurse of the discreditable occurrences which have been witnessed, the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) in the ex- ercise of the authority vested in him by virtue of his office has dismissed the old and highly-esteemed organist (Mr. El J Durm in); ordered the voluntary, hard-working popular choir not to enter the chancel and occupy the choir seats ; objected to the appointment of wardens and sidesmen ; and ' turned away a number of the teachers and workers in the Sunday school. His authority has been recently exercised ' to a still further degree, for a few days previous to last Sun- day he informed Mr. ana Mrs. Stacey (who see to cleaning the church) that their services would be dispensed with as he could not bind himself to pay them. As oar readers will be aware, the greatly respected curate (the Rev. H. E. Sm;th) has been suffering from ill-health I for a few weeks past, and at the request of his medical attendant be left the parish. He, however, returned on ' 8 iturday, and preached in the Church on Sunday morning. ' The attendance was not very large—there being less than a ' score of adults present. As usual, the organist was Mr. Perob3rton, of Liverpool, and about half a dozen girls did duty as a choir. No incident occurred to interrupt the ser- vice; and everything passed off quietly. But in the after- noon an extraordinary scene took place in the Sunday school I —the principal parties to which were the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) and the curate (the Rev. LI. E. Smith), and one result has been the immediate resignation of the latter gentleman, it being understood that he will not again officiate either in the church or Sunday echool. So far as can be learned the step has been taken in consequence of what has been termed the arbitrary and high handed action of the vicar, which has tended to still farther increase the bitterness already existing against him. The parishioners of St. John'e are well aware of the deep and hearty interest which the Rev. H. E. Smith has taken in Sunday school work. Since his illness and consequent absence from school many of the scholars did not attend the school, but on Sunday, when it was known that he would again be pre- sent to teach them, there was a goodly number in attendance. Shortly after the school opened the Rev. T. It. Matthews entered the class, and his subsequent action gave rise loan extrat*dinary scene. So far as can he ascertained, it appears that the Vicar informed the curate that some of the young men present in the class must leave the room as they had not attended school regularly.—The Rev. 11. E. Smith said he did not see any reason why they should leave, whereupon the Vicar mentioned several by name and again called upon them to withdraw. The curate remarked that they had always been regular attendants when he was present, and he could not sac his 9cholars dismissed like that. He informed the scholars mentioned that he thought they had better not leave the school. The Vicar intimated that the curate did not know all the circumstances of the caee, and the curate added that he thought he ought to do. The Rev. T. R. Matthews said the scholars had not been respectful, and he must have rules to carry on the school. The curate replied that they bad always been respectful as far as he was concerned, had always been very attentive and regular in attendance. The Vicar said be was not going to be dictated to like that, and he would not be spoken to in that manner. The curate again said that he thought the scholars should not leave the school, whereupon the vicar hastily took the class register containing the names of tll3 scholars and drew his pencil through them, one after the other, and shortly afterwards left. The action of the vicar created considerable astonishment, and for a time the scholars scarcely knew what to do. They closed their Bibles, and it is needless to add that they were not in a very pleasaut mood for the rest of the afternoolL

On the following day the vicar visited the house of Mr. Smith, who, however, was not at home. At the vicar's request the curate subsequently went to the Vicarage, where be saw Mr. Matthews. We learn that in the course of the conversa- tion the vicar said he thought all the unpleasantness had better be brought to an end; and the curate replied that he did not know what was meant by that expression. He asked. the vicar what he meant. Mr. Matthews said he meant that he thought he (the mate) had better go "When ?" asked Mr. Smith, to which Mr. Matthews replied "As soon as you like." The curate thereupon said " Very well, I will go to-morrow." The interview was shortly' afterwards brought to a close, Mr. Smith. who was entitled to six months' written notice, waiving that right. This step on the part of the Rev. H. E. Smith caused a deep impres- sion throughout the parish, and many expressions of sym- pathy and respect Sr him wsre heard.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST NEW SCHOOLS. LAYING OF MEMORIAL STONES. In unfavourable weather, but under circumstances of an encouraging and gratifying character, the Primitive Metho- dists of Earlestoren laid memorial stones of new school pre- rouses on Saturday afternoon. The event marks an epoch in the history o' Primitive Methodism in the district. The friends of the sauce formerly met with moch opposition and difficulty in the nropagation of their principles, and for some years prior to 1863 no suitabloplace for public worship or for instructing the young by moans of a Sunday school could be obtained. But about the year mentioned special efforts were pat forth towards attaining the greatly desired treetieg place, and this was ultimately attained. As they met with an insurmountable obstacle in the fact that they could not secure any suitable plot of land on which to erect a school or chapel owing to certain restrictions placed on the land, the Primitive Methodists of that time selected a plot in Legh-street, ostensibly upon which to erect cotta,ge houses. As a fact two cottages were erected, but one large room was placed overhead, and this large room was afterwards utilised both as a Sanday school and chapel. Though in- convenient in many respects the place was better than none, and formed a central meeting place for the Primitive Metho- dists of the district. The friends and school children rapidly increased in numbers; and after the lapse of ten years the congregation was so large and influential that they secured the removal of the restrictions which had formerly existed upon the lend, and the present chapel was built upon the adjoining plot of land. Since that time the original room has simply done duty as a schoolroom; and success of a most gratifying character has attended the efforts of the workers in the Sunday school. But the inconvenient and incommodious features of the premises were apparent to almost everyone, and for a long time past the teachers and scholars have keenly felt the need of bettee school accommodation. The present preraisas were in every respect unfit for the efficient working of the schools, and though there are 31 teachers and over 200 scholars at present oonnec ad with the school there cannot be any doubt that the numbers would have been much larger but for the unfavourable circumstances by which they were sur- rounded. With the view of doing more and bettor work amongst the young the trustees decided to erect a good plain building to accommodate a much larger number of scholars, and the land in Lord-street. immediately behind the chapel and the school premises was taken upon a lease from Mr Legh. The new school premises will stand upon over 800 square yards of land, and towards the estimated cost of £BOO about £2OO have been raised including the amount raised at the laying of the memorial stone, on Sat- urday last. The style of the building will be gothic, with a frontage to Lord-street, and the building will be of a plain though thoroughly substantial and convenient character. The schools will consist ef a large room G 2 feet by 26 feet, to seat 50. adult persons, with Ilya classrooms, each 1,4 feet by 10 feet, and a library and entrance vestibule placed along one side of the large room. At the back ot the large room will be an infants' school, 21 feet by 14 feet, with a connecticg lobby 4 feet wide between the twe rooms. The main room will have live roof principals, and will be celled up the spars and across the collar beams; the height to the square of the room being 15 feet, and to the ceiling in the centre 19 feet. Ample provision will be made for ventila- tion of all the rooms by upright tubes for inlet of fresh air, and air exhaust chamber above the ceiling for outlet of via- -1 ted air. E tch room will be very well lighted by means of large windows. A low pressure hot water heating apparatus will be provided in a cellar at the back of the infants' room, and this will warm the whole of the building. The infante' room and one of the classrooms will have open fire grates so that the rooms can be used for week night meetings. A tea bailer rill be provided in the cellar, and separate yards and conveniences for boys and girls will also be provided. The internal woodwork will be best quality pitch pine, twice varnished, and the walls will be of local bricks with Ruabon terra-cotta ornamental strings and Halifax stone dressings. The roofs will over- hang at eaves and at gables. The whole of the ceilings will be plastered, and the wall will have two coats of lime white and size. Messrs. Maxwell, Tuke. and Hurst, of Southport, are the architects, and the works are being carried out under their superintendence by Mr. Joseph Pennington, builder, Earlestown. It is estimated that the total cost, including architects' commission, heating apparatus, and gas fittings will be under £BOO. Unfortunately for the proceedings on Saturday afternoon the weather turned out very unfavourable. In the earlier part of the day the sun shone brilliantly, but shortly after noon threatening clouds gathered overhead, and soon rain began to fall. This wee followed by peals of thunder, and the rain ultimately descended in torrents. Notwithstanding the downpour, however, the school children and friends be- gan to assemble at the pld school in Legh-street about two o'clock, and as the weather "cleared up" a little a proces- sion was formed. In front was a, large double-poled banner containing the words, "Primitive Methodist New Schools, Lord-street. Earlestown ; stone laying three p.m.; tea at five o'clock. Come and help us." The banner was a white one, and the letters—blue and red—had been splendidly painted for the occasion by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, the resident minister. In the procession there also walked the Rev. J. M. Eairbourne (Wesleyan minister), Rev. D.S. Prosser,pf Walk- den, Rev. F. N. Shimmin, Rev. A. Cobb (Wesleyan, from Canada), Messrs. T. Clark, James Woods, Bevan, &a.; while the proceseionists were led by the Lowton Temper- ance Brass Band. In a drizzling rain the principal streets of the town were paraded; after which the scholars and friends gathered round the site of the new building. There was a large crowd of interested spectators. Among the gentlemen in attendance were the Revs. F. N. Shimrnin, D. S. Prosser (Walkden), J. M. Fairbourne(Wesleyan), W, C. Tayl er (Bap- tist) Messrs. B. B. glover, H. Thornton (Warrington), Woods, Lane, and others. The proceedings were com- menced with the singing of the hymn "Before Jehovah's awful throne," after which the Rev. J. M. Fairburnee read a portion of the 29h chapter of theist book of Chronicles. —The Rev. A. Cobb then offered up a prayer,which was suc- ceeded by an address from the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, who said that according to their programme the first stone was to be laid on behalf of the Sunday school by Mr. James Woods, who for many years had sustained the office of superintendent. He was pleased to be able to state that at a very largely attended teachers meeting, when the question came up as to who should be honoured on that occasion without a single exception the teachers held up their hands for their superintendent—(hear, hear)—and he the Rev. F. N. Shinn-rein) took that as an expression of the kindly spirit prevailing between Mr. Woods and themselves. He drew from that fact an assurance that the school would prosper, for where unity obtained between superintendent and teachers they might fairly hope for success in the work of training the young, and he was quite sure they were not present with a divided vote on the question. Before the stone was' laid by Mr. Woods on behalf of the school, a bottle was to he deposited in a cavity which had been ar- ranged for it. The bottle contained documents of an interesting character, includrng a copy of the Prlnzitive Methodist World, a circuit plan, and a plan of the Sunday school, a list of the trustees, the names of the architects who had the building in hand, and a coin of the realm. He had to present to Mr Woods a copy of their connexional his- tory, beautifully bound in brown morocco and inscribed in the following manner :—"Presented to Mr James Woods by the trustees on the occasion of his laying, by request of the teachers, a memorial stone of the Primitive Methodist New Schools, Earlestown, sth July, 1884." He bad the greatest pleasure in handing tilt volume to Mr Woods for his ser- vices to the school had been valuable, and he trusted by God's blessing he would be spared to do good work in the future. <Applause )—Mr James Woods then proceeded to formally lay the stone. He afterwards thanked the friends for their presence that day, on behalf of the Suaday school,' with which, he said, he had had the pleasure to be identi- fied for upwards of 20 years. He remarked that in pence and halfpence the Sunday school children had raised about £4o—(applause)—and he thought from that that they ought never to despise tbe day of small things,' in addition' they had received £l7 10s from the general school fund, making a total of £57 103 from the Sunday school. (Ap- plause.)—The Rev F N Shimmin stated that the next stone was to be laid by B B Glover, Esq, of Newton-le-Willows. He (Mr, Glover) had a practical interest in the work, as be was a superintendent of the school connected with the Rev. J. Allatt's church in Crow-lane; and by helping the Primi- tive Methodist cause be was showing his catholicity of spirit. He had great pleasure in handing to Mr. Glover a splendidly worked solid silver trowel bearing the following inscription:—" Presented to B. B. Glover on the occasion of his laying the memorial stone of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Earlestown, sth July, 1884. 2ad Chroni- cles, ix. B."—Mr. B. B. Glover then laid the stone, after which he said that occasion reminded him of an event which took place over 30 years ago, when his father laid the foundation stone of the Primitive Methodist Chapel at Orrell. He then received a trowel, which had since caused them very many happy reflections, and he hoped the trowel received by him that day would do the same to him and his children, when they had an opportunity of coming forward to help the Primitive Methodist cause. When their com- mittee asked him to take a part in the work that had c tiled them together that day, he found it difficult to meet the request with a refusal. Hs had an interest in the work of Primitive Methodists that went far back and extended to some of his earliest recollections. He had seen much of that work, and knew something of the men who did it during many years of close and even inti- mate connection on his part with the mining industries of that part of Lancashire. He was ready to say both by word and actiob that day that the enlarged acquaintance had not lessewed the interest referred to, but on the contrary bad led him to honour the zeal and devotion which the Primitive Methodist Connexion brought to bear on all their efforts to promote tha highest and best interests of those among whom they laboured. It had to be remembered that as a Christian community they dated their birth frem a year in which some of the men were born who were now in the foremost ranks of every department of life, and yet be found

from the annual report of the Primitive Metho- dist Sunday Schools submitted to the Confer- ence that they had schools to the number of 3,074, teachers to the number of 57512, being an increase of 364 over last year; the male teachers being 38.413 and females 19,099 The scholars of their schools numbered 376,346. He also found that the Rand of Hope was very prosperous, having 83,959 members. The financial state of their schools was also satisfactory. They were now raising about £60,000 per annum, or in other words between £l,OOO and £l,lOO per week for Sunday school work. Their history was a short history for a Christian Church, but it was an , honourable and an encouraging history. Not only had they toiled successfully in some of the lowest and most unpromis- -1 places at home, but. if they turned to the mission field they would find that they had chosen countries and districts in which the climate had been so deadly that the Primitive Methodist cause might almost he looked upon as constituting the forlorn hope of the gre a army of Christians. All present that day were not Primitive Methodists, but they were ready and, willing to give honour where honour was due, and all ready M acknowledge that the members of those churches could justly claim that they had proved their faith by their work. An assembly4ike that illustrated the oneness of Christian life in connection with diversity of religious opinion and of modes of worship. As Christian communities they were as many as the W 3709 of the sea, but at the same time they were one like the ocean. It was a great work in which Sunday sahool teachers were engaged, and on their labours depended to a large extent the welfare of the Christian Church in the future. The foundation stones were being laid that day for the benefit of those who would come after them; they were laid in the strong belief that the crowning glory of man- hood and the honour and safety of an empire were to be found in its Christian life and in its religious conviction. With that expression of his sense of the duty they had asked him to undertake, it only remained for him to declare that the stone was well and truly laid in the earns of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. (Applause.)—The Rev. F. N. Shimmin next called upon Mr. Henry Thornton, cf Warrington, to lay the third memorial stone, and presen- ted to that gentleman a handscene silver, trowel bearing a similar inscription to that on the trowel handed to Mr. 1 Glover. After the ceremony of formally laying the stone Mr. Thornton in a few reirearks declared the stone well and, truly laid, and he hoped they would soon find the pre- sent chapel too small. As they were erecting a school for 500 children there were parents somewhere, and he hoped it would not be long before they found it necessary to increase the accommodation of the chapel. (Applause.)—The Rev. F. N. Shim nin intimated that Mr. Glover and Mr. Thornton had each handed over to him the sum of £3O. (Applause.) —A collection was next made, after which the Rev. D. 8. Prosser, of Walkden, delivered an address, in the course of which he said that Mr. Glover had given them some valu- able information regarding tne denomination with which they were connected, and he hoped they would well ponder over the facts he had given thorn. He remarked that that day in Mancheeter Mr. Mundella was being entertained at a banquet, and he supposed the welcome be would get would be largely due to the fact that he was associated with the carrying out of the educational work of this country in connection with the present Government, The Sabbath schools prepared the way for the Education Act of 1870, an Act which had accomplished much good; which Was destined ultimately to exterminate ignorance from their midst, and placed a good education within the reach of the poorest family in the land, and which had put a ladder at the foot of every boy and girl who had ability by which they could climb to the very highest position and influmice which education gave. He held that that act would not have been written upon the statute book for many years had it not been that public opinion was created, developed, and, matured through the labours of the Sunday schoo's. Millions, it might be said, of Englishmen and women had received the only education they ever had in the Sunday school, but now the state was attending to the secular and the church had time and op- portunity to devote herself to the spiritual. The church Would still have to look to the Sunday achool In her efforts to win the entire country to sobriety, morality, and godli- ness; and the Sunday school had the training of the rising generations upon her hands. They had begun the erection of that school under happy auspices; perhaps the only mis- fortune so far had been the weather, which was not all that could be desired. He hoped there would be nothing worse than that however, and he hoped that when the building was completed it might for a long number of years be the home of united and earnest Sunday workers. He prayed that the work of God might prosper in the neighbourhood, and that His blessing might rest upon all their sister churches. (Applause). This concluded the proceedings; but a large number of friends proceeded to lay "bricks " upon which they after- wards placed certain sums of motel,. TEA MEETING.

After. the proceedings connected will the laying of the memorial stones the company adjourned to the Viaduct In- stitute, where a substantial tea was partaken of. Upwards of 400 set down, and the room presented an animated ap- pearance. The tables were bedecked with plants and fl3wers. A well attended meeting was subsequently held in the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. Samuel Davies, of Manchester, and tJaere were also present the Revs. F. N. Shimmin, T. Cobb, W. C. Tayler, Messrs. B. B. Glover, H. Thornton, T. Clark, and others. In his opening address, the Chairman narrated his experience of early Methodism, and pointed out that through small, earnest, and-devoted efforts great success had attended the movement by the blessing of God. They were celled upon to carry on the work, and they were responsible for it, and he was glad to see that his friends at Earlestown felt their responsibility, and were putting forth efforts for the extension of the Kingdom of Christ. (Applause.)—The Rev. F. N. Haimmin referred to the Primitive Methodism of the past and said he believed that the success which had attended the efforts of their forefathers was mainly due to the spirit of perseverance, industry, faith in God and love for man, which they had manifested. After a brief allusion to the old school and chapel, the Rev. F. N. Shimmin went on to say that in erecting the new school they did not want to hurt any • other church or school in Earlestown, but simply gather up the hundreds of children who did not attend any school. They had raised for the memorial stone laying £157 103 9d, and he wished to express his sincere gratitude to the public of Earlestown for the very liberal way in which they had been disposed to help them. (Applause.)—The Rev W. C. Tayler expresed his pleasure at being amongst them, and said he rejoiced at the success which had attended their labours since they commenced in Earlestown, and the enthusiasm they had thrown into the day's proceedings. He sincerely hoped the new school would be opened free from debt.—The Rev. A. Cobb also addressed the meeting, point- ing out that the Sabbath schools were engaged in a most important work, and exhortinA them to enter heartily into the work.—On the motion of Mr. T. Clark, seconded by , Mr. Bagnall, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the stone layers, Messrs Woods, Glover, and Thornton, to which Mr. Glover responded; and a vote of thanks the brick- layer, the Rev. D. S. Prosser, and to the friends who had kindly given the provisions for the tee was passed, on the motion of Mr. Dickens, seconded by Mr. J. Jackson. A col- lection was then made in aid of the school fund, and the Rev. F. N. Sbimmin in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman, speakers, those who had made the tea, to the band who had given their services,and to the friends who had kind- ly lent the flowers for the tea tables, stated that £164 03 10V had been raised as the result of the entire day's proceedings. (Applause.)--Mr. Ormond seconded the vote of thanks, which was duly passed, and the meeting concluded with the Benediction. -

NEWT ON COMMISSIONERS: MONTHLY MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Com- missioners was held at the TovveHall,on Monday afternoon, when there were present—Messrs. Gooch (in the chair), J E Pardey, B B Glover, J W Emmett, Thomas Hunt, Thomas Forster, J E Woraley (law clerk), R Brierley (surveyor), and Dr. Watkins (medical officer of health). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Watkins read his re- port for the quarter ending 30th May, which showed that the number of births was 51 males, 54 females, total 105 ; deaths-20 males, 15 females, total 35; excess of births over deaths 20 males, 15 females, total 35. The births were at the annual average rate of 3660, and the deaths (precisely one-third of the number of the births) 12 20 per 1,000 of the estimated populttion. The statistics presented many facts as subjects for congratulation ; (a), the lowness of the rate; (b), the absolute immunity from epidemic disease; (e), the comparatively low infantile mortality-25 71 per cent.—and not one child died in the month of June; (d), 34 28 per cent. of those whe died had attained 60 years of age and upwards, thus from.6o to 70 years 8, from 70 to 80 years 1, and from 80 to 90 years 3; and finally (e) there was not a single death in the whole quarter from injury, accident, or violence. Whilst the general health of the. township had been re- markably good, he regretted to have to record a very un- healthy period for the inmates and officials of the Reforma- tory School. A careful record had been kept of all the cases of sickness occurring in the institution, and they had been largely in excess—both in numbers and severity—of any year since the school was built. The causes for that were not internal. He had no hesitation in pronouncing the disease to be epidemic in character, i.e, peculiar to the locality, the cause of it in the polluted state of the Newton brook. A special committee of the Board had recently in- spected the brook; he knew that they were convinced of its ' excessive pollution, and it now only remained for action to speedily follow up conviction. He had to direct the atten- tion of the Board to the increasingly contaminated water flowing into the east end of the lake.—On the motion of Mr. Glover, it was decided to refer the report to the Sanitary Committee. CEMETERY AND SEWAGE Womm—At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee, on the 16th June. The following plans were submitted and approved :—Mr. Galli- Otani amended plan, house and shop, Sankey-street: Thos.

thei'delai from June 16th to July 2nd ILMr. Brierley replied that the pians had to be completed and altered.—Mr. Pardey stated that the matter was one of a very urgent character, and produced plans and letters to show that he (Mr. Pardey) had not delayed the matter. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE : A DOUBTFUL QUES- TION.—Aftor the minutes of the School Attendance Commit- tee (which contained no item of interest) bad been tead. Mr. Emmett stated that at previous meetings of the Board he bad been ruled out of order for asking that the minutes of the committee should be confirmed by the Board. He should, however, like to know whether he was really out of order or not. Taking a commota sense view of the matter it seemed to him that he was not out of order. He thought they had no right as a Board of Commissioners to spend the ratepayers money unless the ratepayers knew what they were spending it upon —The Chairman said he thought Mr. Emmett had been out of order because the committee was under different regulations entirely to the other commit- tees.—Mr. Fairclough said he thought there had never been any objection to the minutes ‘)eing read, but simply to a resolution confirming thorn. It was thought that that reso- lution was unnecessary.—Mr. Pardey : Or any discussion on them.—The Chairman : There was no objection to the minutes being read to the meeting of the Board, but only to any discussion upon them.—Mr. Emmett said he had un- derstood the chairman of the committee to say that it was a concessieng to the Board to have them read at all.—The Chairman : Yes, that is so. He (Mr. _Worsley had since received formal notice of appeal, but, be did not think it could be heard this side of neat Christmas. This was 311 the basTness of public interest.

OUTBREAK OF FEVER. Considerable alarm has been occasioned at Earlestown by rrnmours of a serious outbreak of scarlet fever in the town, but as will be gathered from what follows the reports have been greatly exaggerated. At the monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners on Monday afternoon, Mr J W E.nmett mentioned the outbreak by ask- iog the Surveyor if he had not received a latter calling at- tention to an outbreak of fever at Earlestown.—Mr BrierleV replied that he had not.—Dr Watkins (who bad just read his report on the health of the district for the last quarter) replied that that matter did not interfere with his present report which was only for the last quarter.—Mr Emmett : I understood that you had received a letter from a medical man calling attention to it.—Mr Brierley : Simply the usual notification calling attention to it, and for which they get a fee of 2.3 t3d for each case —Mr Emmett : There are three deaths in one house.—Mr Brierlev : No ; no.— Dr Watkins : There are four cases of sickness and one death. There are three infected'houses.—Mr. Emmett: I understood there were three deaths. " In that case a certain suggestion has been made and I thought it was coming befctre the Com- missioners in the letter. However, I think it, is only right to call the attention of the Commissioners to it. The father of the family was advised to stop away from his work for a week on account of the fever being in the house, and he has lost his week's wages. He was asking me as a Commis- sioner whether it would not be more advisable to isolate the cases in some way by stopping the father from going to work and about the neighbourhood carrying the fever with. him. In reply to that, I said I did not know whether the Commissioners had power to do anything of the kind—that is pay the father from stopping away from his work. I shall be glad to know whether as a body we have that power- -Mr. J. E. Worsley (law-clerk) : I should think not, It is a thing for which we should very likely be surcharged. Dr. Watkins: There is a very special thing in the Act which points the other way, and that is that a man will be subject to a penalty of £5 if he goes out of a house.. It is only to be met by private benevolence.—Mr. Emmett said he hact wondered whether there was anything in the Act by which they could maintain a min for stopping off his work.—Mr. Hunt: The only power we have Is to remove them to & hospital, and then we cannot remove them against their wilt- -Dr. Watkins: I don't know where the case has come from unless it has been iinported.—Mr. Brierlev : I think it must have been brought into the town by strahgere corning- -Mr. Hunt; At the races, I should say.—The matter then dropped.

div.p: MR. A. J._MUNDELIA, 31.P.,1N

MANCHESTER. Mr. Mundella, vice-president of the Council on Educatior, has during the last few days paid a visit replete with aduca- tional interests to Manchester. On Saturday the right hon. uentleman opened the new Art Museum in Queen's Park. Among those present, in addition to the members of the Corporation, were the Bishop of Salforee. Sir I'. Cunliffe Owen, Principal Greenwood, Professor Roscoe, Mr. John Slagg, M.P., Mr. Henry Lee, M.P., Professor Gamgee, Alderman Samuelson (Liverpool), Sir Joseph C. Lee, Pro- fessor Boyd Dawkins, Mr. Swire Smith, dec. Mr. Mundella, after being welcomed by the Mayor, received a gold key and an address.—in reply, he said the founding of the Queen's Park Art Museum furnished an additional illustration of the noble part which Manchester had taken in the great educational movement of our time. The very parent and founder of our elementary education system as now ad- ministered by the department with which he was connected was Sir James Kay-Shuttleworth. (Applause.) He was the man who obtained the first small grant of £30,000 to as- sist the elementary education of the people of this country. He was the first man who administered it neder the Com- mittee of Privy Council. But there WAS another man whose advocacy was nene the less eflective,who gave an impetus to this movement in Manchester which had never slackened, and from that day to this that inan,whose disciple he was willing to confess himself, had always combined in himself the ele- ments of the greatest statesman and philosopher and pro- phet of this century—Richard Cobden. (Applause.) There are no nobler, there are no abler speeches, there are certainly none more logical or more closely reasoned than those which were made by Richard Cobden 30 or 40 years ago on this subject of education. He spoke to Mr. John Bright only three or four nights ago about Cobden's interest in education. (Applause.), " Why," said Mr. Bright, 'don't you know that I first made his acqualatance when a very young man at my father's house when he came to Roch- dale to address a meeting on education ? It was the sub- ject that lay nearest his heart at that time, but he felt the first thing was to find the people food, and then to do what he could to get them education, and so he set to work to educate his countrymen on the great fiscal and economic question which he carried ultimately to a triumphant issue." Proceeding, Mr. Mundella said : I remember very well the first speech I ever made in. Manchester was at a conference at the Manchester Old Town Hall about 18 years ago, when Mr. Bruce, now Lord Aberdare, and Mr. Forster took the chair on alternate days. Man were gathered together at that conference from all quarters of the United King- (loin to advocate a great and national change. On that occa- sion I moved and carried, to the dismay of many gentlemen who were then present, a resolution in favour of a national compulsory system of education. I remember how I was re- monstrated with, how I was told that I had rained the pur- pose of the conference, and The Times spoke of pie as a visionary, indulging perhaps in amiable dreams, the dreams of a well-meaning enthusiast; but the article went on to say that the day was distant, if not impossible, when any such system could come into operation in this country. Gentlemen, I have lived to realise my dream. (Applause.) When the museum wit started no member of the Parks; Committee had any idea that it would grow to the dimen. alone it has now assumed, Much of its success was due te the great labours of Sir P. Cunliffe-Owen. (Applause.) When all the bills were paid it would be found that the building and its fittings bad not cost £lO,OOO, and in this WAS included a number of cases which had been purchased by the Corporation. Applause.)' If a similar result could be obtained in the other parks at a similar cost the money would be well spent. (Applause.)—On Sunday, Mr. Main- della worshipped at the Cathedral, and on Monday paid an early visit to the Kindergarten Training College, Alexandra- road. At a subsequent lunch, the Mayor of Manchester stated that all his children had received instruction in Kin- dergarten schools, and the success which they met with after- wards in other schools and in colleges was, in his judgment, attributable to the excellent effect which the Kindergarten system of instruction had had upon them. (Applause.) Mr. Mundella, in company with the Mayor apd Mr. Oakeley afterwards visited the Jewish School in Derby-street, Chest- ham. They were shown over the school by Mr. Edward Michas (the president), and by several members of the committee. Mr. Mundella also drove to the Manchester Mechanics' Institution and Technical School in Princess- street, and was shown over that building by Mr. Oliver Hey- wood (the president of the Institution), Dr. Watts (chair- man of the Council), Mr. Reynolds (the secretary), and several members of the council. Mr Mundella said he was much pleased with the manner in which the institution had been converted into a Technical School, and stated that from what he could see those who were at the head of it were working in the right direction.—The crowning event of the visit was the opening of the Central Board Schools, Deansgate. Mr. Mundella, in speaking of the work of the Manchester School Board, wished all school boards were like it. His office would be much easier were rates nowhere, higher than in Manchester. He desired to abstain from all political references; education was not a parte or political question. (Applause.) If he wanted an illustration of that, he could point to gentlemen round that table; but he would point to one who was absent-to the good deeds and good works of the Chairman of your School Board, Mr. Herbert Birley—(applause)—than whom no man had done better service to Manchester in the way of making provi- sion for elementary education. He spoke of him not merely , as chairman of a School Board, but as a man who had at the same time managed 20 voluntary schools, and in both capaci- ties he had done excellent service. Having mentioned that every scholar in that school would learn drawing, and thus to express with the band any tneeanicil work or any idea that ran through his Vain as to the work he might be en- gaged in in after life, he said education in England bad been, especially in the elementary schools, too literary. What was wanted was that children should learn the dignity of labour; that they should carry their brains into our indus- tries; that they should feel the pleasure of being inventors, mechanics, engineers,draughtsmen, and designers; that they should superintend, direct, and control labour, and feel that was the highest aspiration a man cauld have. Their Town Hall was worthy of a great city like Manchester, but that £30,000 spent on those schools was the best investment, he ventured to say, that Manchester had made for a long time. He believed money had never been better laid out than in that central school, and as the representative of the Edu- cation Department he thanked them. He thanked the Board over which Mr. Birley presided for their courageous, liberal, and enlightened policy, and he trusted that from that school would go thousands of the citizens of Manchester to bless and honour the city to which they belonged. (Loud applause.)

EARLESTOWN GOSPEL MISSION.—A miscellaneous enter- tainment in connection with this mission was held in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday evening, when Mr. John Clarke presided. Several selections of music by the choir were much appreciated. THE EARLESTOWN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.—At a recent meeting of the Committee of the Earlesto wn Association Football Club, the honorary secretary (Mr. James Duxbury) intimated that owing to the pressure of his business engage- ments he was compelled to resign the post; and Mr. David Davies, of 63, Sankey-street, was unanimously elected to fill the vacancy. GOOD TEMPLARS' MElrrom—At the session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of flood Tetnplars, held in the lodge- room , Bridge-street, on Monday evening, Bro. George E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. There was a goodly number of members preseht. After several items of business had been transacted a selection of readings, recitation, clic., was given by some of the members.

A MEETING WITHOUT SPE&IIERS.—On Wednesday after- noon the "bellman " and town•crier of Earlestown announced throughout the district that a meeting of colliers to consider the notice of reduction of ten per cent. ia wages would be held on the Market Ground, Earlestown, at half- past six that evening, and that Mr John Cross, of St. Helens, the miners' agent, woul I address the gathering. A large number of men assembled on the Market Ground. There was every prospect of an enthusiastic gathering, as altogether about 200 men turned up. Half-past six came and passed, but no speaker or anyone to conduct the meet- ing arrived. After eight o'clock the men 13“.gan to disperse, but it was an hour or 80 after that time bJfore the Market was clear, considerable disappointment being expressed at the non-appearance of the gentlemen who had been the means of calling th 3 meeting. It was stated that the gen- tlemen who should lute addressed the meeting were pres3nt at a conference between the masters and men in Liverpool, and could not get away in tune to attend the meeting at Earlestown.

THE ANTI-VACCINATION AGITATION AT EARLESTOWN. The agitation which is being carried on at Earlestown against the law of compulsory vaccination is evoking much interest in the town and neighbourhood. The dismissal oF the recent summonses, under circumstances recorded in our last issue, appears to have given great satisfaction to the local anti-vaccinators, and it has been decided to again en- gage Mr. Thomas Duxbqry, of Blackburn, in future cases that may be brought up at the Town Hall. A large number of the defendants who were summoned about a month ago to show cause why their children should not be vaccinated have had summonses served upon them this week for refus- ing to comply with an order of the magistrates ordering them to have their children vaccinated. We understand that out of the 17 persons then summoned but two or three have consented to have their children vaccinated, and it is be- lieved the others are determined to resist to the "bitter end." The committee appointed at a recent public meeting to draw up the rules of the newly-formed Anti-compulsory Vaccina- tion Society have held one or two meetings, and rules for k governing the society have been issued.

Babbage, the mathematician, was' one' day breakfasting With Rogers, the poet, when the conversation turned on the Modern fashion of plate-glass windows. The poet abused the fashion, and declared that he caught a severe cold a Short time before from sitting with his back to what he thought was an open window, but which was, in reality only a large pane of glass. Babbage replied that with him the effect of imagination had once acted in the reverse way; " for," said he, "while travelling, I found I had lost my night-cap, and, to avoid catching cold, I tried to persuade . myself that I had it by tying a piece of packthread round 131.7 head. It succeeded perfectly, and I caught no cold, Which I should assuredly have done without this trick of self-deception." "Mosx WIDLINGLY !"—The following story is told of the tenor Gayarre during his recent sojarn in Paris. He was invited one evening to dine with the Baroness de X. On arriving at the house, he received an intimation from one of his friends that the hostess intended to ask him to sing after dinner. He approached the piano under the pretext of examining some pictures that hung near It, and in the course of his inspection he contrived, unobserved, to lock the piano, and to abstract the key. Soon after dinner, the guests having returned to the drawing-room, the baroness aPnroached him and begged him to sing. "Most willingly, madame," responded Guyarre with alacrity. Then she tried the piano, and was surprised to find it locked. Search was made in all directions for the key, but naturally in vain. Then there was some talk of breaking the lock; but to this the hostess would not consent, as the case of the instrument Was a very handsome one, and she did not wish it to be in- lured. So the evening passed off without music, and, when the great tenor went away, he let fall the key of the piano on the floor of the ante-chamber, where it was discovered the next morning, to the amazement of the baroness, who could not imagine how it got there. div.head: ON WIDOWS.
div.p: ON WIDOWS.

Fuller says, in his Holy State, that "the good widow's grief for her husband, though real, is moderate" and it is my object to illustrate the old divine's text by two famous and most ancient stories. In society a miss is, not to make a pun, amiss. Your sixteens and seventeens are always at sixes and sevens among the men. They are so walled about by what is proper and what is not proper, that they can do nothing but sit bolt up- right with their arms folded. Their sitting, walking, riding, dancing, talking, are all carefully graduated to the proper. They start when you speak to them, as a pigeon does when it sees a hawk, and take hold of a man's arm as though he were made of phosphorous; and are bound to look silly, and take refuge under mamma's wings,' if the air be tainted by the ghost of a possible impropriety. In Spanish society young ladies are danced with, but never spoken to; but no more of them. But a widow, as soon as the becoming sorrow is over, which soon takes place, is always gay, always charming. In the first place, there is the lively widow. She knows how to talk to men and how to treat them: In the second she does what she pleases, and Miss Scandal has to shriek, "Row improper!" in- a whisper. In the third place, she never grows old. A spinster is on the wane at five and twenty; and at forty, even Echo would be afraid to answer her, for fear she should consider it an offer! but a.widow at thirty is on the " wax," and in her prime at forty; at least so says the song. I wonder that all women do not wish they were born widows t'and`that failing, and the occasion presen- ting itself, do not emulate the fifty Misses Danaus, in the mythology, who, in their haste to become widows, stabbed their husbands on the-wedding night. The Rev. Dr. Sterne remarks, that "the Lord tempers the wind to the shorn lamb." Bereaved married people must be shorn lambs. I have heard widowers a fortnight after the sad event humming Gai! Gai! de profundis I—and widows finding the breeze of a most comfortable temperature, and keeping up a cheerful live-man-loving spirit behind their impenetrable black veils, just as the sun shines as brightly as ever behind the darkest thunder-cloud. The first tale is that of the matron of Ephesus, told with infinite spirit by La Fontaine in his Coates. He took it from Boccaccio. It is to be found in Petronius, will had it from the Greeks. They borrowed it from the Arabians, who, in their faro, owe it to the Chinese. Da Heide has it in his version. The origin of most of our every day stories is as completely hidden in the obscurity of bygone ages as the name of the inventor of the plotigh. Once upon a time there lived in Ephesus a lady renowned for her beauty and her wit, but most of all for her intense affection for her husband. _Mothers cited her as an example . .

to their daughters, and husbands were for ever singing tier praises to their wives. In short, the whole town esteemed itself tacky in possessing within its walls each a model of virtue. But, alas! the husband died. Far from being con- soled by a will full of legacies in her favour, the widow abandoned herself to the most distressing grief, and sobbed and groaned so bitterly and so loudly, that all the neigh- bourhood was in tears. Frantic with the loss she resolved te denoild into the tomb with her husband, and to die on his bosom. A faithful maid servant accompanied her, after trying in vain to bring back her mistress to the love of lifo. She wished to.feed her eyes to the last upon the bier of the deceased, and this was the only aliment she intended to allow herself. One day passed in sighing and weeping, ' and her grief omitted nothing irhich is necessary in such cases.

AOOther dead body was lodged not far from this tomb, but very differently. Ms monument was a gallows, and himself his only epitaph—a warning to all thibves I A soldier watched him night and day, and was threatened with install( death if the body was removed. During the night, the sentinel perceived, to his great surprise, a light flashing through the crevices of the tomb; and stealing toward it, heard many soft oh's and alas's. Entering, he was amazed to see two pretty women in tears, and inquired politely what motive could induce them to inhabit so melancholy an abode? The widow did not, of course, deign to answer, but I the servant explained to him that they had resolved to starve themselves to death for love of the deceased. The soldier explained as well as he was able, what life was, and asked leave to take his supper in their presence, if they would eat nothing themselves. They gave him permission. Animated by the beauty of the lady, and assisted by the maid, who began to tire of starvation, he pleaded so warmly MI so well, that ttio slam @ consented, by degrees, to forget her "dear departed," and to estow herself upon him. Just as they had ratifle. the compact by a kiss, under the nose of the defunct, he heard a noise without, and rushing to his post, found the body gone! Overwhelmed with shame and fear' he returned to the tomb acquainted the ladies with the fate which awaited him, and bade adieu to his bride. "What!" said the servant, "shall we allow you to be hung for such a trifle? No! no! One body is like another. Let us hang up our old master. No one will know the ! difference !"

The mistress consented; the "dear departed" was sus• pended in the place of the thief; and the soldier imme- diately left the guard-house for the palace of the matron of Ephesus. The other story is from the Zadig of Voltaire, and illus- trates the same characteristic trait.
One day Zidig's wife, Azora, returned from a walk, swelling with rage. "What is the matte*, my dear ?" said Zadig: "what can have happened to put you so beside your- self ?"

"Alas !" said she, "you would would be as indignant as I am, if you had only seen what I have witnessed. I went to console the young widow Corson' who not long since erected a tomb to her husbaud, near the bro.* which flows through yonder meadow, and vowed to the gods to remain at the tomb so long as the waters of the stream should flow by it." "There is an estimable woman for you ?" said Zadig ; " she sincerely loved her husband." "Ah !" replied Azora, "if you only knew what she was doing when I visited her I" "Well, what? sweet Azora.” "She was labouring to turn the course of the stream !" Azora was so vehement in her condemnation of the young widow's conduct, and overwhelmed her with so many hard names, that Zadig was displeased with so great a parade of virtue. _ .

He had a friend named Cadow, who was one of those young men whom his wife thought better behaved and more moral than most others. He had made him his confidant, and promised him a large sum if his plan succeeded. When Azora, who had been passing a day or two at the house of a relation, returned to town, the servants in tears announced to her that her husband had died suddenly the night before, and had been buried that morning in the tomb of his ancestors at the bottom of the garden. She raved, tore her hair, and called the gods to witness that she would not survive him.

. _ That evening Cador asked permission to see her, and they wept together. The next day they shed fewer tears, and dined together. Cador informed her that his friend had left him the greater part of his property, and hinted that it would be his greatest happiness to share it with her. The lady wept, grew angry, but allowed herself to be appeased. The conversation became more confidential. Azora praised the def.nct, but confessed that he had maay faults from which Cador was exempt. In the midst of the supper Cador complained of a violent pain in his liver. The anxious lady rang for her essences, thinking that perhaps one among them might be good for the liver complaint. She regretted deeply that the great Hermes was no longer at Babylon; she even deigned to touch the side where Cador experienced such intense pain. " Are you subject to this cruel complaint ?" said she compassion- ately. "It sometimes nearly kills me," replied Cador, "and there is only one remedy which soothes it, and that is to apply on my side the nose of a man who died the day bef ere. "That is a etrange remedy!" said Azora. . " Not so strange,' he answered, "as Dr. Arnold's apoplexy

bags." Dr. Arnold was a Babylonian of those days, who pretended to cure all diseases by means of a bag suspended about the neck of the patient. This reason, and the great merit of the young man, de- cided Azora. " After all," said she, "when my husband passes from the world of yesterday into the world of to- morrow over the bridge of Tchinavar, the angel Asrael will not refuse to admit him because his nose a little shorter in the second life than in the first." So taking the razor in her hand, she went to the tomb of her husband, bathed it with her tears, and approached to cat off his nose as he lay extended in the coffin.—Zadig sprang up, holding Vs nose in one hand, and seizing the razor with the other : "Madam !" he cried, "say no more against the widow Corson! The idea of cutting off my nose is quite equal to that of turning a watercourse 1." And this is the end of my story. The most sincere of us, alas! are always hypocrites, but never so much as when we bring our grief before the eyes of the world .—From Ben Brierley's Journal.

MINERS' WAGES.—The Committee of the West Lancashire .Coalowners' Association and representatives of the miners n.iet at Liverpool on Wednesday to discuss the wages ques- tion. The masters having insisted on the necessity for the proposed reduction of ten per cent, the colliers' delegates asked for a postponement of any change for a month in order that they might ascertain the feeling of. the men; but the coalowners said the notice must be adhered to, and with this understanding the meeting terminated. STRIKE'S IN TEE WEAVING TRADE—The Committee Of the North Lancashire Power-loom Weavers' Association have endorsed the action of the Preston weavers who have struck work and declared the operatives entitled to strike pay. The advance for which the weavers have turned out was promised at the beginning of the year conditionally on the state of trade warranting it. There is no change in the relations of employers and operatives in the Burnley cotton trade. Meetings were held in several weaving towns on Wednesday evening, and at all of them resolutions were passed to contribute Zd per IGOM per week in support of those on strike. Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth has telegraphed offering mediation or arbitration in the Burnley cotton strike.

BEAM CHAMPAGNE.—The champagne districts of the Conti- nent produce some 300,000,000 bottles annually. Only one- haft of this quantity is exported. and yet England and America alone are said to consume more than twice this vast production. From whence does the balance come ? From the apple orchards on both sides the Atlantic! Yes, it is these apple orchards that are responsible for most of the cheaper champagnes. Now CANtarACE& CO. are offering, an AMERICAN CIDER CHAMPAGNE—the PURE JUICE of American apples—which they might easily pass oft as a champagne at ten trues the price : but they prefer to call a spade a spade! They are confident that everyone who tastes this most delicious and wholesome beverage, will, like Oliver Twist, ask for more.—Advt.

The Australians met the Eleven Of England team at Hudders- field on Saturday, the game ending in a draw, the Australians win h three wicket a to fall, wanting 154 runs to save a sin.,le Inning n dereat.—wltst n,niv sta runs to get to win the Players began their second innings against the Gentiemen, at the Oval, on Saturday. when the Players won the match by nine wicket,. —Nearly 1,100 runs were scored in the county contest between Sussex and Kent, which ended at Brighton, on Saturoay. in a draw greatly in favour of Sussex, The home tram, which had made 176 nuns overnight for the loss of two wickets in their second tunings, putt. gather the enormous total of 464. Of this number Jesse Hide, who went in at the fall of the sec md wicket at 134 played a grand innings of 112, being eventually got lid of at 314.—At Rochdale on Saturday, the Philadetphian en icketers achieve.; a decisive victory over the Oastleton cub defeating them by an Innings and 10 runs. This was the eleventh match played by the Philadelphians, of which they have won five, lost three, and drawn three. At Atgburi hon Monday the twelfth match in the Philadel- phians' tour was commenced in dull weather and in the pre- sence of few spectators. The Americans put together 185 and Liverpool had totalled 22 when the stumps were drawn for the day. On Tuesday the Philadelphians beat their opponents by four runs, the finish being most sensational. At the fall of the fifth wicket the home eleven only required 18 ruin, to win, of which numbsr the remain ing batsmen only realised 13, mainly due to the fine bowling of Lowry, who was well sup- ported by the field. It is only just, however, to say that the Liverpool gentlemen lost the match in a great measure through their anxiety to obtain the rut s in the few mlnu. es remainiug for play. the last wicket falling just on the stroke ot seven. Score: Liverpool, 283; Philaaelattans, 287 --On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday the Gentlemen,. Players match WAS play el at Lords, re•ultiog in the Gentlemen gaining a victory , , over the Players by six wi, kets The march was splendidly I contested from start to finish, all three days producing excel- lent cricket On Wednesday when the gentlemen went in to get 204 runs required to arm, the first two wickets fell for 29, and the chances looked certainly in favour of the Players. Then Messrs. Grace and Steel partnered, and by magnificient cricket put on 137 runs when On y were tvether. In the four innings there were exactly 1,000 runs scored The committee of the Marylebone Club have passed a resolution to the following effect i•—" That the committee of the Marylebone Club having learnt with regret that Barnes and Flowers, two professionals engaged on their staff at Lord's, refused to play for the Players of inland v. Austra- lians at Sheffield on June 30, one of the representative matches, do by this resolution express their strong disapproval of their want of public spirit." .

Owing to the unpropitious state of weather it was impossible to make a start on Thursday, in the match arranged between England and Australia Thewickets were pitched and the urn- res went out Into the field soon after twelve o'mo..lc. Then the rain set in steadily aad made such a mess of the ground that tie idea of commencing the game was abandoned.--At Brighton on Thursday, Bur ey in their first innings made 177 against Sussex. Ellis for Sussex had made eight wh m the stumps we e drawn for the day.

The Rev C H Collyns, secretary of the British Temper- ance League, died at his residence at Sheffield, on Tuesday. The Maori King and suite attended on Tuesday, a tem- perance fete at the Crystal Palace. The king addressed, in his native tongue, a meeting presided over by Sir Wil- fred Lawson.

THE POLICE AND THE Sr. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIA- TION.—On Thursday week 32 officers of the St. Helens county constabulary were present at the examination in con- nection with the St. Helens centre of the St. John's Ambu- lance Association. The examiner was Brigade-Surgeon E. Nicholson, A.M.D., and a report which has since been received from that gentleman shows results of a most en- couraging character. Every one of the candidates passed successfully, and the men are worthy of commendation for the evident care and attention they devoted to the lectures, delivered by Dr. Jardine. The following are the names of the successful candidates —lnspectors Joseph Keighley and Matthew Whittaker, Police-sergeants Edmund Pollitt, Samuel Ross, Charles Gilligan, William F. Montgomery; Police-constables James Cottara, Edward Caunce John Massey, James McHenry, Thomas Peters, James Blicliffe, David Chrystal, Win. Chrystal, William Simpson' John McDonald, Robert Pope, Walter Reeves, James Stelker, David Marsh, Elisha Millett, Benjamin Brocklebank, James Watters, Peter Dutton, John Henderson, Robert Rhymer, William Duerden, George Groarke, Win. Kendall, Alexander Young, George Tempnall, and Richard Morton. A LIVELY Die-maul/ice'. At GREENBANIE.—The particu- lars of a somewhat lively row at Greenbank were learned at the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, when a respect-- ably-dressed young woman named Bridget Shearon, was charged under a warrant with Using threatening language to Winifred Churchill, and also with wilfully damaging some windows of the dwelling house occupied by Mrs. Churchill.—Mr. Swift appeared for the complainant, and stated that his client resided in Bold-street, while the de- fendant formerly lived in Liverpool-street. Since the issue of the summonses, however, the defendant had been residing elsewhere, and had only just surrendered upon the warrant issued against her. It seemed that for some few weeks or a fortnight previous to the 17th Ante, Greenbank had been in a lively state and Mrs. Shearon and Mrs. Churchill had been more or less mixed up with the occurrences in the locality. On the morning of the date mentioned, Mrs. Churchill was at home when Mrs. Shearon came to the window with a large stone in her hand and she deliberately smashed two panes of glass, after which she threw the stone away. She then got the poker and a frying, pan and smashed all the windows in the house. During that dis- turbance she used very violent language towards Mrs. Chur- chill and threatened to kill her.—Several witneeses were afterwards called on both sides, and the Deneh ultimately fined the prisoner 5s and coats. •

FATAL CABLITAGH ACCIDENT.—WhiIe the Rey. Mr. Keith, minister of the Established Church, of Lybster, near Wick, was out driving on Saturday, the horses tookfright and ran off. The carriage was upset. and Mr. Keith thrown out on the road and received injuries from the effects of which be died in a few hours.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. A WIDNES CONTR eCTI)R CHARGED WITH THEFT. At Widnes Petty Sessione on Wednesdev, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and H. Gaskell, jun., Robert Smithson, carter, Lugedate-road, and night-soil contractor to Widnes Local Board, was summoned to answer a charge of stealing a,pair of reins, vain 4s, the property of Alice Lightfoot.— Mr. W T lin-band was for the complainant, and Mr. J. Agoowles for the defendant —Mr. Husband said Mrs. - htfoot kept the Golden Bowl public-house, Widnes, and on Friday afternoon last two of her carters were passing deem Lugsdale-road in charge of a horse and cart, when ate defendant emerged from his house, and seizing the nurse's head took the reins off, and had retained them. This was a high-handed sort of proceeding that ought to meet with condign punishment. If Smithson had any claim to tne • reins he bad a particular remedy in detinue in the County • Court. Had the horse been restive when the reins were re- Moved, it might have run away, and the lives of the public might have been endangered.—Robert Lightfoot, brother- in-law and manager for the complainant, deposed that the reins (produced) had been in Mrs. Lightfoot's possession for 12 years, and the defendant had no right whatever to them.—Thomes Simcock, jun., and Richard Brenton, certers at the Golden Bowl, confirmed Mr. Husband's state- ment of the occurrence, and identified the reins. The reins were also sworn to he Mrs. Lightfoot's property by John Spiers, carter, Moss Bank-road; Thomas Sitncock, sane and John Smith, carter, Midwood-street.—Ch tries Smithson, carter, brother to the defendant, most emphatically stated that the reins were his brothers, and pointed to certain 'identifying marks. He offered, amid laughter, in court to "back." his opinion by £lOO to a shilling—For the defence Mr. Knowles contended that the case ought never to have 'been brought into the police curt. He admitted that the reins were taken by Smithson, but when seizing them he distinctly said "these are mine," and the witnesees for the prosecution had partly admitted that. If Smithson was wrong is 'lie proceeding, Mrs Lightfoot had her remedy tor each an offence which was characterised in common law AS a treapass for which they could claim &Linage. If any Serrious damages were proved in the Coanty Court they I should be pleased to pry them. Mr Knowles quoted from Stoae's Justices' Manual to show that a thing taken on a I claim of right was not felony, and he pointed out that the openness or secrecy with which the thing was done had an , important bearing on the off,nce, and constituted the dis- t:notion between felony and trespass. Smithson took the reins openly and in a claim of right, and he (Mr Knowles) should submit that there was no charge whatever against him, and that the court had no jurisdiction.—Mr Gossage said the Bench thought Mr Smithson did not feloniously in- tend to steal the reins, but was under the impression that the reins were his. They therefore bad no jurisdiction in the case. but considered Smitheoa's proceedings most im- proper. `TERRIBLE FATALITY IN A SEWER AT WIDNES. Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner,. held an inquest at the Widnes Accident Hospital, on Thursday, on the body of Peter Griffin, wile died on Tuesday afternoon from injur- r• es teceived whilst working in the new sewer in Lower llouee-lane. Deceased was in the sewer when a skip, filled with clay, MO being hauled up by a steam crane. The I machinery became out of order, and the skip fell back into the excavation and buried the deceased beneath its weight. Mr. C. H. Lewin was present on behalf of Messrs. Evans and Lewin, contractors; and Mr. J. W. Knowles for the rela- tives of the deceased.—John Griffin, of Nelson-street, de• osed that the deceased was his brother, and lived at 17, I.,ke-street. He was unmarried, and followed the employ- j ment of a contractor's labourer.—John Carricker, of 44, Cromwell-street, Widnes, said he was an engine driver in the employ of Mears. Evans and Lewin, and was at present working at the new sewer in Lower House-lane. The ex- cavated clay was brought out of the sewer by means of skip, which was worked by a moveable steam crane. He had been in charge of the crane for the last three weeks, and some time ago be was in charge of it for six or seven months. On Tuesday the deceased was in the sewer with two other c:t,n named Small and Luke. At the point where they were , working the sewer would be about 15 feet deep. The skip , containing clay had been drawn to within four or five feet of the top when the" key " went out of the drum of the crane. Immediately the heavily laden skip descended repidly into the sewer. He put his foot upon the brake, but ee it would not act, he shouted as loudly as he could, as did also the banksman. The deceased had no right to be Loderneath the skip when it was being wound up, and he Lad frequeatly heard the foreman tell the men to stand out of the way. He made a thorough inspection of the ma- chinery at one o'clock on Tuesday, and everything was than in proper order.—By Mr. Lewin :We had never known a like accident before. The drum was the last pLece where they would have expected an accident, and nothing he could have done would have prevented the occurrence. —By Mr. Knowles He bad had fifteen years experince as an engine driver. He had pulled te pieces and, fitted up the crane he was now working. The crane was only about 12 months old.—By the Coroner: The key which he had new put in the drum had a :bead on it; the old key, which was not headed, was put in by the maker of the crane.—Michael Small, labourer, deecribed how the skip fell upon the deceased, who, he said, ought to have kept clear—common experience told him to keep clear of the skip. The man on the bank had frequently told them to stand clear.—Thomas Cammiskey, binksman for the contractors, deposed to warning the men to stand away when the skip was being wound up.—Mise Downie, eue.tren at the hospital, said the deceased was admitted on Tuesday last, suffering from iejaries to the abdomen and the lower part of the body. Dr. O'Keeffe was with the de- ceased; who died at half-past three.—The Coroner having summed up, the foreman of the jury said they would like to &mew what weight the crane was capable of lifting, and what it was lifting at the time of the accident —Thomas Dibble Lewin, the contractor, said it would be quite sire to lift two tons weight with the steam crane. When the iron skip was filled the weight would be about 15 cwt.—After conferring in private for some time the jury come to the conclusion that the deceased came to his death accidentally, and contributed to the result by negligently not standing clear of the skip.—Mr. Lewin said no one regretted the acci- dent more than Mews. Evans and Co. The deceased had to relatives in Widnes except his brother, and the firm meant to pay the expenses of his burial. They could not do anything more than that.—The foreman remarked upon the kindness displayed.

6USFICIOUS DEATH OF A CHILD AT WIDNES. INQUEST AND VERDICT. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner for the honour and fee of -Batten, opened an inquest at the Prospect inn, Weston, into (because 4.,," death of the infant son of Wm. Atherton, farm labourer, Kings7ooCl. It appeared that Atherton's wife died about six weeks ago, end her child was put out to nurse with Mrs. Ribbert. of Wesion Point. On Friday last week ties e(1 died at the house of Mrs. Whitby, but as the child, although seven months old, only weighed a little over ' °lbs.' Dr. McDougall refused to give a certificate of death until the coroner had been made acquainted with the facts. lllr. James Coll:er was foreman of the jury.—William , Atherton said big wife died on the 15th May. She nursei ' the deceased child up to her death. When his wife died he rnt the child out to nurse with Aon Hibbert. big wife's etster.in-law. The child was always a weakly one, and I white it was with Mrs. Hibbert he saw it about once a,l week. On Monday. the 30th of June, be took the child from Mrs. Hibbert because she had not time to look after It,' en account of one of her own children being ill. The child was always clean, and seemed to be taken care of.. He had ' seen it taking food. He heard no complaint before be moved the child. Since be moved it be had beard that Kra. Hibbert had not taken care of the child. He bad beard that she had not bees seen with it ie her arms. He had lean Mrs. Hibbert with it when be was there. He did not pay Mrs. Ilibbert a fixed sum, but he had given her 6s MI for the whole of the time she had bad it. Last week but 1 one he left her some money,but she would not have it. Mrs. filbbert bad three children at home. He did not expect the &lid to live as he thought it was wasting from the birth.— The Coroner said be had not had a p•st-mortem examina- tion made, but from what he had heard since he came there he was inclined to tbink it was a case in which such as ex- amination should be made in justice to the people who had had the child under their care, so as to clearly decide whether the child bad received proper attention or net. It would, therefore, he better to adjeurn the inquiry until the doctor could make such an examination.—The inquest was then adjourned until Tuesday at 12-30.—The adjourned in- (lorry evis resumed on Tuesday at the time and place fixed, before Mr. T. J. Ridgway.—lnspector Atherton, of ft uncorn, was present on behalf of the police.—The evidence g.ven by the father on the last occasion was read, and tkerf or. Dwell was sworn. He said the child was brought to his surge-11r by Mrs. Hibbert shortly after she had taken charge of it. Be exemined the child. It seemed to him to be pining and wasting away. He did not detect any speci- fic disease ; but he believed that the child was suffering _trout diarrhoea. Be prescribed for the child, and told Mrs. Hibbert that she must be careful about its diet. He had also teen the child when attending Mrs. Hibbert's children at her own house. He could not tell whether be ever prescribed for the child again. From the first it Was a question with him whether medicine wonld ever do it ay good. The child always appeared to be in a cleanly eats. Had be been called upon to give a certificate of death, he shonld have stated that the cause of death was imironnis. The child was continually crying and pining. The child WAS a very small one.—Mrs. Hibbert, after beinz cautioned by the Coroner, was sworn, and said she was the Wife of William Hibbert, a quarryman, of Weston Point. The deceased was placed in her charge five weeks last Thursday, when she fetched it from King,wood. It wa • tbffi in a very weak state. She took it to Dr. Heenan the ' ot lo w ing morning. He prescribed for it, and she carried out his instructions.—The Coroner: Did von ever give the child any paregoric of any deacript ion —Witness : No, Sir. Cr. Ragnall asked whether it had been used to" Mothers' friead," and I said it had. Dr. Bignell said I must not give it any more. In reply to further questions, witnelse said one never gave the child any paregoric, opium, or anything of that sort. She parted with the child because her own was ill, and the docter ordered her to give it up. She did everything she could for the child, even neglecting her own baby to attend to it.—By the Foreman : The father did no' want her to give the baby up.—The Coroner: Are you sure the doctor ordered you to give it gin P Witness : yes. Be asked me whether it was troubled with the bowel complaint and said I might give it a drop or two of gin in its fond occasionally. Martha weh,rhy, wife of Thomas Whitby, labourer, of Wes- ton, deposed that she took possession of the child on Monday week at the request of the father, who wished her to keep it for a :crtnight. She went down to Mrs. Ilibbert's house

The fact that the father had heard that the woman with whom he put the child to nurse had not done her duty, and the furthti- consi- deration that the child at the age of seven months weighed less than an ordinary child I Ought to do at birth, were strong reasons why they should ascertain the exact cause of death and free any persons who had had to do with the child from blame if I they deserved to be free from blame, and if they were respon- sible that the blame might be put on the right shoulders.
