They thought she had done her , duty whilst she had the child. I WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. 1 The monthly meeting was held in the Board-room, Victoria-road, on Thursday afternoon. Present: Messrs. .T. S. Tirnmis (chairman), Rev. Father Clark, Bradshaw, Deacon, Imison, Glover, and Denby (clerk.) EDUCATION IN TEE DISTRICT: INTERESTING STATISTICS. Mr. Deacon said that during the holidays the attendance j officers were employed in taking a census of the children of , the district, the results of which were now submitted to the I Board in a tabular form. Mr. Deacon reviewed the table at , some length, remarking that it showed that the total number lof houses in the town was 5,092, of which 4,524 were in- I habitsd, an increase of 216 inhabited on the previous year. I He was glad to be able to report that in very few instances I indeed were there two or more families living in the same house. As a general rule each family had a house of its own, and the instances in exception of that were compara-1 tivelv few. With regard to the accommodation in exiottng I schools, there had been various alterations during the past year, and there were now places for 778 more children 1 than last year. The increase had been at Simms Crosse West Bank and St. Mary's, and a decrease at St. Luke's. The number of children between the ages of three and thir- teen was this year 6,665, last year 0250, being an increase 'of 415. This was rather remarkable because for the last three 1 years there had been practically according to the census no I increase, the figures being 1881, 6,191 ; 1882, 6,236 ; 1883, 1 6,250; so that in these years there had only been an In- crease of about 50 children, whereas between thityyear and last there had been increase of 415 in attend Inca at school which was very marked indeed. That increase must cur- respond with an increase of population, which must be con- siderably larger this year than it was last year. The access of accommodation was nominal only, because they had a much larger number of school-going children than was shown by the deductions in the tables. They would observe that one column in table two was labelled Ditton. The reason for that was that there were come chil- dren whose parents lived in the town sent to schools in Dit- ton. These were children who attended badly the schools in Whines, and he supposed the Board had shown the parents that they could not allow their children to attend badly In Widnes, and so they tried to send them to Ditton. They bad- hid the parents before the committee, and informed them that although their children were going to Ditton they were still liable to the authority of the Board. Last year out of 6,250 children 1,155 attended no school, while this year out of 6,665 children only 1,187 attended no school, white was , a very small increase. The number of children between three and five years on the rolls was rather smaller, being this year 336, last year 405. Personally, he thought this WAS a fact not to be regretted, as it was rather a mistake for children under five to attend school. So long as they attended .regul-arly when they a' teined that age it seemed to him to be unnecessary to send them before five. They would also notice that the number of children between 13 and 14on the rolls was much decreased. This year it was 177, last year 217, and the number had been steadily decreasing for the last four years. That must mean that the children were passing through the standards much earlier, and would show that children had plenty of time after reaching five years of age, to get through the necessary standards. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND THE SHLP' CANAL. Yesterday afternoon a special meeting of the Warrington General Purposes Committee- was held in the Town Hall to consider the advisableness ct voting a sum towards promo- ting the Ship Canal Bill. There was a good attendance of members. amongst those present being the Mayor (in the chair)., Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Kean, and Pickmere ; Councillors Broadbent, Dion, Greening. Taylor, Marsh, Bur3eBs, Whittle, Mackie, and Bolton. After some discus- sion, it was proposed by Alderman Burgess that a sum of money equal to id in the .f.,', which was in round figures estimated to be 4;500, be voted out of the borough rate in promotion of the Manchester Ship Canal, and that a special meeting of the Council and a meeting of the ratepayers, necessary under the Boroagh Funds Act, be called to wathorise the expenditure of that sum of money. This motion was earnestly supported by the Mayor, Aldermen lean and Pickmere, Dr. Mackie, and others. Exception was taken to the resolution. by Alderman Holmes, and Coun- cillors Broadbent, Burgess, Bolton, and Whittle. Ultimately the resolution was carried by a considerable majority. It may be mentioned that the General Purposes Committee is a committee of the whole Council, so that it is in every way probable that a resolution passed by it will also be car- ried at a Council meeting, though, of course, it is by no means impossible for such a resolution to be negatived by the full Council.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

Sir,—" Cap'ain Cattle ' has jumped to conclusions which are certainly not suggested by nay former letter. I did not say that I should withhold my vote at the next election unlese one of the tw• candidates at present before our constituency coincides with my views upon the very im- portant question of Sunday closing. What I shall certainly do will be to vote, and to vote for the man whose opinions are nearest alike to my own. It I cannot get the whole loaf I will keep myself from positive starvation by taking as much of it as I can possibly obtain, and in the meantime push my views with all the energy and persuasion I am possessed of. "Captain Culle," with the same guileless honesty which characterised his famous prototype, proves my case admirably. He admits that public-houees are not fit for "even social reformers to meet in on a Sunday." He tells as also "how unfit some of the publicans are for the posi- tions they hold," and that "a proper state of thing would tumble such men (publicans) out of their houses: "He (that is, •Catain Cattle's' publican,) evidently thinks the public exist for his benefit, and not he 4or their conveni- ence." Where is the ideal publican who carries on his busi- ness in such a style as leads his cueomers to believe that he exists for their convenience,and not they for his benefit? Such a man certainly does not live in our day, whatever may have been the case hundrecla of years ago. But to come to the main question—why should public houses be kept open on Sundtys at all? To take the lowest line of argument, I say that ttlf opening of these places on Sunday 'a, 'Elle cauga of thousands of Meta and women "'oaring to keep their nosey to the grindstone (and what a grindstone it is) seven days to the week, and not merely six." Again, every other manu- facturer, merchatat, shopkeeper, and employer of labour is I compelled by both law and custom, except under extraordi- ' ---‘, circumstances to close his place and liberate his e:'^rk- t people for the "day of reef," and why should this particular trade be exempt from so salutary a regulation? Again, "Captain Cuttle" must know that it is not the moderate drinkers among our countrymen who are the best supporters of the public-bons. It is rather threw men who nearly every &turd ,y and Sunday of their lives make a practice of getting drunk, or at any rate, of taking so much liquor as to be more or less "hoed," and it is mainly for these men, forsooth, that public houses are to be kept open on Sundays. Sunday drinking is the most fruitful cause of " playing " on Monday, and I am free to assert that no proposal is so cal- culated to bmetit the working dames in particular, together with their wives and families, as the shutting up of all drinking shops on Sunday. I am net anxious to " drive " anybody into either chapel or church, and except that I ob- ject to the extra labour which would be incurred I am , quite prepared to go far the opening of museums and read- ing rooms on Sundays, or for any other measure which is cal- culated in the smallest degree to brighten the lives and lighten the loads now borne try my fellow-men. I value " education "as highly as "Captain Cuttle " does, but at the same time my eyes are not closed to the fact that in the alums of our great towns are to be found to-day shoals of men whose lives are the most depraved and besotted, but whose early education was far superior to anything which ordinary individuals can hope for. How is it, then, that these men fall, and "taillike Lucifer?" Simply beotsse the tempt ations to drink abounding on every hand, and the customs of" society" have waged war against their morale and setbdued their force of character. en conclusion, let "Captain Cattle" tell us in what sense, morally, physically, politically, socially, or religiously, any man can possibly be benefited by spending his Sunday or any portion of it in sitting drieking in a public-house.—Yours, (rec.. SOCIAL REFORMER.

div.head: STATE CHURCH.
div.p: THE STATE CHURCH.

Sir,—The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in his efforts to defend that relic of az intolerant age—the State Chnrch—places himself in a somewhat ridiculous position. He entirely for- gets that not only the Church, but the thousand and one drones that are li-Ang on its resources, have ceased to minister to the wrotts of the people. Instead of being the temple of God the Church is the home of an intolerant sectarianism, and her clergy aspire to control the human conscience in a manner that has become simply intolerable. In the correspondence- you publish the Rev. E CE Carleton displays himself in hiz true colours; instead of being a preacher of good-will, -whenever he has the opportunity, he swings the tomahawk and; likea true Irishman, calla upon somebody to' tread on the tail of my coat." Poor fellow, his character being so well known, no one cares to waste time on him, so he rushes off to Mr. W. Crosfield; and in a most "nefarious" manner attempts to draw that gentleman out on a subject upon which all. sensible men havedong made up their minds.

Mr. Carleton seems to think it impossible for the linger to be placed upon any especial Act which distinctly and in so many words established the Church. Now I should think that anyone descending to theme of such scornful words as are contained in the letters published, would do well to keep his own ground as clear as possible. Is Mr. Carleton aware that in no instance is the word church referred to previous to Henry VIII. time as the Protestant Church 2 Of course he knows this, the word not having then been coined. He knows full well that the Chuck of Rothe was the church referred to, not only up to this date but for long after. Every Act, and they can be pointed to without number, enforcing the payment of tithes was are Act establishing the Church. Every Act granting special privileges to clergymen gars them a.social position superior.to that of other ministers of the Gospel, and so far established them. Every Act deter- mining the pains and penalties to which the careless, and those who.wonid not conform, should be subject, was an Ant intended to weld together a pious fraud, a despotic cristo- cracy, and a kingly rule. These three, acting on a people priding themselves more on their martial achievements than on any eflacatisnal code, have so far sustained ua.ae nation. To-day the people are- determined none of three shall exist any longer as privileged classes. Jost at present it is not quite clear which must go fiist. The House of Lords seems determined to commit suicide, so for the present we leave it. _ _

Our reverend friend hints at--a word he does not mention. Guessing at the word, perhaps- ho means robbery, in plain English. Well, there is net moat in a word, but will be kindly tell us-voters what he means by the following sentence? "Of course, the only form ;n which Christianity NVAS pre- sented to the people at that time wax a Church forra." I have troubled myself some little ti find out the meaning of the word Church. Dr. Vance Smith, who is, I suppo3e, equal to the Rev. Mr. Carleton in scholarship, tells us "that it is not, aad moot be, the exoluaive property of any single communion." I conclude from this that any body, of men, however numerous, or however insignificant, have a right to the term, and that no body has a right to arrogate to it- self ouch a position as the Established Church of England tries to do. The Rev. gentleman speaks of Congregationalism as "a thing of modern growth." Why, be might say the same of the clothes on his back. Was it a usual•thing for the Apostles and early Fathers to take themselves- off to tlae Lakes of Killarney to the utter neglect of their flock P Did "the Christian rulers of ancient times "' pay Bishops , to sit in a House of Lords to vote in favour of pigeon shoot- ing ? To read at Church that all men are equal in the sight of God, and yet are unequal in a Franehise Bill? From the Test and Corporation Acts down to the [lariat Act , the Bishops have made us feel that they are an integral por-, it on of the State. This State Church that has taken so many Acts to establish it now clasps civil society with the arms of an octopus. Little by little. it sucks and exhausts every movement with which it beoomes connected, and threatens to stifle and kill all around it. It has become rich beciuse there has been a great namber of simple souls who thought to obtain grace from on high by giving or bequeath, log wealth and property to its inatitutiorm. . To say the Church is not established is to confess weak- ' ness. "Point to the act and repeal it," say these equivoca- tors. They forget the history of the Church lies open for the liberators, as for the defender to read. Pope Gregory protested against the temples of the heathen being destroyed. "Let holy water be made and sprinkled In the sai,d temples, for it is requisite they be converted from the worship of devils to the service of the true God." I rather think Abbot Melitis (A. G. 601) was an instrument for putting in- to use the word about which our Rev friead is so dioident at using. If the Church is tot Establialied by law, bow is it that until the year 1867 all parishioners were liable for

div.head: POLITICAL cm's: THE PEERS AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.
div.p: THE POLITICAL cm's: THE PEERS AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.

ii;-dia;i;iOiii-n 'the Hop-tie-of kwda Tttesday nicht on the Franchise Bill the Minority included the two Arch- bishops and ten Bishops, viz, Bath and Wells, Carlisle, Chichester, Durham, Ely, Exeter, Manchester, Oxford, St. Asaph, and Winchester. The following five Conservatives also voted for the Bill, viz , the Duke of Norfolk, Earle Jer• sey, Leitrim, and Wernyss, and Lord Haldon. The Duke of Marlberough and Lord Tennyson identified themselves with the Liberal party by voting in this lobby, and Lords Bramwell and Alcester and the following Independent Liberals were also with the Ministers, v'z , Earls Fitz- william and Fortescne, and Lord Stratheden and Camp- bell. 1 The majority comprised only dye Liberals, viz, the Mar. gals of Clanricarde, Earl Gosford, Viscount Torrington. and Lords Stanley of Alderley and Fitzhardinge. Bat one Bishop—Gloucester and Bristol—voted against the Bill. Lprd Napier of Magdala voted with the Conservatives, and Lords Ravensworth and Brabourne also went with their party. Noticeable a.nongst the absentees from the division are Earls Grey and Dunraven, and Viscount Sherbrooke. Thirteen Bishops did not vote, viz., London, Norwich, Bangor, Worcester, St. Alban's Hereford, Peterborough, Lincoln, Salisbury St. David's, Rochester, Lichfistd, and Liverpool. The division was taken in a vary full House, the fullest probably within living memory, 351 Peers voting out of a tot il of Just over 500 (excluding Peers of the Royal blood). The largest number voting hitherto was in August, 1880, when the Compensation for Disturbance (Irelamt) Bill was rejected by 292 to 51, giving a total of 433, or 18 less than Tuesday night's. Next in point of number was that on the second reading of the Irish Church Bill, when 325-176 to 119—vote1 and 18 paired. A noticeable coincidence, too, is that the majority on that occasion was the same as on Tuesday night. On the occasion of the rejection of the De- ceased Wife's Sister Bill the House numbered 32?-165 t) 158; and on the Vote of Censure in February last the House numbered 282-181 to 81.

It is intsresting to compare the divisions in the Lora on the Reform Mlls of 1831-2. Even in the divisions in the former year, and when voting by proxy was permitted, the total votes reerded was only 357-199 to 158. In the fol. lowing year,when the bill was a second time rejected by 184 to 175, the total was 359—an increase of two. On the occa- Mon of the third reading of the bill the House numbered'Unt 128-106 to 22. The Times, in ita' second edition of Wednesday, published the following :—"lr. Gladstone has had a conference with his colleagues this morning as to the crisis, but a full meet- ing-of the Cabinet will not be held until later in the dayk The Prime Minister ia being urged by many of his suppor- ters in the House of Commons to dissolve, but there are stiong reasons agamet this course, and the impression le- general that there will be an autumn session." The Cabinet held an informal meeting early on Wednes- day, and in the afternoon reassembled at the official resi- dence of the Premier. The Council at for three hours. Sir Charles Dilke, going fresh from the Council to a meet- ing of Liberals in promotion of the candidature of Lord Kensington and Mr Caine for Middlesex, very soon allowed- it to appear that there is to be no immediate dissolution. He repudiated the idea that because an irresponsible and unre- presentative body like the House of Ler& had chosen to re- ject the Franchise Bill, therefore the House which had pas- sed that bill by a practically, unanimous vote should ba " sent aboutits business." The general feeling of the Liberal party would, he thought, be in favour of re-1 presenting the bill again and again to the House of Lords until it was passed. He announced that Mr. Gladstone had called a general meeting of his followers in the House of Commons for this. afternoon, at which he would explain the course he intended to take in the House at four o'clock. Commenting on Lord Salisbury's "extra- ordinary rashness," Sir Charles said the remark that "matters were going on charmingly in Egypt from a Con- servative point of view," might be answered by the state- ment that matters, were going on charmingly in the House of Lords from is Radical point ot view. The did not believe that the majority of the Peers would continue to follow Lord Salisbury. The House of Lords possessed great powers on the condition that it used them with scrupulous modera- tion. If they were used to thwart the will of the people, as expressed by planing so many Liberal Governments in power' since 1832, the result must be disastrous to the Pears. The right hon. Baronet warned Lord Salisbury that his reign was disputed in the constituencies if not in the Legislatne, and asserted that the Conservatives of Lancashire were in favour of the Franchise Bill being passed at once. If the Lancashire Conservatives spoke out their voice would be heard. He gave instances of Tory obstruction in the House, and said that the question of the method of transact- ing public business would be one of the most important W;th which the constituencies would have to deal in the coming struggle. The proposal to bold a great Reform demonstration in lyde-park on Monday, the 21st inst., has been eagerly ,enepted, and is being promptly acte4 upon in all parts of he country. The increased communications arriving,eyester- day at the Committee-rooms, 18, walhroek, conclusively show that the result of the Franchise Bill division in the House of Lords has had the immediate effect of spurring the provinces to action. The National Reform Union, in the North, is arranging demonstrations of its own, but al- ready inquiries and resolutions, evidencing hearty co-opera- tion, have been forwarded to London from Liberal associa- tions in such remote parts as Staffordshire and Norfolk, as well as from counties nearer the home district. The war- cry printed upon the yellow hand-bills. circulated broad- case, is given in the taking headline, "The Peers and the Franchise," and the Demonstration Committee, sanguine as they were, have been astonished at the ready response to it. MEETING OF THE LIBEL PARTY.—THE DECI- SION OF THE GOTEENMENT. There were 256 Liberal members of the House of Com- mons at the meeting of the party which was held on Thurs- day afternoon in the large room of the Foreign Office, A considerable crowd waited outside in the quadratagle to watch their arrival, and on the appearance of the members of the Cabinet and other leading men there was consider- able cheering. Mr Gladstone, Mr Bright, and Mr Chamber- lain had an especially warm reception. The meeting had been convened for balf-past two o'clock, and by that time most of the members had already assembled in the hall, which proved none too large for the purpose. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH CHURCEI CHOIR.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH CHURCEI CHOIR.

. PRESENTATIONS TO MR. TIMSON. The annual trip of the members of the Stockton Heath Chuch choir was held on Tuesday. The place chosen this year was Chester, at which ancient town a very pleasant day was spent in visiting the Cathedral, the " Rows," and other places of interest. The party proceeded to Chester in wagonettes, and on their arrival there they sat down to a substantial dinner, at the conclusion of which Mr Joseph Whitlow, senior chorister, on behalf of the choir and many of the congregation, presented Mr T 11 Timson, the retiring organ'st and schoolmaster, with a valuable case of electro- plate and cutlery (worth about twelve guineas.) In making tht presentation, Mr Whitlow said he was happy in that way to express his own feeling and the feeling of the other members of the choir of their indebtedness to Mr. Timson for his unwearying efforts in teaching them and in bringing the choir to its present excellent condition. Mr Timson, in acknowledging the present, said it would be peculiarly acceptable to him as proving that, amidst all the trouble and difficulty he had bad during the past six months, he had many staunch friends in Stockton Heath. He had endeavoured, whilst in charge of the choir and school, to do his duty to the best of his ability, and he took their gift to be an expression of feeling on the part of a large number of parishioners that they were convinced that he had done his duty. He felt regret at leaving so many friends, but be was pleased to saa that in Il.ina Stockton Heath to take charge of the Guild Hall Schools, Bury St. Edinonda, he was im- proving his position and entering upon a lar- ger field of usefulness.—lt may be mentioned that the boys in the day school at Steckton Heath have presented Mr Timson, their late master, with a very Iloafd hst;emeet:orra,vel ?Ilan gt hheaigr, bienh aol frd; eitdo sohneewo ft their ah pa r,ri rdescol iion(..l older scholars also pfesehted Mr litTlSOrt wil:u A handsome copy of Dicken's "Great Expeetailoias." Last av evening's service being the last at which Mr Timson was to officiate as organist and leader oi the choir, there were many of his old friends preeent ; and in the course of the eervice three psalms were sung to chants of Mr Timson's own composing. It would seem that all the soreness of feeling caused in Stockton Heath by the recent dispute between the vicar and Mr Timson has not disappeared, and it is now said that her- tain members of the choir have expressed their intention of resigning their positions in consequence of the very cavalier manner in wh.ch their protest against Mr Timson' s dismis- sal was treated by the vicar and other managers of the school. Many of Mr Timson's friends are also disposed to congratulate him on the fact that in hie new sphere of labour he will not be so directly under the influence of clerical management as he has been at Stockton Heath.

The Municipal Council of Paris have decided in fa-our of proceeding with the National fete notwithstanding the eholera ; the military reviews will also take place. The Commission could not conclude its labours on Friday, and therefore another meeting will be held n-a-t,,iis to the date being fixed for the second, meeting of the Co ifersnee. RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN buoTLAND —The train which left Glasgow for Rucklyvie, on Thursday night, left the rails at Strathblane, owing to a subsidence of the ern:34Hk- ment from the floods. The driver, Robert Mallon, and Wm. Rodger Younger, a. carrier, of ,Campsie, who was on the en- gine, were killed outright, and the fireman and driver were serious scalded. The carriages, fortunately, kept the rails, and only the engine was damaged by falling down the em- bankment. The carrier was riding on the engine with Mal- lon, and thus met with his fatal injuries. So much damage was done on this section wf the North British Railway, that ' it could not be used at all yesterday, and traffic has been diverted to another route.
TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN SEIEF7IELD.-A MOTHER ANA FOUR CHILDREN MURDERED:

Some time during Thursday night a terrible tragedy was committed at Sheffield by a man named Joseph aycock, a hawker, who lived in the Irish quarter of the town. He bad a wife and fear children. He was a Ma 3 of violent temper, frequently quarrelled with his wife, and had only recently come out of prison for an assault upon her. Just before midnight a neighbour heard the wife scream, but as this was a common occurrence no attention was paid to it. As the inmates of the house did not appear yesterday morn- ing, another neighbour went to the door soon after 10 t o'clock to see what was the matter. She then found Lay.. cock's wife lying dead in a pool of blood on the floor with a terrible gash in her throat, her head being nearly severed from her body. Going upstairs she found haycock's four children lying in bed dead, with their throats also cut, and haycock himself leaning against the wall with ' blood flowing from a wound in hill throat. He was alive, but unconscious. The police were communicated with, and when they entered the bedroom haycock begged not to be removed, and said "Let me die here." There was scarcely a vestige of furniture in the room, and one of the murdered children was lying perfectly naked. Her head was almost , sev• red from the body. The other children had on ragged shirts. 'lhe murdered woman had all her clothes on, audit is evident that, after murdering her, haycock went upatairs and completed his terrible work. The murders were com- mitted with a large carving knife. Laycock, who was taken to the hospital, is expected to recover. It is said that early ' on Thursday night haycock went to his wife's mother, and told her that be intended doing something desperate during the night. She begged him not to do 80, and at length he said he would not. The poor woman had assisted to main- ' taid her husband and children by purchasing and selling Ibottles. "She was very bard working, and but for her husband would have been houseless. She was far advanced in pregnancy. The tragedy hae naturally created much. I sensation in Sheffield,

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four O'clock. LORD SALISBURY AND TILE FRANCHISE BILL...*The eiarq of ULIt•BURY drew attention to the Prime Minis- ter's speech at tile naeirsa ()Mee yesterday, and emphati- cally denied that any overtures had been made by the Go- vernment to him with regard to the Franchise Bill, and complained that the Prime Minister had misrepresented him. —Earl Granville and Earl Csirns rose together, and, neither Riving way, the House divided on the order of pre- cedence, when 27 voted for Lord Granville and 26 for Lord Cairns.—Lord GRANVILLE read notes of a private conversa- tion with Lord Cairns on Tuesday night, and explained that Mr. Gladstoue, speaking of Lord Salisbury as declining to discuss the Franchise Bill with a rope round his neck, and, considering people to be enfranchised as wild beasts, were intended as a summary of Lord Salisbury's opinions, and not as a quotation from his speech.—The Lord Chan- cellor, Lord de Lisle, and Lord Waveney took part in the subsequent discussion, and the subject dropped. The orders of the day were disposed of and the House adjourned. The House ran at four o'clock.

div.head: EXCITING SCENE
div.p: EXCITING SCENE

Lord R. CHURCHILL wished to know howe wben, and by whom the offer of a compromise was made to the House of tords on the Franchise Bill, and whether the published report of Mr. Gladatone's speoch at the Foreign Office was correct. —Mr. Glans-rose said the report was correct as regarded the offer of a compromise. It was made by Earl Granville to Earl Cairns, and cleaned, be- cause it did not add anything to, the assurances already given, but afterwards some written,words came that the com- promise would bearcepted if the Government agree to insert in the Franchise Bill a clause that it abauld take effect on the first of January am, unless an acawas passed providing ter an earlier date. The offer was not made as private and confidential.—Sir S. NORTIICOTE said the compromise was made two hours after the debate com- menced, and as private and confidential. He denied the correctness of the words attributed to Lord Salisbury by the Priemier that he (Lord Salisbury) declined to consider Redistribution with a rope round his neck. Such a statement could only have been made, to prejudice 7.10 rd Salisbury. Mr. GLADSTONE justified the words need in his speech. He denied that the offer of a compromise was made as private and confiden- tial. It was the last offer on the altar of. peace —Lord R CHURCHILL moved the adjournment of this House, and in- sisted that the offer was private and confidential. If not, he asked why wee it not made to the House of Lords. He ac- cused Mr Gladstone of traducing Lord Salisburv.—Sir S NORTIECOTE said he had the authority of Earl Cairns to say he understood the offer was private and confidential.—An angry discussion ensued—Mr GLADSTONEV repelled the charge of traducing an adversary, and said Such imputa- tion was diseraceful, amiclut tremendous cheering. He again ineisted that the offer of a compromise was neither private nor confidential. Mr GIBSON contended that the impression of Earl Cairns was correct, as he heard the conversation between Earl Granville and Lord Cairns.— Sir W. HARCOURT defended the offer of a compromise, and with regard to the House of Lords, he did not wish to speak disrespectfully of that body, but he severely- condemned dm conduct of men who had misled that assembly by coercing an unwilling raajority. As to whether the offer was private the country could judge by results and be was sure it would be of opinion that everything had been done by the Liberal party and its illustrious leader to bring the Bill to a successful conclasion.—Mr.Gonsr. contended that he offer of a compromise was made to lead Lord Salisbury and LA Cairns into a trap.—After observations from Mr. McLiver, Mr. COWEN said he felt that the result of the 'present discuselon would be to induce the Home of Lords te pest the Pranchise Bill in October.—Mr. .1. Loarrnau :tholicbt,abe compromise offered by the Government a ,worthless sham —The discussion was continued by Mr. Macfarlane, Mr, Schott Rooth and Mr. Healy—Mr. WHIT- RUED trusted that after the explanations that had.been made that night, the Howie of Lords might yet re-consider their decision. Lord R. Cannon-ma expressed deep regret for using words personally huraul to the Prime Minicter. Hewes su- ffering from vexation when he (lid so. Aa regarded a com- promise, if the Goversmaent were willing again to approach the Lords, he would willingly do all in hie power to avoid two Houses entering into conflict. —Mr. GLABSIiONE ex- pressed satisfaction &. the observations of the noble lord, and said if a comoromisa oouid be brought about the Govern- ment were still in the same spirit—The motion for ad- journment of the Howse was withdrawn. Mr. Mowx calledaattention to the half-past twelve o'clock rule.—The House- was counted, and forty members not being pre sent, it adjourned at a quarter to one.

STOIKH OF WEAVERS.-0a Wednesday nearly the whcle of the weavers employed at the Cockhedge Mills by Messrs Armitage and Rigby, struck work to consequence of the firm respiring the operatives to pick their pieces whilst weaving them. It bas been, it is stated, the custom of the weavers to pick their pieces when they are completed, but the employers now require them to do this work whilst the piece is tv.dng worked, as is done in other cotton mills. The mills contain over 1,000 lsoms, and the weavers, who nom - her some hundreas, turned out on Wednesday. When they left work they indulged in considerable hooting and shout- ing. On Thursday the strike was terminated, and the heal resumed work, we Aro informed, at the taaStare terms.

FRODSHAM. CROSTIELD SUNDAY Scnoora—The scholars attending this school had their annual treat on Tuesday, when they were taken in special carriages by rail to Beeston. The children were regaled with a' capital tea, and all the ar- rangements were successfully carried out. The sch.lars were delighted with the exceptional character of the treat. • CAMPING OUT OF VoLUNTEERS.—A bout forty members of the Frodtham Volunteer corps marched from the Town Hall, Frodsham, to the station on Saturday afternoon headed by the band, en route for Conway camp. Each man carried a knapsack, and the company were much ad- mired for their smart appearance and soldierlike bearing. FREE CHUTICH SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Special sermons were preached in the Methodist Free Church. Frodsham, on Sun- day, by Mr J W Chisholm, of Liverpool, in aid of the Sun- day school fond, and the annual treat to the scholars was given on Tuesday, when the children spent a pleasant after- noon at Mr Percival's farm, Godscroft, near Frodsham, where a substantial tea and a round of amusements were pro- vided for their enjoyment. CATTLE SALE AT FRODSILAIL—MC Steward held his usual fortnightly sale of fat and store stock on Tuesday. There was a good attendance of buyers, dud a fair quantity of atock on offer, comprising several fat cows and heifers, 150 fat sheep, including 80 prime fat lambs; 12 fat calves, dm. Fat beasts made from £l7 to £22 7s 61; fat sheep, 42s to 57s Cld ; fat lambs, 30s 61 to 565; fat calves, 20a to 425. Beef and veal tfade rather lower. Sheep and lambs fully maintained former prices. FRODSHAM Fauna Carscrt Towma.-1 he work of res- toration of Frcdsham Parish Church,vihich has so recently been carried out, did not extend to the tower through lack of funds. It was hoped that the tower would have stood for some years, but in consequence of certain indications of weakness, it has been decided to discontinue the usual peal of bells, and on Sunday the welcome sound was hushed for a season. That the vicar and churchwardens had acted wisely was on inspection only too apparent, as a slight crack which was previously notice Ole on the south side of the tower appears to be gradually extending, and on the north side the masonry bulges out considerably. It is estimated that £2,000 will be required to provide a tower which would correspond with the substantial and ornate character of the restored fabric.
